en: The Mahāvaṃsa Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Official and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, there was a great assembly of Śākyas in the kingdom of Kapilavastu who reflected among themselves:
"In what place was our Buddha, the World-Honored One, born in past lives?
What was his surname?
What was his clan?"
"What are the causes and conditions for this?
Having reflected thus, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"In past lives, where was the World-Honored One Śākyamuni born?"
What is his clan?
What is his lineage?
By what causes and conditions [did he come to be]?
"We now wish to go to the Buddha’s presence to inquire about this matter, so that we may receive and uphold it according to the Buddha’s teaching.
Having spoken thus, they went with the great assembly of Śākyas to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down in their respective places.
At that time, the great assembly of Śākyas from the kingdom of Kapilavastu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While we, the great assembly of Śākyas, were dwelling within the vihāra in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, we suddenly reflected:
"In what place was our Buddha, the World-Honored One, born in past lives?
What was his surname?
What was his clan?"
"What are the causes and conditions for this?
We do not know; therefore, we have come with the assembly of Śākyas to the place where the Buddha dwells to inquire about this matter.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound it for us, so that we may hear it and receive and uphold it according to the teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to sever the doubts of the assembly, spoke this meaning to the Śākya multitude, saying:
"I did not wish to proclaim this meaning previously.
For what reason?"
Should any Māras or non-Buddhists hear this matter and further slander it, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama speaks of his own excellence; he says only what he likes and does not say what he dislikes—what benefit is there in this?"
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was present among the great assembly; he rose from his seat and gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance, not for a moment averting his eyes.
The World-Honored One said to him:
“Maudgalyāyana!”
Those Śākyas wish to hear about my past lives: where I was born,
what my family name was,
and what my clan was?
"By what causes and conditions [is this]?
Now, with a sincere mind, please explain it for us.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana among the assembly remained silent in contemplation; after a short while, he gathered his saṃghāṭī robe and placed it by his head, lay down on his right side with his head as a pillow and his feet stacked one upon the other without moving, and entered samādhi.

Furthermore, he observed the past lives of the World-Honored One—the place of birth, his clan, his lineage, and the causal circumstances—and understood them as they truly are without error; he then emerged from meditative absorption and sat once more upon his original seat before the great assembly.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the assembly of Śākyas, saying:
"Through meditative concentration, I have observed the past lives of that Gautama. When the world was being destroyed, after those beings passed away, they were reborn in the Subhakṛtsna Heaven.

Having been born in that heaven, their faculties were complete and their physical forms were majestic; no suffering arose, their bodies and minds were at ease and joyful, and their radiant forms moved freely through the air."
They took celestial sweet flavors as their food and drink, and their lifespan was long, with none meeting an untimely death.

At that time, the great earth produced a vast expanse of water that filled the void of space; it was like the waves of the great ocean stirred by the wind, or like boiled milk whose water has become clear and cool—this was the pure and supreme "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) consumed by all sentient beings in those later times.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana again addressed the assembly, saying:

"When that kalpa is destroyed, those beings who were born in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, having exhausted both their merit and lifespan in that celestial realm, will pass away from the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven and be reborn in the human world. The bodies they are born with will be like those in the celestial realms—dignified and majestic in appearance, with no deficiency in their sense faculties, and possessed of vast, exquisite beauty. They will naturally possess bodily radiance that constantly shines forth, and they will enjoy long life and bliss, moving freely through the air."
At that time, there were no sun, moon, or stars; there were no years, months, seasons, or such measures of time, nor were there any signs of male or female sentient beings;
the "taste of the earth" (pṛthivī-rasa) emerged as their food and drink.
Thus, the taste of this earth was sweet, exquisite, and subtle; after sentient beings had eaten it, they conceived an attachment to it.
Subsequently, their craving for its flavor increased, suddenly causing their bodies to become heavy and all their radiance to vanish, whereupon the world became entirely dark.

At that time, sentient beings saw this world as entirely shrouded in darkness; filled with various forms of alarm and distress, they gave rise to sorrow and affliction. Consequently, the sun, moon, and constellations appeared in the world, whereby day and night, as well as the seasons, were first distinguished.

In this way, sentient beings have long lifespans and are free from illness and affliction; however, those who are excessively attached to the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) suffer a decline in their physical appearance and become ugly, while those with little attachment maintain a naturally upright and majestic physical form.
Thus, according to the mental discriminations of their hearts, these two types of appearances—the black and the white—are the fruits of their retribution.

Those sentient beings, harboring mutual hatred and jealousy, committed unwholesome deeds; because of these unwholesome acts, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) immediately vanished. Due to its disappearance, the minds of all sentient beings were filled with burning distress, and they spoke thus:
"Now we have nothing to eat! This is profound suffering!"
"How profound is this suffering!
He further reflected:
"How has the supreme essence of the earth (rasa) vanished?"
"How shall future sentient beings obtain food?
This will cause them to suffer from affliction and exhaustion, being unknowable and inexpressible.
At that time, within the great earth, before long, earthen cakes (pṛthivī-piṇḍa) appeared; their flavor was exquisite, fragrant, sweet, and delicious, like the kārṣikāra flower.

When sentient beings eat this earth-cake, their bodies are nourished and strengthened, they enjoy long life and peace, and their physical forms become upright and dignified while their vigor increases.

However, if some sentient beings greedily consume it in excess, their physical appearance deteriorates; whereas those who consume it sparingly maintain their original appearance without such decline. Due to this distinction between the two types—black and white—they begin to criticize one another and engage in unwholesome deeds, causing that earth-cake to vanish and become invisible.
Because they do not see it, sentient beings again give rise to suffering and affliction, speaking these words:
"Deep suffering! Deep suffering!"
Again, he reflected:
"How has the earth-cake, from which beings were born, vanished?
I do not understand its meaning; yet all sentient beings have already come to suffer the afflictions of hunger, exhaustion, and fatigue. What shall future beings eat?"
Not long after this, for the sake of those sentient beings, forest creepers (*vanalatā*) arose again, their color exquisite and their fragrance and taste sweet and delicious.

Sentient beings such as these, consuming these forest creepers, saw their physical strength increase, their lifespan become long, and their forms become upright and majestic, endowed with the marks of a human being.

Furthermore, among those sentient beings, those who were greedy for food saw their physical appearance diminish, while those who were less greedy retained their original appearance. Thus, these sentient beings distinguished between two types of appearances—black and white—and, by engaging in mutual criticism and practicing unwholesome karma, the forest creepers vanished and were no longer seen.
Having failed to see him, they cause all sentient beings to give rise to mental distress and speak these words: "Alas!
Alas! How bitter!"
How has such exquisite flavor vanished?
We do not understand its meaning;
how shall we obtain food and drink?
Not long after this, within the great earth, there arose naturally a superior-flavored fragrant rice; that rice ripened naturally according to the seasons.
At that time, sentient beings took it and ate it; it was exceedingly fragrant and delicious, nourishing their limbs and extending their lifespans for a long duration.
Consequently, at that time, while eating fragrant rice, they gradually perceived an obstruction within their bellies and immediately reflected:
"How may this be removed?
Having formed this thought, two organs were produced, with the male and female forms appearing distinct from one another.

At that time, sentient beings became increasingly attached to forms, fragrances, and flavors. Toward those they held dear, they made various offerings of incense, flowers, and clothing, and further comforted and gladdened them with gentle words so that they might rejoice.

If there were sentient beings whom they did not love, they would immediately disparage and revile them in various ways, or even strike one another with tiles and stones, thus performing unwholesome deeds.

Furthermore, for those sentient beings, all that was the True Dharma (saddharma) in the past has now become non-Dharma; what was the Vinaya in the past has now become non-Vinaya; even the divisions of day and night are distinguished through inverted conceptualization.
It is just as if someone were to measure charcoal with a bushel-measure, yet acts with such uneven and improper conduct—it is exactly like this.
"Because of their perverted perceptions, the True Dharma was regarded as false; consequently, even the fragrant rice disappeared.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Śākya assembly, saying:
"Because the fragrant rice had disappeared, those sentient beings went about searching for rice seeds in various places every day, desiring to plant them."
At that time, there was a man who was by nature indolent and greedily attached to wealth and profit; although he possessed rice seeds, he could not bring himself to sow them.
Another man, having learned of this, said to him:
"You have rice seeds; give me a small portion, for I wish to sow them."
That person said:
"I have fragrant rice for my own use; if you now desire it, I shall give it to you.
However, return the rice to me after one day, two days, or even up to seven days."
The person said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
‘If it is not returned within one day, two days, or even seven days, it shall be returned within half a month or a full month.
Having spoken these words, he then reflected to himself:
‘Previously, this fragrant rice grew spontaneously without being sown; it required no labor and was enjoyed at will. Now, however, it must be cultivated with effort.’”
"Now that I have obtained this rice seed, it must dwell in the fields where I exert great effort continuously day and night before it can grow.
Having thought thus, his heart was filled with anguish, and he wept with tears of sorrow.
Furthermore, he reflected:

"In past ages, all sentient beings possessed upright and handsome physical forms, with their faculties complete and human characteristics fully endowed. Their bodies and minds were at ease and joyful, their bodies emitted radiance, they moved freely through the air, and their lifespans were long and far-reaching; the 'earth-flavor' they consumed was like celestial food.

However, at a later time, because they gave rise to craving and attachment for this delicious food, their bodies became heavy and their radiance was extinguished; consequently, the world became entirely dark."

Furthermore, among those sentient beings, those who consume little food do not suffer the deterioration of their physical forms, while those who consume much food suffer the deterioration of their physical forms. Based on this distinction between the two types—black and white—they disparage one another and engage in unwholesome conduct.

Consequently, at that time, the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) vanished, and the "earth-cake" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) arose; its appearance was exquisite, it was sweet and fragrant, it strengthened the sense faculties, brought joy to body and mind, and extended the lifespan.

Those who ate little did not suffer a decline in their physical form, while those who ate much suffered a deterioration of their physical form. Due to this distinction between the two types—the fair and the dark—they began to disparage one another and committed unwholesome deeds.

At that time, the earth-cakes also disappeared. Not long after this, forest creepers (*vanalatā*) arose; their appearance was exquisite and their taste sweet and excellent, like the food of the gods. They nourished the limbs and extended the lifespan.

Those who ate little did not suffer any decline in their physical form, while those who ate much saw their physical form diminish. Due to this distinction between the two types—black and white—they began to disparage one another and engaged in unwholesome conduct.

At that time, even the forest creepers vanished. Thereupon, a natural fragrant rice grew from the earth; its grains were fragrant and delicious, reaching four finger-widths in length. It ripened according to the seasons, its flavor was sweet and exquisite, nourishing the limbs and extending the lifespan.
Because the craving of sentient beings increased due to this, all the fragrant rice also disappeared and was no longer seen.
"Therefore, those who now seek this rice seed must dwell in the fields and exert great effort before it can ripen.

Although the rice was produced, the grains gradually became smaller; thereupon, sentient beings became greedily attached to the benefits of the land, extensively occupying the fields and competing to plant more. They committed unrighteous acts, harboring thoughts of theft, and even stole from the seeds planted in the fields of others.
At that time, there was a man who saw this theft of rice; after [the theft] had occurred once, twice, and even up to three times, he said to him:
"You have rice of your own—why do you not use it yourself? Why do you commit theft against another?"
"From this day forward, do not steal rice again.
Despite hearing these words, the thief did not reform his ways and continued to commit theft at a later time.
When the former man saw him again, he rebuked him, saying:
"I have already admonished you previously not to commit theft; why then do you act as a thief once again?
He then assembled many people to collectively reprimand and adjudicate him.

Furthermore, at that time, he selected one person of great merit from among the multitude and established him as the Lord of the Fields (Kṣetrapati), dividing the lands equally so that all were made equal, and ordering that anyone who did not follow the law be subdued.
When the crops in the fields have ripened, a small portion is yielded as a reward for the landowner.
In this same way, the landowner receives and practices the precepts, comforts the world by adjudicating according to the Dharma, and immediately subdues those who require subduing.
"From this, the Kṣatriya lineage was established in the world, and he was named King Samadatta. That king had a great minister named Sattva.
Later, that king fathered a crown prince named Priyaputra, and the king had a great minister named Ihaka.
At that time, King Priyaputra fathered a crown prince named Sumitra, who had a great minister named Tīraka."
At that time, King Kalyāṇamitra again fathered a son named Uttara; he had a minister named Aparājita.
King Uttara had a son named Śīlavant; he had a minister named Tāraka.
Upon the crown of that king’s head, a fleshy tumor grew; it was soft and supple, and he constantly brushed it with *tūla* cotton so that it caused him no pain.

Later, the tumor ripened and burst spontaneously, giving birth to a boy who was virtuous and handsome, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and beloved by all. Consequently, he was given the name King Mūrdhaja (Crown-Born).
As soon as he descended from the king’s head, he entered the inner palace.
At that time, within the inner palace of King Śīlavant, there were sixty thousand palace women, each with milk in her breasts, who all said to the king:
"I have milk in my breasts; I wish to nurse the prince."
For these reasons, he was also named King Manu.

At that time, all sentient beings in the world gradually increased in wisdom; they were able to engage in subtle reflection and to weigh and discern minute matters, whether they were right or wrong, as well as various arts and crafts. Therefore, he was given the name *manuṣya*.
"At that time, the six great devaputras possessed immeasurable lifespans, and they had six great ministers:
the first was named Sattva;
the second was named Ihara;"
Third is Tilaka;
fourth is Aparājita; fifth is Taraṅga.
The sixth was named Manuja.
These six great ministers were wise and possessed great intelligence; they were capable of governing the world and possessed great majesty and power.
At that time, a fleshy tumor grew on King Mūrdhaja’s right thigh. This tumor was soft and supple, and it was constantly brushed with *tūla* cotton so that the tumor remained free from all pain.

Later, when the pustule had ripened, it spontaneously burst open, and a boy was born with a dignified and handsome form endowed with the thirty-two marks. He was named Nīru; possessing great wisdom and immeasurable merit, he became a Golden Wheel-turning King who ruled over the four continents.
"Subsequently, on his left thigh, King Nīla also developed a tumor. This tumor was soft, and he constantly brushed it with *tūla* cotton; though it was a fleshy growth, it caused him no pain.

Later, it ripened and spontaneously split open, giving birth to a boy who was handsome and exquisite, endowed with the thirty-two marks. He was named Upanīla; possessing profound wisdom and immeasurable merit, he became a silver-wheel-turning monarch (*rājā cakravartin*) ruling over the three worlds."
“Later, on the upper part of King Upāriṇa’s right foot, a fleshy tumor arose. This tumor was soft and supple; even when brushed with *tūla* cotton, it caused no pain whatsoever.

Subsequently, as the tumor ripened, it burst open of its own accord, giving birth to a boy whose physical form was majestic and endowed with the thirty-two marks. He was named Śinirū, possessed profound merit and wisdom, and became a copper-wheel-turning monarch (*tāmra-cakravartin*) who ruled over two worlds.”
"King Śinilu had a fleshy tumor upon his left foot; this tumor was soft and supple, such that when brushed with *tūla* cotton, it caused no pain whatsoever.

Later, the tumor ripened and burst open of its own accord, giving birth to a boy of upright and handsome appearance, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man. Named Maṇilu, he possessed profound merit and wisdom, and became an Iron-Wheel-Turning King who unified the entire world."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Śākya assembly, saying:
"In this manner, the succession of royal thrones has continued until now, numbering in great abundance.
Thus, King Saṃmata had a son named Rājaka; Rājaka had a son named Sumitra."
King Kalyāṇamitra had a son named King Uttara;
King Uttara had a son named King Śīlacārī;
King Śīlacārī had a son named King Mūrdhaja.
King Mūrdhaja had a son named King Nīla;
King Nīla had a son named King Upnīla;
King Upnīla had a son named King Śinīla.
King Śrīṇika had a son named King Maṇicita;
King Maṇicita had a son named King Rucira;
King Rucira had a son named King Surucira.
King Suruci had a son named King Mucinda;
King Mucinda had a son named King Mucilinda;
King Mucilinda had a son named King Agra.
King Agra had a son named King Agnīdhra;
King Agnīdhra had a son named King Vagnīdhra;
King Vagnīdhra had a son named King Sagara.
King Sagara had a son named King Mahāsagara;
King Mahāsagara had a son named King Śakuni;
King Śakuni had a son named King Mahāśakuni.
King Mahāśaṅku had a son named King Śaṅku;
King Śaṅku had a son named King Upaśaṅku;
King Upaśaṅku had a son named King Mahāśaṅku.
King Mahākuśa had a son named King Sūnṛśaṇa;
King Sūnṛśaṇa had a son named King Mahāsūnṛśaṇa;
King Mahāsūnṛśaṇa had a son named King Praṇaya.
King Praṇaya had a son named King Mahāpraṇaya;
King Mahāpraṇaya had a son named King Praṇana;
King Praṇana had a son named King Mahāpraṇana.
King Mahāpraṇada had a son named King Prahaṅkara;
King Prahaṅkara had a son named King Pratāpa;
King Pratāpa had a son named King Vāmiru.
King Vāmiru had a son named King Mīrumata;
King Mīrumata had a son named King Ariñjaya;
King Ariñjaya had a son named King Rariñjeśma.
King Rājeśvara had a son named Nārjeśvaradatta;
King Nārjeśvaradatta had a son named Ariṣṭasamanta.
In this manner, the princes and their descendants succeeded one another, totaling one hundred great kings, all of whom resided in the city of Potalaka.
From the last of these kings was born a son named King Arindama; because that king possessed great majesty and power capable of subduing all enemies, he was called King Arindama.
In this manner, the succession of this prince’s descendants upon the imperial throne continued without interruption; there were fifty-four thousand kings who resided in the city of Ayodhyā.

Furthermore, the last of these kings fathered a son named King Aparājita. The descendants of that prince succeeded one another, inheriting the imperial throne, and there were sixty thousand such sovereigns who resided in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
To that last king was born another son named King Nuprasaha; his descendants succeeded one another as eighty-four thousand kings, all of whom resided in the city of Kṣemavatī.
From that last king, another son was born named King Brahmadatta; his descendants succeeded one another as thirty-two thousand kings, with their capital at the city of Hastināpura.
The last of these kings fathered another son named King Haṣtitīrtha; his descendants succeeded one another until there were five thousand kings, all of whom resided in the city of Takṣaśilā.
The last of these kings fathered another son named King Śatarīsa; his descendants succeeded one another as thirty-two thousand kings, all of whom resided in the great city of Uruśā.
From that last king, another king was born named King Nāganandi; his descendants succeeded one another for thirty-two thousand generations of kings, all of whom resided in the great city of Duduna.
After that last king, another king was born named King Jayasena; his descendants succeeded one another as eighteen thousand kings, with their capital in the great city of Campā.
To that last king was born another son named Nāgadeva; his descendants succeeded one another as twenty-five thousand kings, with their capital at the city of Tāmraliptī.

The last of these kings fathered a son named King Benevolent (Renwang); his descendants succeeded one another for twelve thousand generations of kings, all of whom likewise resided in the city of Tāmraliptī.
The last of these kings fathered a son named Sāgararāja; his descendants succeeded one another as eighteen thousand kings, with their capital at the city of Dantapura.
The last of these kings fathered a son named King Subuddhi; his descendants succeeded one another as twenty-five thousand kings, all of whom resided in the city of Rājagṛha.
The last of these kings fathered another son named King Śatānīka; his descendants succeeded one another as one hundred kings, all of whom likewise resided in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Upon that last king, another son was born, named King Mahāsena; his descendants succeeded one another as a lineage of one thousand kings, who resided in the great city of Kuśāvatī.
To that last king was born another son named King Sāgarasena; his descendants succeeded one another as one thousand kings, with their capital at the city of Potalaka.
From that last king, another son was born named King Śatānīka; his descendants succeeded one another as eighty-four thousand kings, all of whom resided in the city of Kuśāvati.

After that last king, another king was born named King Mahimukha; his descendants succeeded one another until there were one hundred thousand kings, all of whom also resided in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

From the last king, another king was born, named King Mahīpāla, also known as King Bhūmipati; his descendants succeeded one another for one hundred reigns, with their capital in the great city of Ayodhyā.
From that last king, another king was born named King Lokadhara; his descendants succeeded one another for eighty-four thousand generations of kings, all of whom resided in the city of Mithilā.

After that last king, another king was born, named Mahādeva; his pure conduct was stainless, and his descendants succeeded one another as eighty-four thousand kings, all of whom likewise resided in the city of Mithilā.
"In the lineage of that last king, another king was born named King Nimi;
that king in turn begot King Māndhātṛ; King Māndhātṛ begot King Nalika-nimi-khaṇḍu;
and King Nalika-nimi-khaṇḍu begot King Rūpa-khaṇḍu."
King Rūpakarṇa fathered King Karṇamañca;
King Karṇamañca fathered King Karṇapūrṇa;
King Karṇapūrṇa fathered King Sūnṛśas.
King Sūnṛśa begot King Sunṛśa; King Sunṛśa begot King Surudhasena;
King Surudhasena begot King Dāmasena.
King Dharmaśena was reborn as King Vinīta;
King Vinīta was reborn as King Mahāvinīta;
King Mahāvinīta was reborn as King Vinītasiṃha.
From King Vainateya was born King Aśoka;
from King Aśoka was born King Vigataśoka;
and from King Vigataśoka was born King Prabhāsavat.
King Bharasvata begot King Jarasvata;
King Jarasvata begot King Mṛdumāra; King Mṛdumāra begot King Aruṇa.
King Aruṇa fathered King Niṣadha; King Niṣadha fathered King Renu;
and King Renu fathered King Śaṅkaraka.
King Śaṅkaraka begot King Ānanda; King Ānanda begot King Ānandīśamukha;
King Ānandīśamukha begot King Jñānaka.
King Jñānaka gave birth to King Sañjñānaka;
King Sañjñānaka gave birth to King Jñānaśrava;
King Jñānaśrava gave birth to King Anupama.
According to the records, King Nāpana was succeeded by King Prajñāpana;
King Prajñāpana was succeeded by King Ajita;
and King Ajita was succeeded by King Parājita.
King Parākṣita begot King Pratīkṣita; King Pratīkṣita begot King Supratīkṣita;
King Supratīkṣita begot King Mahāmalla.
King Mahāmāra gave birth to King Vahana;
King Vahana gave birth to King Somadeva;
King Somadeva gave birth to King Nṛtavāhana.
King Nṛcatvaha begot King Naśadānu; King Naśadānu begot King Śatadānu;
King Śatadānu begot King Navadīdānu.
From King Nābhaediṇṇa was born King Sīyakaḍḍhanna;
from King Sīyakaḍḍhanna was born King Vijayaḍḍhanna;
and from King Vijayaḍḍhanna was born King Nemiyaḍḍhanna.
From King Nṛpatuṇḍa was born King Naśaratha;
from King Naśaratha was born King Śataratha;
and from King Śataratha was born King Navatiratha.
Nāvadīratha King further gave birth to Citraratha King;
Citraratha King further gave birth to Nṛcitraratha King.
In this manner, seventy-seven thousand kings, father and son in succession, resided in the capital city of Saṃkāśya.
Furthermore, the last of these kings begot another king named King Amarasena;
that king had a son named King Nāgapāla, and one hundred kings in his lineage, father and son in succession, resided in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Furthermore, the last of these kings begot a son named King Kṛkin.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān Kāśyapa appeared in the world. When that Blessed One was a bodhisattva, he maintained the precepts and pure conduct, and having made great vows to seek unsurpassed awakening, he became the Regent in Tuṣita Heaven. When the conditions were ripe, he descended to be born in the palace of King Kṛkin; he renounced his throne, practiced the path, and attained Buddhahood.
"At that time, King Kṛkin had a crown prince named Sujāta.
This King Sujāta, in turn, fathered a prince; in this manner, descendants succeeded one another until there were one hundred kings."
That last king again fathered a son named King Karṇa; in his later years, two princes were born:
the first was named Gautama, and the second was named Bharadvāja.
This prince, though fond of the royal palace and craving the position of sovereignty, constantly reflected upon how to bring comfort to the world while attending to his kingly duties.
At that time, Prince Gautama further reflected:
"Sentient beings are submerged in the cycle of birth and death within the three miserable realms; they revolve through suffering and find it difficult to escape."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to his father the king, prostrated himself with his head at the king's feet, and said to him:
"I no longer take pleasure in the royal palace; I wish to practice the holy life in the mountains and wilds and seek to go forth into homelessness."
The king then said to him:

"You are my son; all the lands and the royal throne, as well as the ministers and high officials, are as if held between my fingers and palms. For what reason do you so lightly abandon them to seek to leave the household life?"
Gautama replied: "Great King!

I contemplate the three realms as being like an illusion or a magical transformation; they possess no solidity or substance, and are impermanent from moment to moment—how could they be fit for attachment or delight?"
"Today I take my leave of the King to go forth into homelessness.
Having heard this, the King, knowing his son's resolve, immediately granted him permission.
At that time, there was a rishi on the mountain named Kṛśānuvepavyanu, who dwelt and practiced his austerities in a hut made of grass within those mountains.
Then the youth Gautama went to that place, leaping for joy and prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground to pay homage at the feet of the seer. He addressed the seer, saying:
"I have come here from the royal palace to serve you, O Seer; I pray that you will accept me."
Thus, when the seer observed that the prince’s resolve was firm and steadfast, he accepted him as a disciple.

Thereupon, the youth gathered fruits and provided water in the mountains to serve the seer; through such diligent toil over many months and years, the master, seeing that the youth was persevering without retreat, bestowed upon him a name and called him "The Seer" as well.
Later, when his father, King Karṇa, passed away, the younger brother, Brahmanarāja, succeeded to the throne and administered the affairs of state.
At that time, the seer Gautama, knowing the king had died, said to his former teacher:
"I can no longer gather fruit and provide water in these mountains; I wish to go to the city and dwell there."
The teacher then said to him: "Gautama!
Previously you came here and dwelt well in the mountains and wilds; for what reason do you now go instead toward the cities and towns?"
As you depart now, do not enter the city; instead, pitch a hut and dwell in a secluded place near the city of Potalaka, guarding your sense faculties and practicing the holy life with diligence.
Having heard these words, the youth Gautama immediately went to a secluded place outside the great city of Potalaka, where he erected a hut, fixed his resolve, and devotedly cultivated the holy life.
The Sūtra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Sūtra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Subject Dharma-bhadra, the Great Master Mingjiao, by imperial decree:
"At that time, in the great city of Potalaka, there was a courtesan whose physical appearance was upright and dignified, and whose form was exceptionally exquisite."
At that time, there was a man named Mṛṇāla who became deeply infatuated with this woman; he then bestowed upon her gold, silver, precious jewels, and exquisite garments.
Later, at another time, there was yet another man who also conceived a passionate attachment for this courtesan and said to her:
"I shall give you five hundred gold coins for your use; you may follow me and enjoy our pleasures together."
Upon hearing this, the courtesan immediately set out with him and ordered her maidservant to go and inform Mṛṇāla:
"I am currently occupied elsewhere and have not yet had the leisure to visit you."
Upon hearing these words, Nalā immediately told her maidservant:
"If she returns home, have her come quickly to the garden where I dwell.
The maidservant returned to her own quarters and reported the matter in full to the courtesan.
Upon hearing this, the courtesan had little inclination to go; the maidservant, knowing her refusal, went again to Mṛṇāla and related in detail the courtesan’s breach of agreement.
Having heard this, the man became enraged and sent a maidservant to persuade her,
saying, "Bring her quickly to my garden.
Having received these instructions, the maidservant used various means to entice the courtesan, who then set out.
Having seen this, the man rebuked him, saying:
"From the past until now, I have constantly provided for you with clothing, precious goods, and wealth; why do you now turn your back on me?"
He then took up a sharp sword and killed that courtesan.
At that time, Gautama’s hut was near that grove; Mṛṇāla secretly took the sharp sword he had been carrying, placed it inside the hut, and then fled.
At that time, the courtesan’s maidservant cried out in a loud voice,
"A man has been killed here!
Having heard this, a great multitude went together to the hermitage where the seer resided, and there they found his sharp blade with fresh blood still upon it.
The crowd rebuked him, saying, "You are a seer; why have you committed such a killing now?
Having spoken these words, they immediately bound the seer's hands with ropes and led him into the city to the presence of the king’s palace.
The crowd said:
"This is a renunciant seer who has abandoned the holy life (brahmacarya) to practice impure conduct;
furthermore, he has taken the life of a courtesan with a sharp sword."
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with rage; he immediately ordered him out of the city and commanded that his limbs be pierced with wooden stakes.

Once the royal decree had been proclaimed, the rishi appeared wearing a garland of flowers upon his head and clad in green robes, surrounded by attendants who held weapons in their hands and shouted aloud:
"This is a bandit who violates the precepts and takes human life!"
At that time, the rishi was entirely without fear or dread; upon reaching the city gate, he submitted to the royal law.
Then his former teacher, the rishi Kṛśāśvavaiśya, came to the hermitage and, not seeing his disciple, went forth to search for him gradually through the surrounding areas.
Suddenly, he saw his disciple with his hands and feet bound, upon a wooden stake, undergoing such suffering.
When the Master saw this, his hair stood on end with shock; weeping with tears of sorrow, he asked his disciple:
"How can you have such a transgression?
Furthermore, how will you endure these various sufferings and afflictions in your body, with such pain day and night?"
The disciple replied,
"Great Seer!
When I search for any pains within this body, they are entirely unfindable."
The teacher asked,
"Why do you abandon such suffering and distress?
The disciple replied:
"I make this sincere vow before my teacher: if there is truly no pain in this body of mine, may my teacher’s body immediately become the color of gold.

Having made this vow, in the space of a single kṣaṇa, the teacher transformed his own body into the color of pure gold, which all the people witnessed. For this reason, he was given the name the Golden Sage (Suvarṇarṣi).
At that time, the disciple again asked the teacher, saying:
"Where shall I be reborn when this life of mine comes to an end?
The teacher replied:
"According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, if one has no heir, there is no place for rebirth.
The disciple replied, "When I was a youth, I took no pleasure in the royal palace; I renounced my position and left the household life—how could I have a son?"
The teacher then said to him:
"Why do you not now reflect upon the pleasures you enjoyed while in the royal palace?
The disciple replied:
"This body of mine now undergoes such suffering under the king's law; how could I possibly think of my former pleasures?

At that time, the golden-hued seer, possessing great supernormal powers, caused a great wind and rain to descend from the midst of space within a mere kṣaṇa, drenching the disciple’s body so that he attained coolness, was freed from all suffering and distress, and was restored as before.
Consequently, the disciple thought of his former joys and gave rise to a lustful mind, whereby two drops of semen fell upon the ground.
At that time, the seer Gautama had four reflections:
first, reflection upon himself;
second, reflection upon sentient beings.
Third, he contemplated the attainment of Buddhahood by all sentient beings;
fourth, he contemplated all Buddha-fields.

Having thus reflected, his two drops of semen coalesced into two eggs. Every day at sunrise, they were illuminated by the sun, and before long, the eggs spontaneously broke open, giving birth to two boys of exquisite and upright countenance.
The seer Gautama took these two boys and entered a sugarcane grove to settle there;
however, Gautama soon passed away, succumbing to the heat of the sun.
At that time, the Golden-Colored Rishi entered the garden and asked,
"Young man! Who are you?"
The youth replied,
"I am the son born of Gautama. Upon hearing this,
the Golden Sage felt great joy in his heart and took the two boys back to his hermitage to raise them.
Because at the time of his birth the egg was caused by the sun's rays, he was given a name and established the Solar Clan as his first lineage;
furthermore, as he was the son born of Gautama, Gautama was established as his second lineage;
and as he was born from his own body, Āṅgirasa was established as his third lineage.
Because they were raised by being nurtured within a sugarcane grove, the Sugata caste was established as the fourth varṇa.

At that time, there was a great king named Brahmadatta; when that king passed away, no son succeeded him to the throne. The ministers and high officials deliberated upon this matter, not knowing who should be consecrated to the royal position.
A certain great minister addressed the assembly of ministers, saying:

"King Kārūṣa has an eldest son named Gautama, who has renounced his father’s royal throne to dwell among the mountain forests and serve the ṛṣi Gārgya Vaiyāsana. He is of the Śākya lineage and is fit to succeed to the consecrated royal throne."
Having heard this, the ministers immediately went into the mountains to the place where the seer was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and said:
"Great Seer!
In the past, King Karṇa had a crown prince named Gautama; where is he now?"
The Great Seer replied,
"He passed away long ago," and then related the preceding events in detail to the ministers.
Having heard this, the great minister felt deep distress in his heart and thought,
"We have now committed a most grievous offense.
Having spoken these words, he saw that the two youths possessed dignified and handsome physical features, and he asked:
"Who is this? The Golden Immortal replied,
"This is the son born of Gautama."
Upon hearing this, the ministers were all filled with joy and exclaimed, "This youth is of royal lineage.
They immediately appointed him to succeed to the consecrated throne of kingship; therefore, he was given the name King Ikṣvāku.
"After this king, his descendants succeeded one another, and there were one hundred Ikṣvāku kings who resided in the city of Puṇḍravardhana.
That last Ikṣvāku king fathered four sons:
the first was named Ulūka-mukha;"
The second is named Kāraṇī;
the third is named Haṣṭināga;
the fourth is named Sunābhaka.
After the four princes had been born, at a later time, the queen passed away; the king was immediately overcome with grief and distress, resting his chin upon his hand in deep sorrow.
At that time, there were great ministers who, seeing that the king was unhappy, addressed him together, saying: "Great King!
Why do you harbor such sorrow and distress, with such a displeased countenance?"
The king replied:
"Because of my queen, I have now suddenly encountered impermanence and this suffering.
Having heard this, the minister addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard that the neighboring small kingdom has a king who has a daughter endowed with great merit and virtue, of exquisite and peerless beauty, fit to be a queen for our country.
The king said to his ministers, "That small kingdom's king wishes to invade our territory; how can we form a marriage alliance?"

The minister replied, "There is another small kingdom that has also given birth to a girl of exquisite beauty and superior excellence; if she were taken as a consort, she would be perfectly suited to Your Majesty’s heart.
Having heard this, the king immediately dispatched an envoy to that small kingdom to convey the king's intent, desiring to betroth her daughter and establish her as queen.
Having heard this, the minor king was filled with joy and consolation, and he addressed the envoy:
"If the Great King wishes to marry my daughter to serve as his queen, and if she should bear a son who shall succeed him to the position of consecrated king, I shall grant my consent."
The envoy returned to his country and reported the matter in full to the King.
Upon hearing the report, the King was deeply displeased and said:
"I have an eldest son who is rightfully entitled to succeed to the throne; how can a mere child be established as king?"
The minister replied, "For now, simply marry her; whether the child born later will be a son or a daughter remains uncertain.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately sent gold, silver, precious jewels, fine silks, bolts of cloth, and ornaments for the body to welcome her home to his kingdom.

Afterward, she carried the child for a full nine months and gave birth to a son whose physical features were dignified and handsome; on the day of his birth, the ministers offered their congratulations.
The King asked, "Now, what name should I give to this son of mine?"
The great minister reported, saying:

"That minor king has accepted his daughter as a consort so that a noble prince may be born to succeed to the precious throne. We now request a name for him; let it be named King Nanda. Let eight ladies be appointed as wet nurses to raise and nourish the prince."

"At that time, the Great King wished for his eldest son to succeed him to the throne. When the minor king learned of this matter, he was filled with indignation and immediately dispatched an envoy to detail the previous events:
'Previously, you promised that the son born of my daughter would be the king; why have you now yourself violated your word and agreement?'"
"If Deva acts in this manner, I shall immediately lead a vast army to suppress and destroy your kingdom.
Upon hearing these words, the great king was overcome with grief and distress, and he said to his ministers:
"To set aside the elder and establish the younger is contrary to principle."
The ministers submitted this report:
"That minor king possesses a powerful mind and is skilled in military combat; if he raises his weapons to invade our borders, we shall surely suffer defeat and loss.
If you dispatch your eldest son to go abroad quickly, then our kingdom shall be spared from the calamity of war."
Upon hearing these words, the king remained silent and did not grant his consent.

At that time, the ministers devised a stratagem and immediately constructed a royal park on the outskirts of the city, filled everywhere with pavilions, ponds, flowers, and fruits, as well as groves, hills, lakes, flowing springs, and soaring galleries.
Furthermore, with agalloch, sandalwood, and various precious necklaces, they adorned the palaces and pavilions in every way.
At that time, the eldest son of the great king went out of the city with his ministers and officials for recreation; seeing this grove, he inquired of those around him:
"To whom does this belong?"
The attendant replied, "This is the royal garden.
Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately turned his horse back; his attendants then entreated him, requesting that he enter briefly to view it.
The Crown Prince replied,
"How would I dare go to the royal garden of the Emperor?
The attendant spoke again:
"If it be ministers or commoners, they shall not enter; however, there is no hindrance to the king’s eldest son enjoying himself here.
At that time, the prince immediately entered the garden to play music and sport.
A high minister petitioned the king, saying:
"The imperial garden previously commissioned has now been completed; we pray Your Majesty will come to view it.
Upon hearing this report, the king immediately visited the site and approached the park; suddenly, he heard the sound of music, and his heart was filled with suspicion.
The minister replied,
"The crown prince was previously making music here. Thereupon,
the king became violently incensed:
"I have created this garden and never yet visited it for recreation; how is it that the Prince has entered first to make merry?
His offense is grave and cannot be pardoned—he must be banished from the kingdom.
Though the ministers remonstrated and pleaded, the King’s anger did not cease, and he immediately issued a decree:
"I grant you permission to depart from the city with your servants and kinsmen, provided you leave within seven days.

Having received his father the King’s command, the Prince immediately departed from the great city of Puṇḍravardhana with his ministers and beloved relatives, settling himself at a place not far from the city;
the King then sent word for him to reside in a more distant location.

"At that time, on the banks of the river Bāhulī by the side of the Snowy Mountains, there was a rishi named Kapila, who maintained pure brahmacarya and practiced the Way while dwelling in a hermitage."
The Prince again took his attendants and lived with the rishis, sustaining his life by hunting birds and beasts.
Later, the Prince recalled sensual desires, and his countenance became emaciated and haggard.
The rishi questioned him, and the prince spoke in detail:
"I thought of sensual pleasure and thereby brought about this suffering.
The rishi replied:
"Do not engage in sexual acts with your own elder sister; otherwise, you may do as you please.
The Prince became deeply attached to the many men and women, and his youthful frolics and clamor increased day by day.
The seer’s mind was not tranquil and his faculties were distracted;
he then said to the prince, "I now wish to go elsewhere to establish a dwelling.
Upon hearing this, the prince felt deep shame and remorse.

"The Great Sage has practiced here for many years; his realization of the fruits of the Way is already complete and cannot be moved. This day, I shall lead my retinue elsewhere to seek a place to dwell."

Upon hearing this, the rishi was deeply gratified in his heart; he immediately selected an exceptionally auspicious site near his hermitage, sprinkled water from a golden pitcher upon the ground to mark the boundary, and had the prince reside there.
Thereafter, as the population flourished and the retinue multiplied, they built a city according to the boundaries and established a kingdom named Kapilavastu.
Later, guided by a wise man, another city was constructed called Aṅgāpuri; the king also designated this city as his capital.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka asked his minister,
"Where is my crown prince now?
The minister replied:

"Currently, he resides in the city of Kapilavastu on the banks of the Bhagirathi River to the south of the Snowy Mountains. He has established two great cities as his capital, where ministers, officials, commoners, and kinsmen are numerous and prosperous, like those of a great kingdom."
Then King Vīrucaka, the Ikṣvāku, bowed his body and lowered his head, asking the great minister:
"My child is indeed capable of such a feat.
The minister replied:
"Because the Prince’s benevolent virtue has brought about such magnificent prosperity," they established his clan name.
After King Ikṣvāku Vṛṣadhvaja passed away, Śākya succeeded to the throne.
The Muni had a son named King Uruvilvākāśyapa;
King Uruvilvākāśyapa had a son named King Jyotiṣka;
King Jyotiṣka had a son named King Kṣemadatta.
King Haṃsa had a son named King Nubhruka; King Nubhruka had a son named King Ubhruka.
In this manner, fifty-five thousand kings succeeded one another in their lineage, all residing in the great city of Kapilavastu.
"After him, there was another king named Daśaratha; after King Daśaratha, there was King Navatiratha;
after King Navatiratha, there was King Śataratha;
and after King Śataratha, there was King Citraratha."
After King Citraratha was King Vararatha;
after King Vararatha was King Dṛḍharatha;
after King Dṛḍharatha was King Daśadhanu.
After King Daśadhanus came King Navatidhanus;
after King Navatidhanus came King Śatadhanus;
after King Śatadhanus came King Varadhanus.
After King Varāhadhanu came King Citradhanu;
after King Citradhanu came King Dṛḍhadhanu, who was the foremost in archery in Jambudvīpa in the south.
At that time, King Dṛḍhadhanu had two sons:
the first was named King Khaṅkhānu,
and the second was named King Siṃhanāda.
At that time, King Śuddhodana begot four sons:
the first was named King Śuddhodana;
the second was named King Śuklodana.
The third was named King Droṇodana;
the fourth was named King Amṛtodana.
King Śuddhodana had two sons:
The first was named Siddhārtha;
the second was named Nanda.
King Śuklodana had two sons:
The first was named Śatānīka;
the second was named Vairāṭa.
King Droṇodana had two sons:
The first was named Mahānāman;
the second was named Aniruddha.
King Amṛtodana had two sons:
The first was named Ānanda;
the second was named Devadatta.
King Śuddhodana had a daughter named Subhadrā.
King Śuklodana had a daughter named Prajāpatī;
King Droṇodana had a daughter named Gopā;
and King Amṛtodana had a daughter named Mṛgajā.

Siddhārtha had a son named Rāhula; this son of the Buddha was of the lineage of King Viśvāmitra of the past. Having now encountered the age of a Buddha, he followed the Buddha into the homeless life, fully realized the nature of birth and death, skillfully severed the cycle of saṃsāra, and attained the rank of sainthood by realizing the true emptiness.
When Mahāmaudgalyāyana had spoken these words, he rose from his seat and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Return to your original seat."
Excellent, excellent!

That you are able to explain to the bhikṣus the matters concerning the lineage from which the Śākyas were born in the past brings the bhikṣus great benefit and ensures their peace and security for a long night.
At that time, the assembly of Śākyas were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced accordingly.
Then, King Śuddhodana, the ruler of the kingdom of Kapilavastu, possessed great merit and immeasurable wealth; his people flourished and his land was prosperous and abundant.
Not far from here there is a kingdom named Devāṅgulīpura, where there is a king named Supratiṣṭhita. That country is immensely wealthy, with gold, silver, and precious jewels filling every place.
That king has a queen named Narmadā, whose physical form is upright and majestic, and who is endowed with all the auspicious marks.

Within that kingdom there was an elder who, having planted roots of goodness in past lives, possessed profound merit and virtue; his retinue was flourishing and his treasuries were numerous, like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.

At that time, the elder possessed a garden park, complete with various plants and famous flowers, flowing springs and bathing pools, pavilions, terraces, and towers, and nothing lacking in its array of exotic beasts and auspicious birds.
At that time, King Sūprabuddha, together with his queen, consorts, and retinue, came to this garden to enjoy music and play.
Then, the queen, seeing the various flowers blooming brilliantly in this grove, felt a sense of love and delight and said to the king:
"I desire this garden for my constant enjoyment."
The king said to his consort:
"This grove belongs to a householder; how could we obtain it?
As the king, I shall have one constructed myself."

He immediately commanded the people of the realm to extensively develop a park and garden, featuring springs, ponds, terraces, and pavilions of such peerless excellence that it was named the Lumbinī Garden.
At that time, King Sūprabuddha pondered for a long night:
"How may I now give birth to a son who shall become a Golden-Wheel Turning King?"

While he was reflecting thus, his queen suddenly became pregnant; after carrying the child for nine months, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was upright and beautiful, endowed with all auspicious marks, and preeminent in the world for her merit, wisdom, and excellence.
When the multitude beheld these marks of merit, they all said:
"How extraordinary!
This must have been created by the gods of the Vaiśravaṇa heaven, or perhaps it has been produced through magical illusion."

After the girl was born, on the first day, the second day, and up to the twenty-first day, the king gathered his kinsmen and ministers to celebrate with music for the girl; he then bestowed upon her a name, naming her Māyā.
The girl’s physical form possessed eight breasts, and the physiognomist prophesied:
"In the future, this girl shall give birth to a noble son who will succeed to the position of an anointed king."

Furthermore, at a later time, another daughter was born, whose exquisite and auspicious features were preeminent; at the moment of her birth, a great radiance appeared, illuminating the city and its surroundings with extraordinary portents. On the day of her celebration, she was given the name Mahāmāyā.
The physiognomist divined:
"This girl shall give birth to a son endowed with the thirty-two marks, who will become a Golden Wheel-turning King.
At that time, King Subhūmat heard that the crown prince of King Śaṅkhaṇa possessed such noble virtues, and immediately dispatched an envoy to inform the king of that country:
"I have two daughters:
the first is named Māyā;
the second is named Mahāmāyā."
"When they were first born, physiognomists prophesied:
'If these two daughters later bear sons, those sons will possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and become Golden Wheel-turning Kings.
Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana said to Prince Śuddhodana:"
"King Śūrpāraka wishes to give his two daughters to you as wives; should you later father sons by them, they will surely become Universal Monarchs (cakravartin).
He then dispatched five hundred members of the Śākya clan to go there and welcome the maidens.
At that time, there was a certain clan in a frontier kingdom named Pañcāla, who led a host of soldiers to a strategic pass intending to commit robbery.
When the Śākya community learned of this, they feared they would suffer harm and disaster; they recounted the aforementioned matter and requested that the King accompany them.
The king then said:
"I am now old and weary of military affairs; I shall command my son Śuddhodana to lead the expedition himself. If he achieves a victorious triumph, he may then establish his own vows."

At that time, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra selected and trained his fourfold army, entrusted it to the Śākya clan and others, and sent them with Prince Śuddhodana to slay the evil kinsmen and escort the princess back.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"Regarding the separate vow that Your Majesty previously proclaimed, what is its meaning?
The king then replied:
"You must now take a daughter as your wife; should a son be born to you later, protect him well so that he may succeed to the throne.
After the king passed away, the ministers together installed Prince Śuddhodana to succeed to the royal throne.
At that time, the kingdom was prosperous and its people abundant; the king, together with his queen and the palace ladies, constantly enjoyed happiness.
Then, Śākyamuni Bodhisattva, residing in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, desiring to be born among humans, performed five kinds of observations:
first, he observed the lineage.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"If I were born among the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, my lineage would not be superior; it would not be one from which I am born.
Since the people of that time value wealth and nobility, I shall be born into the Kṣatriya caste."

"If I were born into a low caste, I would not be respected by others; now, in order to gather and transform sentient beings and cause them to take refuge, I must therefore be born into a Kṣatriya family.
Second, the observation of the country.

If that land is most supreme and excellent, possessing superior-flavored sugarcane, fragrant and delicious rice, and robust, powerful oxen; if it is free from poverty, begging, and strife—such a land is called a "central land," and I shall be reborn there.
Yet, fearing that sentient beings might raise disparaging words, saying: "The Bodhisattva cultivated great and victorious causes in the past; why has he now instead been born in a borderland?"
Third, the observation of the timing.

If it is during an eon of increase when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, sentient beings have dull faculties and inferior wisdom; they are not vessels for the Dharma, and therefore [the Bodhisattva] does not take birth.

If it is during an eon of decrease at the time of a hundred-year lifespan, although one is close to the five turbidities, the sentient beings of that time possess sharp and keen faculties and their capacities are matured; therefore, the Bodhisattva descends to be born.
Fourth, he contemplates his superior lineage.

Since the beginning of the eon of formation in the past, the descendants of King Viśvāmitra have succeeded one another down to King Śuddhodana, all belonging to the lineage of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); therefore, the Bodhisattva went there to take birth.
5. Contemplating the Mother’s Body:

"If she is a woman of profound wisdom, immeasurable merit, and dignified features; one who maintains pure precepts and has been granted a prediction of enlightenment by all past Buddhas—then I shall take birth there.
Now, seeing that Māyā possesses these aforementioned virtues and is also of royal lineage, I shall indeed be born there."
At that time, having made this observation, the Bodhisattva again addressed the devaputras of the six heavens of the desire realm:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now descend to be born in Jambudvīpa, taking form within Māyā; you should bring down for me a rain of nectar so that I may experience bliss."
The devaputra replied:
"In Jambudvīpa there are six great evil men:
first, the Elder Kāśyapa;..."
2. Māṣakāriyūpa; 3. Sāryavīracitiputra;
4. Ajita-keśakambala; [5. Kakuda-kātyāyana].
5. Kāṣāya; 6. Nigrahaṇṭi-putra.
Furthermore, there are six other naked ascetics (nirgrantha) in Jambudvīpa:
1. The brāhmaṇa Kūṭadanta; 2. The brāhmaṇa Sūrata; 3. The brāhmaṇa Māgha.
4. The Brahmins who receive from Brahmā;
5. The Puṣkarasāda Brahmins; 6. The Rauhineya Brahmins.
In Jambudvīpa there are also six great mahārathas: first, Ulkāmukha;
second, Aruṇa; [and so forth].
3. Kārima; 4. Suvadana; 5. Paryavrajaka;
"Sixth, the *saṃyamanabaka*.
These eighteen types are difficult to subdue.
At that time, there was among humans a rishi named Ulūka-Kāśyapa, who was already advanced in years and aged.
He reflected and said:

"In this land of superior merit, spanning some twelve yojanas, there is a place within it fit for a Bodhisattva to sit and preach the Dharma. I pray that the Bodhisattva will swiftly descend to the human realm to preach the Dharma for me, so that I may gain great benefit throughout the long night."
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the devaputra of Tuṣita:
"Now, for my sake, cause all the musical instruments to play.
Having heard this, the devas vied with one another to perform their music.

At that time, the Bodhisattva blew the great Dharma conch; its sound was lofty and far-reaching, surpassing all the melodies of celestial music. In this same way, regarding the eighteen kinds of difficult-to-tame sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, the Bodhisattva used unimpeded eloquence to vibrate the great sound of the Dharma, causing those sentient beings to be naturally subdued—just so.
And he spoke in verse:
“The lion’s single roar subdues all beasts; A single vajra-staff shatters the mountain peaks;
Countless asuras are defeated by a single wheel; The darkness of the world is pierced by a single sun.”

At that time, the devas of the six heavens of desire and Śakra, Lord of Devas, beheld the Bodhisattva mounting a six-tusked white elephant, descending from Tuṣita Heaven to enter the womb of Māyā. They immediately sent down nectar to protect the mother’s womb, making it pure and secure, and spoke this verse:
"I behold the Son of Heaven descending to Jambudvīpa, Taking birth within the palace of the Ikṣvāku King;
To benefit sentient beings and fulfill his ancient vow, Like the rising sun emitting its radiance."
The Sūtra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Second.
The Sūtra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, the Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, Mahāmāyā had four kinds of dreams:
first, she dreamed of a white elephant with six tusks in its mouth;
Second, he dreamed that a white elephant descended from the heavens and entered his womb;
third, he dreamed that he himself ascended a great high mountain;
fourth, he dreamed that many noble and eminent persons all came to prostrate themselves before him.
Having had this dream, she immediately informed King Śuddhodana of these matters.
The king asked his physiognomists about the dream, and the physiognomists told the king:
"This lady will surely give birth to a crown prince endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence; if he remains in the royal palace, he will become a Wheel-Turning Monarch."
"If he leaves the household life to cultivate the various pure conducts, he will attain perfect enlightenment and be titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

At the time of the Bodhisattva’s descent and birth, the great earth shook and a vast radiance was emitted; when sentient beings beheld this, they marveled at such an unprecedented event. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the Four World-Protecting Kings each held swords, lassos, bows, arrows, and other weapons to guard the Bodhisattva, so that none of the māras or non-māra spirits and ghosts could cause him harm.
Just as a maṇi jewel and a kāśyaka gem cannot be defiled by any foul or impure dust or grime, so too is the body of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, he caused the mother’s body, both internally and externally, to be as pure and translucent as lapis lazuli, so that she could see the physical form and sensory faculties of the Bodhisattva, clearly and distinctly revealed like a crystal through which a thread of five colors is passed.

Furthermore, it causes the mother’s physical strength to flourish, frees her from all illness and suffering, strengthens her resolve, and enables her to uphold the five precepts with diligence, remaining free from transgressions and all faults.
At that time, Mahāmāyā said to King Śuddhodana:
"Today, I have suddenly felt a desire to drink the waters of the four great oceans.
The king, upon hearing these words, questioned the various physiognomists.
The physiognomist replied:
"Mahāmāyā will surely give birth to a crown prince endowed with all the marks and signs; he shall cultivate the unsurpassed path and attain perfect enlightenment.
However, if she does not drink the ocean water, the physical marks of the crown prince will not be complete."
At that time, there was a man in the kingdom of Kapilavastu named Raktarṣi who was skilled in the arts of illusion.
The king immediately summoned him to the main hall, where he manifested the waters of the four great oceans; the king then took this ocean water and gave it to the queen to drink.
Having drunk this water, he addressed the king, saying:
"I pray that Your Majesty release all sentient beings who are imprisoned and bound in dungeons;
I wish that Your Majesty bestow gifts upon all sentient beings who are destitute of food, clothing, and shelter."
"In this manner, various meritorious deeds were performed.
At that time, Mahāmāyā said to King Śuddhodana:
"I now wish to dwell in the park."
The king then informed King Suprabuddha:
"Your daughter Mahāmāyā wishes to dwell in a garden.
King Suprabuddha immediately dispatched artisans to undertake extensive construction; the site was vast and spacious, with magnificent pavilions and towers, and was named Lumbinī Garden.

At that time, Mahāmāyā went with her court ladies into the garden; seeing the Aśoka tree in full, fragrant bloom with its leaves spread and flowers opening, she immediately grasped a branch of that tree with her right hand, intending to give birth to the Prince. Seeing the multitude of people surrounding her on all sides, she showed a look of modesty.
The Lord of Devas, having perceived this, then sent forth wind and rain, causing the multitude of people to scatter and flee in all directions.
At that time, the Lord of Devas further transformed himself into an old woman and stood before the lady, intending to take the Prince.
At that time, when the Prince first emerged from his mother’s womb, his body was like a mountain of gold, with the color of pure gold, such that his elderly nurse could not catch him as he descended.
The Prince said to her:
“Release me, release me, Kauśika!”
"I have been born myself.
At that moment, the great earth shook violently, emitting a vast radiance that illuminated the world everywhere; when sentient beings saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, beholding these auspicious omens, circumambulated the Crown Prince three times, prostrated at his feet, and exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Today I have given birth to a son of great manly virtue and merit, who shall bring me long-lasting and excellent benefit.
At that time, the Prince’s physical marks were perfectly complete; he was translucent both within and without like lapis lazuli, with no dust, grime, or impurity adhering to him at all.
He took seven steps in each of the four directions; toward the east, signifying the supreme state of Nirvana.
The south symbolizes the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings;
the west symbolizes liberation from birth and death;
and the north symbolizes the eternal severance of saṃsāra.
At that time, the devas and humans in the void held white parasols to cover the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head;
furthermore, the devas sent down two kinds of rain—
either cool or warm— to bathe him by pouring over his head.

Furthermore, the devas and nāgas in the sky performed celestial music and rained down mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, as well as aloeswood, sandalwood, powdered incense, tamāla incense, and exquisite garments.
At that time, the devas in the midst of the void spoke these verses:
"The Great Muni, born of goodness, With marks adorned by a hundred merits;
Having exhausted all defilements and dust, He has realized unsurpassed enlightenment."
"Able, within his perfect body, To emit great radiance;
It shines universally throughout the world, Dispelling all the darkness of ignorance.
When the devaputra had spoken this verse, four kings each gave birth to a son. In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Aruṇa gave birth to a crown prince. The king reflected, saying:
"When my son was born, the world was pure, serene, and peaceful; therefore, I shall name him Praśāntayana.
In the city of Rājagṛha, King Mahāpadma gave birth to a crown prince. The king reflected:
"When my son was born, there was a great radiance that could illuminate the world; therefore, I shall name him Vimiśra."
In the city of Kuśinagara, King Śatānīka begot a crown prince. The king reflected:
"When my son was born, the world was filled with light and heaven and earth were radiant; therefore, I shall name him Udayana."
In the kingdom of Ujjayinī, King Ānandanimiṇu begot a crown prince. The king reflected:
"At the time of my son's birth, there was great radiance and no darkness whatsoever"; thus, he named him Prajyotita.
Thus, these princes were all Bodhisattvas who had been born there through the power of their holy inspiration.
Furthermore, not far from the city, there was a great mountain named Kiṃśukagiri.
In the mountains there was a seer named Asita, who constantly dwelt upon that mountain practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

At that time, the seer had a nephew named Nārada, who attended upon the seer seeking to hear the essentials of the Dharma. The seer then explained to him the teachings on good and evil, and because of this, he went forth as a renunciant.
When the Bodhisattva was born, a great radiance shone upon the world. Nārada saw it and, struck with wonder and uncertainty, entered his hermitage and asked his teacher:
"This light that now illuminates the world is like a mass of suns."
"How has it come to be?
The Master replied, "This radiance is like the color of pure gold; cool, serene, and illuminating the three realms—this is an auspicious omen of the Buddha's birth."
Narada said to his teacher,
"I shall now go there to pay homage to the Bodhisattva seer.
He replied:

"He possesses great majesty and virtue; surrounded and protected by devas, nāgas, and spirits, he cannot be seen. When you hear that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has entered the kingdom of Kapilavastu, you should go to him; you will obtain great benefit."

Furthermore, at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth, five hundred white elephants and five hundred attendants were born simultaneously; treasures from within the earth spontaneously emerged, celestial nectar descended from the heavens, and all the minor kings came together to offer their congratulations.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, beholding these various and most excellent auspicious omens, spoke to himself:
"My son has been born endowed with great auspiciousness; he is able to fulfill all merits and accomplish all virtuous deeds. He should be given the name Sarvārthasiddha (Accomplisher of All Aims)."

Furthermore, in the city of Kapilavastu there was a yakṣa deity named Śakravardhana. Whenever any sentient beings had a son or daughter born, they would take the child to the temple of the deity to have them bow before the yakṣa and seek his protection.

At that time, King Śuddhodana also had the Prince ride in a chariot made of the four precious substances to visit that shrine; as they reached the temple courtyard, a yakṣa came out to welcome him and prostrated before the chariot.
King Śuddhodana said: "The supreme devas pay profound respect to the Bodhisattva; he should be given the title 'Son of Heaven' (Devaputra).

Furthermore, the members of the Śākya clan are of fierce temperament and difficult to subdue. Yet, upon seeing this Bodhisattva’s physical form—so dignified and majestic, his countenance so serene and refined—they look up to him with reverence. Consequently, they turn their hearts away from pride and arrogance, becoming gentle and compliant as they gaze upon him in silence. For this reason, he shall be named 'Silent One' (Mauneya)."
At that time, King Śuddhodana addressed the palace attendants:
"Tend to the Prince with diligent care; nurse him at the proper times, bathe him, and adorn him; protect and cherish him with all your heart so that he suffers no harm."

"When my son was born, the heavens rained down ambrosia. When the physiognomists examined him, they saw that he possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man. If he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning King, fully endowed with the seven treasures—the golden wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the queen treasure, the treasurer treasure, and the military commander treasure—surrounded by a thousand sons. This is truly rare; he is courageous and fearless, capable of vanquishing all enemies."
At that time, the physiognomist spoke in verse:
“The precious golden wheel with its thousand spokes, With hub and spokes perfectly complete;
Traversing the four quarters through the air, It returns to its original place in an instant.”
The elephant-treasure is most preeminent, white as a conch or snow;
it roams throughout Jambudvīpa, meeting no obstruction wherever it goes.
The horse-treasure possesses full majesty, its blue neck a rarity in the world.
Constantly traveling through the void, coming and going like the turning of the wind;
this supreme maṇi jewel radiates light for one yojana;
like when the bright moon emerges from the midst of the night’s darkness.
The Woman-Jewel is rare in the world, subtle and most exquisite in her beauty;
she attends the Wheel-Turning King and can know his every thought.
The Treasure of the Storehouse possesses great majesty and virtue, capable of presiding over the treasures of the world.
Treasures within the sea and beneath the earth, the King shall cause them to appear at once.
His minister of war possesses great power and can command the fourfold army—
elephants, cavalry, infantry, and chariots— so that wherever they go, none dare oppose them.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again asked the physiognomist,
"What are the thirty-two marks of my son?
The physiognomist replied:
"The thirty-two marks are as follows:
First, on the soles of the Prince's feet there are wheels with a thousand spokes, where the hub, spokes, and rim are all perfectly complete;
second, the Prince's hands and feet are both soft and supple, like *tūla* cotton."
3. The Prince’s hands and feet are like those of a king of geese, with webbed membranes between the toes and fingers, and are the color of pure gold;
4. The Prince’s fingers and toes are slender and long;
5. The Prince’s heels are well-proportioned to his insteps.
Sixth, the soles of the Prince’s feet are level and full, like the base of a fragrant casket;
seventh, his two calves are gradually tapered and rounded, like those of the golden deer king;
eighth, his two arms are long and straight, with hands hanging down that reach past his knees, like the trunk of an elephant king.
Ninth, the Prince’s male organ is concealed within a sheath and invisible, like that of a dragon-horse or a royal elephant;
tenth, a single hair grows from each pore of the Prince’s body, dark blue in color and curling to the right;
eleventh, the Prince’s hair and body hairs are straight and point upward, adorning his golden-hued body which all beings love and delight in.
12. The Prince’s skin is thin and supple, so that dust and grime do not adhere to it;
13. The Prince’s skin is golden in color and radiant, like a magnificent golden pedestal adorned with various jewels, beloved by humans and devas;
14. Seven parts of the Prince’s body—the palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, his neck, and both shoulders—are full and well-fleshed.
Fifteenth, the Prince’s shoulders and neck are exceptionally sublime, each perfectly rounded;
sixteenth, the area beneath both of the Prince’s armpits is fully developed;
seventeenth, the Prince’s countenance and deportment are vast, perfect, and dignified.
18. The Prince’s physical form is cultivated, expansive, and upright, surpassing that of humans and devas;
19. The Prince’s bodily proportions are perfectly rounded and complete, equal in measure to the nyagrodha tree;
20. The Prince’s upper body, from the jaw to the chest, is majestic and vast like that of a lion king.
21. The Prince always possesses a radiance extending one fathom from his face;
22. The Prince’s teeth are forty in number, even and level like snow, pure and closely set, with deep roots, firm and immovable;
23. The Prince has four canine teeth that are brilliant white, sharp, and keen.

24. All food consumed by the Prince’s mouth always attains supreme flavor; he can swallow it correctly, his salivary fluids flow freely, and he is forever free from all ailments, with body and mind in perfect harmony and joy.
25. The Prince’s tongue is broad and pure, capable of covering the face up to the hairline.
26. The Prince’s Brahma-voice is grand and elegant; its resonance vibrates like a celestial drum, and his speech is refined and graceful like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
Twenty-seven: The prince’s eyelashes are deep blue-black in color, like those of a bull king, and are not disordered;
twenty-eight: the prince’s eyes are deep blue-black, with bright white and red rings interspersed, such that the blue and white are clearly distinguished;
twenty-nine: the prince’s facial orb is like the full moon of heaven.
30. The Prince’s eyebrows are curved and long, like the bow of the Heavenly Emperor;

31. Between the Prince’s two eyebrows there is the mark of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*), which curls to the right, is soft as *tūla* cotton, and is so fresh, white, and pure that it surpasses jade or snow;
32. On the crown of the Prince’s head is the *uṣṇīṣa*; the bone of his golden crown is prominent, high, and perfectly round, resembling a celestial canopy.

These thirty-two marks of a great man were achieved by practicing all precepts and wholesome dharmas without exception for an immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas throughout the long duration of past lives, through constant and uninterrupted diligent cultivation; thus, the merit of these marks and signs has now been fully realized.
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva was born in the palace of Śuddhodana, his provisions of food and drink, clothing, bedding, elephants, horses, and all manner of precious jewels were fully provided;
his retinue was flourishing and the royal lineage remained unbroken, such that among humans and devas there was none equal to him.
Had he not renounced the world, at the age of thirty-two he would have become a Wheel-Turning King.
