At that time, after Mahāmāyā had given birth to the Prince, she passed away seven days later and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where she enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses.

At that time, the Prince’s countenance was so upright and handsome that gods and humans could never tire of gazing upon him with reverence and affection; even if a skillful goldsmith of the world were to fashion an image out of gold, it would still not equal his beauty.
Just as the *nāṭaka* stone of the devas emits a great radiance that illuminates everything,
so too is the tranquil radiance of the Bodhisattva’s body.
Furthermore, just as a lotus flower in full bloom rises above the water, its buds fragrant and sweet, so that all sentient beings who see it find delight;
likewise, all who behold the body of a Bodhisattva pay it reverence.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva’s two eyes are pure and clear; looking into the distance, they can see objects within a yojana, including the colors of even the most subtle particles. This surpasses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), as there is no difference between day and night.

Furthermore, the speech and voice of this Bodhisattva are exquisite and resonant like the call of the kalaviṅka bird; they are also like the sound of winged birds dwelling on the Snowy Mountains who, having fed on flowers and water and become intoxicated, call out to one another with voices that are harmonious and elegant—just so it is with his.
At that time, the seer Nārada addressed his own teacher, the seer Asita, saying:
"I shall now go to that city of Kapilavastu to pay homage to the Bodhisattva."
The Master said,
"You may go.
He then employed his supernormal powers with his original teacher and traveled to the city of Kapilavastu.
Not far from the city, the Bodhisattva’s majestic power caused him to lose his supernormal faculties, so that he had to travel on foot to the city and approach King Śuddhodana’s palace.
At that time, the gatekeeper immediately informed the king, who then commanded the attendants to lead him inside.
Having seen him, the king was filled with immeasurable joy; he invited him to take a seat, offered *argha* water, performed music, prepared food, and made various offerings.
The king then asked:
"O Sage!..."
"How have you come here by way of causes and conditions?
Then Asita addressed the king:
"I now wish to see the Great Muni, the Teacher who has accomplished all goals."
The king said, "This prince is currently fast asleep; wait but a moment and you shall see him.
Then Asita requested to approach the bed curtains to gaze upon the prince.
At that time, although the Prince was in deep sleep, both his eyes were wide open and did not blink.
Then Asita spoke these verses:
"When the various devas observe their realms, Their eyes do not blink when beholding objects; The Prince’s eyes are likewise so— They are like those of the gods."
"Though the Bodhisattva sleeps, his observation of objects is likewise so.
When the seer had spoken this verse, the palace attendants and nurses took up the Prince and presented him to the seer.
At that time, Asita, observing that the Prince’s countenance was extraordinary, asked the King:
"Has there ever been a physiognomist who came to examine his marks?"
The Great King replied, “A brahmin once prophesied concerning this crown prince:
‘If he does not leave the household life, he will certainly attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch; if he is able to leave the household life, he will surely achieve Perfect Enlightenment.’”
Having heard this, the seer immediately spoke in verse:
"Formerly I fell into the body of a heretic with false views; Now I have met the Prince of the Wheel of Merit.
He can eliminate afflictions and realize Bodhi, Skillfully expounding the profound treasury of the ocean of Dharma."
Though possessing the perfect marks and signs, you renounced the status of a Wheel-Turning King to become a Great Muni who saves all beings;
therefore, I now take refuge and pay homage to you, praying that I may draw near to you and extinguish my afflictions.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the seer scrutinized his own lifespan to see whether he would witness the Prince attaining Buddhahood.

Having observed thus, he saw that the Prince would depart from that royal city and enter the mountain wilds; at the age of twenty-nine, he would practice austerities for six years among those mountains and realize the deathless extinction, attaining the Unsurpassed Way.

At that time, the rishi again examined himself and realized that although he had encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, his life span was short and he would not meet him for long; filled with profound grief, he could not help but break into tears and weep aloud.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, seeing the seer weeping, was struck with extraordinary wonder and spoke this verse:
"If a person has sons and daughters, Their heart of love and affection can never be satiated;
Yet such a person of exceptional and auspicious marks— Beholding them always brings delight."
Seeing the Crown Prince, the seer asked: "Why do you weep?
If my son is terrified or has suddenly fallen ill, I do not yet know what his condition may be."
"Please explain this to me quickly.
At that time, having heard these verses, the seer Asita addressed the king, saying:
"The Prince will before long attain perfect enlightenment; why then should you have fear for his person?"
Even if great vajras were to descend from the sky, falling like pearls filling the firmament, they could not harm so much as a single hair on that bodhisattva’s body.
No fire in the world can burn him; no great wind can blow him away; no poison can injure him; no swords, blades, bows, or arrows can wound him; and no venomous dragons or fierce beasts can harm him.
Furthermore, this Bodhisattva, having practiced great compassion in past lives, has never abandoned sentient beings, causing those beings to always obtain peace and security.
"How can a Bodhisattva have such fear?
In the void above, Śakra, Brahmā, and other celestial kings constantly provide protection together.

I weep now because I observe that my own life will end prematurely; I shall not be able to hear the profound treasury of the Dharma during this Buddha’s world, nor shall I have any share in the wealth of virtue. It is for this reason that I am moved by grief and weep for myself; I pray that Your Majesty be free from sorrow."
At that time, Asita thought again:
"I possess supernatural powers, yet the Bodhisattva’s majesty has caused them to remain unmanifest; therefore, I entered the royal palace on foot.
If I were now to depart from the city on foot as well, those sentient beings would immediately give rise to a sense of pride [thinking me inferior]."
"The Greatly Transcendent Rishi is stepping forth from the royal city.
Having formed this thought, he addressed King Śuddhodana:
"I now take my leave of the King to depart from the city of Kapilavastu; please have the roads at the four crossroads prepared for me."

At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately commanded the officials to repair the roads, removing gravel, pebbles, and all impure things, and to sprinkle the ground with fragrant water of white sandalwood to purify it. Banners, streamers, and necklaces were erected everywhere, and various exquisite incenses were burned. The king, together with his ministers, elders, and householders, respectfully surrounded him as they departed from the city of Kapilavastu to escort the seer.

Then, having taken leave of the king, Asita proceeded as he pleased toward Mount Kṛṣṇagiri; staying there in the mountains, he practiced meditative concentration and before long attained supernormal powers.
At a later time, his body became slightly ill; by consuming excellent medicines, flowers, fruits, and the like, he was able to recover.
His disciple said to him:
"I have now gone forth from home in order to seek the nectar of supramundane liberation."
"The Master has attained something; I pray you will grant me your instruction.
The Master said, "I have practiced for many years, yet I have still not attained this nectar of immortality myself. How then can I provide it for you?"
Now there is a son of King Śuddhodana named Siddhārtha, who has attained equal and perfect enlightenment and realized the true nectar of immortality.

You should leave the household life under him, practicing the holy life with single-minded devotion to seek liberation; do not harbor notions of lineage, nor notions of self or person, and you will immediately achieve the unconditioned Dharma.
At that time, the seer Asita spoke these verses:
“I have dwelt upon such a mountain, Long cultivating the holy life;
Though I have attained supernormal powers, I have yet to drink the nectar of immortality.”
"Knowing for oneself that the body is impermanent, It constantly abides in arising and ceasing;
A collection of provisional conjunctions— This is precisely the nature of impermanence.

When the rishi had spoken this verse, Nārada was moved by his teacher’s instruction. He prostrated and made offerings, then immediately went to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There he saw five hundred māṇava brahmins reciting the Vedas; knowing these were not the ultimate truth, he did not associate with them, but went instead to the Buddha’s dwelling in hopes of hearing the essential points of the Dharma.

At that time, Nārada, whose clan name was Kātyāyana (the "dǐng yǎ" being pronounced as such), took his clan name as his personal name; because the Buddha revealed to him the essentials of the Dharma so that he attained the bliss of nirvana, he was thereafter named Mahākātyāyana.

Furthermore, while the Prince was in the arms of his nursemaid, he took a golden vessel and ate; having finished eating in a moment, the nursemaid immediately gathered up the golden vessel, but it was as heavy as a mountain and she could not lift it. She then reported this matter in full to the King.

The king went with his palace attendants to retrieve the vessel, but they too were unable to lift it. He then assembled the people of the kingdom to lift the golden vessel together, yet the vessel became even heavier.
They further harnessed five hundred great elephants to drag the golden vessel, but they could not move even a fraction of it.

Why was this? By the supernormal power of the Bodhisattva, he raised a single finger of his left hand and hooked it onto the golden vessel, so that even when the elephant exerted all its strength, it could not move it.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"If the Bodhisattva raises two fingers to hook that golden vessel, even a hundred thousand great elephants could not move it; thus, the Bodhisattva possesses the strength of a thousand elephants.
If these youths wish to compete with the Bodhisattva in playful combat, they are like small swans compared to a great crane—their strength is unequal."
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva was in the royal palace, he entered school to study with five hundred attendants.
At that time, his original teacher brought forth the first book and ordered the Prince to read it;
the Prince replied, "I already understand this book."
The teacher then ordered him to read the second book.
Upon seeing it, the Prince spoke again to his teacher, saying:
"I understand this book as well."
Thereupon, the Preceptor presented the Prince with five hundred kinds of scripts. The Prince said:
"I understand each and every one of these five hundred scripts; if there are other scripts, you should give them to me."
The teacher then replied, "In this world there are only these five hundred kinds of scripts; beyond these, there are none.
At that time, the Prince himself wrote out a script and commanded the teacher to read it.
The Master then sighed and said,
"Since the distant past, my eyes have never beheld such a thing.
The Prince replied:
"This is the Brahma-script; at that time, the Brahma King, knowing that I was destined to succeed to the rank of Wheel-Turning King, transmitted it to me.
He then recited it himself with a subtle and wondrous Brahma-voice.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, from within the void, proclaimed in a loud voice:
"This is the scripture of Brahmā.
Upon hearing this celestial testimony, the Master gave rise to profound faith and understanding.
At that time, the Prince’s maternal uncle was Sāṇḍili, and there was another man named Sahadeva; these two were skilled in the art of archery, and five hundred people studied their craft under them.
Furthermore, these two masters said to one another:

"That Devadatta is coarse-natured and malicious by disposition, and his mind is full of jealousy; we should not teach him the arts of archery, for if we do instruct him, he will surely cause harm to living beings."
"That Siddhārtha, being compassionate, wise, and capable of benefiting sentient beings, is worthy of inheriting and practicing such archery.
There are five types [of archery]:
the first is called "long-distance shooting," wherein the arrows he releases can travel to the utmost distances.
The second is shooting by sound, meaning one can shoot at a target simply by hearing its sound;
the third is shooting with precision, meaning the arrows released hit the mark at will;
the fourth is shooting at the target itself, meaning the arrows released do not miss their mark.
Regarding the five types of shooting at objects, there is nothing he shoots at that he does not pierce and sever.
In this way, the Bodhisattva is well-versed in the five kinds of archery.
At that time, there was a great elephant in the city of Vaiśālī, possessing a handsome appearance and great strength. The people of that country all deliberated together:

"In the city of Kapilavastu, the Great King Śuddhodana has a crown prince named Siddhārtha; an interpreter of marks prophesied that he would attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch, so we have hastened with this elephant to present it as an offering."
He then took various precious ornaments, such as pearl necklaces and jewels, and went toward the city of Kapilavastu to the gate of the royal palace.
At that time, Devadatta saw the elephant as he was leaving the gate and questioned the gatekeeper,
saying, "From where has this elephant come?"
The gatekeeper replied,
"The people of the villages around the city of Vaiśālī have sent this elephant as an offering to Siddhārtha, for he possesses the marks of a wheel-turning monarch."
When Devadatta heard of these matters, jealousy arose in his heart, and he said to his gatekeeper:
"What sovereign power does that Siddhārtha possess?"
He immediately took up his weapon and killed the elephant, which then died.

At that time, Nanda saw the dead elephant and realized it had been killed by Devadatta’s wrath. Desiring to test his own prowess against him in combat, Nanda seized the elephant’s tail and flung it with his hand, so that the elephant was cast seven paces away from its original spot.

At that time, Siddhārtha saw that the dead elephant had been moved from its original place; he knew this was because Nanda had displayed his prowess by seizing the elephant’s tail with his hand and hurling it to that spot.

At that time, Prince Siddhārtha manifested his own majestic power; grasping the elephant’s tail with one hand, he cast it toward the sky, and it passed beyond the sevenfold city walls like a clod of earth thrown.
At that time, those who had presented the elephant to the city of Vaiśālī, seeing that Siddhārtha possessed such great power, spoke this verse:
"We traveled a long distance to bring this elephant To present it to the Wheel-Turning King;
Yet encountering this wicked man, He has slain it on the spot."
Nanda grasped the tail with his hand and hurled the elephant seven paces away;
yet the Bodhisattva, with his great majestic power, cast the elephant as if tossing a clod of earth.
*The Sutra of the Mahāsudarśana, Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle Three.
The Sutra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Minister of State Dismissal,
Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, Dharma-bhadra, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, Devadatta took up his bow and arrows and left the city of Kapilavastu, intending to practice archery.
Prince Siddhārtha, having learned of this, departed from the royal city with five hundred attendants to join him in the practice of archery.
At that time, Devadatta took up his bow and arrows and shot at a tree from afar; the tree, struck by the arrow, fell as if responding to the twang of the string.
Prince Siddhārtha also shot at a tree; the power of his arrow was so great that although the tree was split in two, it remained perfectly upright and unmoved.
Devadatta saw that the tree remained as it was before and, suspecting that his arrow had missed its mark, said to the Prince:
"I have often heard that the Prince is proficient in the five methods of archery; how is it that you shot at the tree and yet could not hit it?"
Having spoken thus, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, reflected from within the sky:
"I must today manifest the power of the Bodhisattva’s supernatural faculties; for if I do not do so, how will sentient beings know that this Bodhisattva is fully proficient in all matters?"
Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested a great wind that blew the tree with the arrowed shaft, causing it to suddenly fall to the ground;
at that time, Devadatta was struck with astonishment and sighed in wonder.
At that time, the Prince further ordered seven *tāla* trees, seven layers of iron drums, and seven layers of iron boars to be set up, commanding the assembly to shoot at them.
Then Devadatta, displaying his own prowess, drew his bow and shot forward, piercing one *tāla* tree;
Nanda followed next, piercing two *tāla* trees.

Prince Siddhārtha then shot accordingly, piercing through all seven *tāla* trees, the seven layers of iron drums, the iron boar, and so forth; his arrow entered the earth and reached the palace of the Naga King.

At that time, the Dragon King beheld the Bodhisattva’s arrow and caught it in his hands; from the point where the arrow had entered, water gushed upward. Thereupon, faithful Brahmins and elders erected a stupa at that site to offer worship, and all the bhikṣus came constantly to pay their respects.
At that moment, Prince Siddhārtha mounted a precious palanquin and returned to the royal city.
A physiognomist divined for the prince, saying:
"When he reaches the age of twelve, if he does not leave the household life, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents and surrounded by a thousand sons."
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy; he immediately assembled his ministers and the Śākya clan and reported the matter to them in full.
At that time, a high minister addressed King Śuddhodana:

"If you wish for the Prince to succeed to the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin), you must quickly select a virtuous lady from among the houses of the public officials, ministers, scholars, and commoners within the kingdom to serve as his consort."
He further commissioned various kinds of exquisite garments, pearls, necklaces, rare treasures, as well as houses and multi-storied pavilions;

having thus prepared these, he selected an auspicious day and had the Prince sit upon the lion throne in the royal main hall. He then commanded all the daughters of the high ministers, officials, elders, and lay devotees to assemble at the palace. If there was a girl of upright appearance and superior merit whom the Prince favored, he would bestow the aforementioned rare treasures and other gifts upon her and take her as his consort.

At that time, King Śuddhodana acted according to the petition; subsequently, on an auspicious day, he summoned Prince Siddhārtha to ascend the royal jeweled palace and sit upon the lion throne, while the assembled maidens all came to attend the assembly.
At that time, there was a young girl named Yaśodharā who did not respond to the summons.
When her father asked for the reason, Yaśodharā said, "Gold, silk, and wealth already exist in my own home; why should I accept gifts from the royal palace?"
The father spoke again, saying:
"When you arrive at the royal palace, once the Prince has seen you, he may choose you to be his consort; how could it be that you are merely granted as a gift of precious jewels?"
Upon hearing this, the maiden immediately donned exquisite garments and adorned her body with necklaces and ornaments, proceeding to the royal palace.

When the prince saw that the maiden possessed such exceptionally auspicious marks and a body radiating light, his heart was filled with great joy. He descended from his lion throne and, according to ancient rites, they exchanged bows; having bowed, they sat down again with palms joined in solemn reverence.
Then the ministers and attendants together addressed the king, saying:
"This young girl is endowed with all the auspicious marks and possesses profound merit and virtue; she is worthy to be the consort for the Crown Prince."
The King immediately issued a decree for twenty thousand young maidens to surround Yaśodharā as they entered the palace together.
At that time, not far from the city of Kapilavastu, there was a great river named Rohiṇī; upon its bank stood a great tree named Sālakaṇṭha, which had grown up at the same time as the Prince.

Before long, this tree grew to a height of one hundred cubits; while the sun had not yet risen, its trunk was so supple that it could be injured by fingernails, but once the sun ascended the heavens, axes could not enter it and fire could not consume it.
Subsequently, the river at the ford swelled with floodwaters and submerged the roots of the tree, causing it to topple into the great stream, after which the lower reaches of the river dried up.

At that time, King Suprabuddha found the Rohitaka River blocked by a great tree, so that the water could not flow through. Consequently, the people within his realm lacked water for their use and dispatched an envoy to the kingdom of Śuddhodana to announce:
"A fallen tree has obstructed the current."
The people of the kingdom were greatly terrified and wished to borrow the Prince’s supernatural power to remove the tree and divert the stream.
At that time, King Śuddhodana remained silent and did not grant permission, saying, "If the Prince goes of his own accord, then let it be as he wishes."
There was a minister named Cūḍā who, having secretly discerned the king’s intention, used skillful means to say to the prince:
"Beside the Rohitaka River there is a park with pavilions, towers, and palaces, adorned with flowers, trees, ponds, and pools; it is most magnificent, and you may go there for recreation."
Upon hearing these words, the Prince immediately departed from the city of Kapilavastu together with his retinue and various ministers, proceeding to that garden to roam and play as he pleased.

At that time, Devadatta saw a flying goose passing through the air; drawing his bow, he shot it upward so that it fell before the Prince. Seeing this, the Prince lamented the injury caused to the creature, extracted the arrow, and released the goose to fly away.
Devadatta sent someone to seize the geese, but the Prince said to him:

"I have resolved upon Bodhicitta and constantly practice acts of compassion and mercy to benefit all sentient beings; I do not wish to see them harmed or distressed. As for these flying geese, I have extracted the arrows and released them so that they may be at peace. You should turn back your mind and harbor no resentment."
Having heard these words, Devadatta remained silent and displeased.

At that time, King Suprabuddha, knowing that his crown prince was nearby in the grove, immediately dispatched the people of the kingdom to the river crossing to remove the great tree; they raised their voices and exerted their strength, the sound of which shook the plains and fields.
Upon hearing this, the Crown Prince inquired of his attendants, and the ministers reported in full:
"This is a group of people sent by King Sūrpāraka to fetch trees from within the river."
Having heard this, the Prince said, "I shall go there myself.
Not far from the river was a great cave where a venomous dragon dwelt; when the Prince arrived before it, the dragon emerged from its lair.
The multitude, fearing that they might harm the Prince, immediately severed the life-force of that dragon with a sharp sword.
The dragon possessed a poisonous breath; those who were touched by it became entirely blue-black all over their bodies, and for this reason, he was named Karuṇāyī.
When the Prince reached the riverbank, he first ordered Devadatta to pull out that great tree; though Devadatta exerted his utmost supernatural power, he could not lift it.
Next it was Nanda’s turn; he pulled with all his might until the tree was slightly detached from the ground.

At that moment, the Prince, by means of his own supernatural power, grasped the great tree with his hand, snapped it in two, and hurled the pieces into the air, dropping one segment on each side of the river. He then addressed the multitude, saying:
"This Śālakalyāṇī tree is a great and excellent medicine; fire cannot burn it, and if one has an ulcerous swelling, applying it will cause it to heal immediately. You all must not forget this."
After the Prince had spoken these words, he immediately mounted his carriage and returned to the city.
At that time, there was a physiognomist who, having examined the Prince, said:
"If he does not leave the home life by the age of seven, he will become a Wheel-Turning King."

As the Prince entered the city and was about to reach the royal palace, there was a daughter of the Śākya clan named Gopikā living in the village of Koliya. She was atop a high tower when she suddenly beheld the Prince’s physical form, so majestic and dignified, and her heart was filled with longing and admiration.
When the Prince saw this girl, he ordered his carriage to halt; he turned his head to gaze at her, and the bow and arrow he held in his hand unconsciously fell to the ground.
At that time, when the multitude of people saw that this young girl possessed such exceptionally auspicious marks,
they all said, "This girl is worthy to serve the Prince.
King Śuddhodana, her father, having learned of this matter, dispatched twenty thousand young girls to surround and escort the daughter of Amṛtodana into the royal palace.
At that time, having taken the consort as his wife, the Prince thought of going abroad to tour the gardens outside the city, and immediately addressed his charioteer, Ājñāta:
"Listen attentively now!
"I am thinking of going outside to tour the gardens and groves; please prepare and adorn for me a fine carriage and horses in accordance with the proper rites.
When Ajātaśatru heard these words, he immediately prepared and adorned a fine carriage and horses in the stable according to the proper rites and went before the Prince.
At that time, the Prince mounted his carriage and went out beyond the city walls; before his horse, he saw an old man with white hair and wrinkled face, leaning on a staff and groaning.
The Prince did not recognize him and asked Āgata,
"Who is this person? Āgata replied:
"This is an old man," [the charioteer] said. The Prince asked,
"What is meant by 'old'?"
Agada said: "The illusory body lacks any solidity;
the four marks shift and change, and the six sense-faculties grow clouded. Rising and sitting require no strength, and one must walk leaning upon a staff—this is called old age."
The Prince asked,
"Can you avoid it? Agada replied:
"How can I possibly escape it?
the Prince asked, saying,
"If you cannot escape it, can I escape it?"
Agada said, "Though noble and base differ, the illusory body is the same for all; as the sun and moon pass in succession, no one can escape it.
Having heard this, the Prince returned home displeased and reflected further to himself:
"The four great elements are but a provisional combination; the five aggregates have no reality. Beginning from youth, one becomes old and decrepit—such a phenomenon is truly and deeply pitiable.
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked Āgata:
"When my son went outside, what did he see?"
Agada said, "When the Prince went outside,
he saw an old man with white hair and wrinkled face.
He then related the preceding events in detail.
Having heard this, the king recalled the words of the former physiognomist who had prophesied that the prince would certainly renounce the world in the future:
"The prince is now dwelling securely within the deep palace, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses; his heart must be so attached to them that he will not renounce the world."
He then spoke in verse:

"The King heard the physiognomist’s prediction regarding the Crown Prince; Fearing that he might later abandon his father to seek renunciation, He now seeks to delight his mind with the five desires, So that through attachment he will surely succeed to the rank of Wheel-Turning King."
At that time, the Prince again contemplated going out of the city to sightsee, and he immediately addressed Āgata:
"Listen attentively!
I wish to go outside the city to visit the gardens and groves; prepare and adorn for me a superior carriage and horse as you did before."
When Agāta had heard these words, he immediately went to the stables and, having adorned a fine carriage and horse according to the proper rites, returned to the presence of the Prince.
At that time, the Prince mounted the carriage and drove out of the city; before his horse, he saw a sick man whose body was emaciated and whose spirit was weak, yet the Prince did not recognize him.
He asked Āgata, "Who is this? Āgata replied:
"This is a sick person.
The Prince asked,
"What is meant by 'sickness'?"

Chanda replied, "When the four great elements of the body conflict with one another, illness arises; the physical form becomes emaciated and wretched, and the mental consciousness finds no peace—this is what is called 'illness.'"
The Prince asked,
"Can you escape it? Agada replied:
"You cannot escape it either.
He asked again,
"Since you cannot escape it, can I escape it?"
Agada replied, "Since all are but illusory forms, why should he alone be exempt?
Having heard this, the Prince immediately returned to the royal palace.
He further reflected to himself:
"This body, a mere composite, is the gathering place of all maladies; how deeply pitiable are sentient beings in their ignorance and delusion!
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked Āgata:
"What did the Crown Prince see when he went outside?
At that time, Āgata recounted the aforementioned events in detail.
Having heard this, the King feared his son would leave the household life; he therefore ordered the palace to entertain and serve the Crown Prince with the pleasures of the five senses.
He then spoke in verse:
“Form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are most exquisite; They delight the heart of the Prince within the deep palace.
If one were to give rise to love and pleasure and become greedily attached, One should not leave the home-life to seek the path of awakening.”
At that time, the Prince again reflected upon going out of the city to tour the gardens, and he immediately addressed Āgata:
"Listen attentively!
I am thinking of touring the parks and gardens outside the city; prepare and adorn for me, as before, a superior chariot and horse."
When Agāta had heard these words, he immediately went to the stables and, having adorned a magnificent carriage and steed according to the prescribed rites, brought them before the Prince.

Thereupon, the Prince mounted the carriage and departed from the city; at the head of his horse, he beheld a dead man whose breath had ceased and whose spirit had departed, appearing like earth, wood, tiles, or stones, devoid of all sensation or awareness, while male and female relatives surrounded him, weeping in sorrow.
He asked Āgata, "Who is this? Āgata replied:
"This is a dead man.
The Prince asked again,
"What is meant by 'death'?"
Agada replied:
"The nature of conditioned phenomena is such that lifespans vary in length; when, all at once, impermanence brings one forever apart from kinsmen, this is called death."
Having heard this, the Prince asked Āgata:
"Can you escape it? Āgata replied:
"Nor can it be avoided," [the physician] replied. The Prince asked,
"If your person cannot avoid it, I ought to be able to avoid it."
Agada replied, "The three realms are impermanent;
arising and ceasing, they do not abide. The body of the Prince is likewise so.
At that time, the Prince’s heart was ill at ease, and he returned to the royal palace.
Having arrived at the royal palace, he reflected again:

"The law of impermanence does not abide for even a single moment; from the realms of form and formlessness, even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no escape from this great affliction of impermanence. How deeply pitiable are all sentient beings!"
Having had this thought, his heart was ill at ease.
Then, King Śuddhodana asked Āgata:
"What did the Prince see when he went outside?"
At that time, Agada recounted each of the aforementioned matters in detail. Having heard them, the king reflected:

"In the past, there was a brahmin who performed a divination for the crown prince; his merit and virtue were profound and thick, and he was endowed with all the auspicious marks. It was certain that he would renounce the world and attain the path of perfect enlightenment."

He immediately ordered that the palace be filled with the various delights of the five sensual pleasures to provide him with every form of gratification, intending to cause him to become attached and abandon his resolve for renunciation.
He then spoke these verses:
"With the great wealth and honor of the five sensual pleasures, I shall delight the Prince, the God among Gods."
"Causing him to have no desire to seek renunciation, entrust him to the supreme station of the Wheel-Turning King.
At that time, Prince Siddhārtha again contemplated going out of the city for an excursion and immediately told Āgata:
"I wish to go outside the city to view the gardens; prepare a magnificent carriage and mount as before and bring it to me."
Thereupon, Ājñāta immediately went to the stables and, having adorned a superior chariot and horse according to the ritual, brought them before the Prince.
At that time, the Prince mounted the chariot and horse and went out to travel and observe.
At that time, the devaputra of Tuṣita thought to himself:

"Now the Bodhisattva has gone out of the city to observe the sights, seeking the conditions for renunciation; I should assume the appearance of a śramaṇa and, carrying an alms-bowl, beg for food before the Prince."
Having formed this thought, he immediately shaved his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and stood at the head of the horse holding an alms bowl.
When the Prince saw him, he turned and asked Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya, "Who is this man?"
Agada replied, “He is a renunciant.
The Prince asked:
"What is meant by 'leaving home' (renunciation)?

Agada replied, "This person realizes the nature of birth and death and vows to sever the cycle of saṃsāra; they cultivate the causes of bodhi to seek the fruit of liberation, shave off their hair and beard, don the dharma robes, and purify both body and mind—this is called leaving home."
Upon hearing this, the prince’s heart leaped with joy; he immediately dismounted from his horse and asked the bhikṣu, “What is this ‘leaving home,’ and what benefits does it offer?”
The bhikṣu replied:

"One who has left the household life severs their affection for kin, does not cling to worldly glory or pleasure, constantly cultivates the pure conduct (brahmacarya), firmly maintains the disciplinary code (vinaya), turns their back on the toils of worldly existence, restrains the faculties and consciousness, allows no false thoughts to arise, and increases in true practice; one who progresses in this manner is called a renunciant."
Having heard this, the Prince sighed in admiration and said: "Excellent!
You are a great man!"
"One who is able to skillfully discipline themselves and skillfully seek [the Dharma] amidst this turbid world is a true renunciant and a true spiritual friend.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself, mounted his horse, and returned to the palace.

While still within the palace, he contemplated with focused intent the way of renunciation; its practice is most sublime and its principle most profound, and he grew weary of the royal court, seeking liberation.
Then King Śuddhodana asked Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya, "What did the Prince see during his excursion? Did he find any joy?
Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya hesitated for a moment and then reported the matter in detail to the King.
Upon hearing the report, the king reflected again:
"The physiognomist once said that if he does not leave the household life, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King.
I must now devise a special expedient to cause the prince to sever his intention to renounce the world."
He then addressed Siddhārtha:
"The village of Kāliṃjara is a strategic stronghold of the kingdom; you must now go there to act as my deputy and ensure that the people of this region live in harmony and joy."

Having heard this, the Prince was bewildered and distressed; day and night he contemplated his goal with single-minded intent to renounce the world, yet as his original purpose remained unfulfilled, he departed for the village of Kāliṃjara.
As he proceeded along the road, five great treasuries of precious jewels welled up from the earth.
The deities who guard the treasuries addressed him, saying: "O Prince!
"These treasuries belong to you, O Bodhisattva; I only pray that you will accept them for my sake.
The Prince replied, "These treasuries are accumulations of various jewels to which sentient beings are attached; they are not what I seek."
When the deity who guards the treasury heard the Bodhisattva’s words, knowing that he would not accept [the wealth], he immediately led his kindred into the great ocean.

At that time, the Prince proceeded by stages until he reached the borders of the village of Kaliṃjara. There he saw many people, each holding farming implements, laboring wearily at plowing; their hands and feet were coarse and calloused, their bodies were covered in dust and dirt, their clothing was tattered and worn, and they were weak from hunger and thirst—thus oppressed by all manner of sufferings.
The Crown Prince, having long harbored compassion, was startled upon seeing him and asked who he was.
His attendants informed him,
"This is a man from among the people employed in the Prince's own agricultural estates."
Upon hearing this, the Prince immediately issued an order:
"Release the able-bodied men and the cattle; let them manage their own livelihoods as they wish, and do not allow the government officials to further detain or inspect them."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went beneath a jambu tree, sat down cross-legged, and entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
His ministers, servants, officials, and citizens likewise stood surrounding him beneath the tree.
During the mealtime, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"The time appointed for the Prince’s excursion has already passed, yet he has not yet returned; I shall go myself to see the Prince."

He immediately prepared his carriage and set out to visit the village; arriving beneath a Jambu tree, he saw that the Prince had entered samādhi, with body and mind unmoving, such that although the sun’s position had shifted, the shadow of the tree did not move.
At that time, King Śuddhodana exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!
O one of great majestic virtue!"
"O Great Man! This is truly rare:
though the sun moves on without ceasing, the shadow of the tree does not shift.
Bowing his head to the ground, he prostrated at the Bodhisattva’s feet and spoke this verse:
“Excellent! O Great Being!
You are truly rare in this world;”
At the time of his birth, he emitted radiance, and the great earth shook in every direction.
Now he sits beneath the Jambu tree; though the sun moves, his shadow does not shift.
All the multitudes see and hear this together; I now take refuge and pay homage to him.
At that time, the Prince arose from his meditative concentration and immediately mounted his carriage to return to Kapilavastu.
Passing through the Śītavana forest, he saw corpses therein—naked, foul-smelling, and with limbs decayed and putrefied—and he conceived a profound sense of weary detachment toward the world.
When the King and the Prince entered the city of Kapilavastu, there was a physiognomist who, observing the Prince’s extraordinary majesty and virtue, told King Śuddhodana:
"If this Prince does not renounce the world within seven days, he will certainly attain the rank of a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
At that time, the physiognomist spoke in verse:
"Great King, you should now know: if Prince Siddhārtha does not renounce the world for seven days, he shall assume the rank of a Wheel-Turning Monarch."
"Ruling over the four great continents, Possessing the seven precious treasures;
When you have attained perfect enlightenment, With the wealth of Dharma, you shall save the world.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the physiognomist departed, and the Prince advanced his carriage, proceeding gradually forward.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Kālakṣama; his daughter, named Mṛgajā, beheld the Prince’s majestic and dignified demeanor and offered him praise.
Before the Crown Prince, she immediately spoke in verse:
"My father has attained the bliss of liberation, And my mother’s body is likewise so;
Since you have been born as this Siddhārtha, I pray that you will become my husband."
"When you have become the Honored One among two-legged beings, And fully realized the Dharma of Nirvāṇa;
When your fame pervades the ten directions— I now take refuge in you and pay homage.

At that time, having heard this gāthā, the Prince’s heart was filled with joy. By the power of its influence, he took pearls and necklaces, passed them through the window, and placed them upon the woman's neck.
When King Śuddhodana witnessed this event, he immediately surrounded the maiden Mṛgajā with twenty thousand palace attendants and brought her into the royal palace.
At that time, the Prince had three consorts:
Yaśodharā, Gopikā, and Mṛgajā.
Furthermore, sixty thousand palace attendants served him morning and evening, yet his mind was free from attachment as he focused solely on seeking renunciation.
When King Śuddhodana learned of these matters, he addressed the three kings:
"A Brahmin has prophesied regarding my crown prince that if he is not made to leave the home life within seven days, he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning King."
"You kings, you must all provide joint protection for seven days and nights.

He further mobilized the populace to construct a city with sevenfold walls and sevenfold moats; the city was equipped with iron gates, upon which bells were hung both above and below. When the gates were opened, the sound of the bells resounded for a distance of one yojana.
At that time, within the inner palace, the Prince amused himself with the palace women through singing, dancing, and music, day and night without distinction.

King Śuddhodana then summoned his ministers and ordered them to provide guard at every location within the harem; furthermore, he dispatched the four divisions of the army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—to patrol and station themselves at the four gates of the city.

At that time, King Śuddhodana was at the eastern gate of the city, King Droṇodana at the southern gate, King Śuklodana at the western gate, and King Amṛtodana at the northern gate; each leading his ministers, they remained awake throughout the night, guarding with single-minded devotion.
He further commanded his minister Mahānāma to patrol the four gates throughout the night without ceasing, keeping watch over the troops and ensuring they did not fall asleep.
At that time, Mahānāma led the group of people on patrol until they reached the eastern gate, where he immediately asked:
"Who is here keeping watch and not sleeping?"
Then King Śuddhodana said,
"I shall now personally provide protection here. Mahānāma replied:
"Great King!
If one does not sleep, there will be no faults.
Then Mahānāma spoke this verse:
"One who indulges in sleep is like one who is dead, And is also like one possessed by a demon;
If one can cease this sleep, Faults will certainly not arise.
At that time, after Mahānāma had spoken these verses, he went to the southern gate and asked again:
"Who is here keeping watch without sleeping?
Then King Droṇodana replied,
"I am here now, guarding with single-minded devotion."
Mahānāma replied: "Great King!
If one does not sleep, there will be no faults."
Then Mahānāma spoke these verses:
"A person's sleep is like death; one must know that the demon of sleep exists.
If one can bring this sleep to an end, faults will certainly not arise."
At that time, after Mahānāma had spoken these verses, he went to the western gate and asked again:
"Who is here keeping watch without sleeping?"
Then King Śuklodana said,
"I am here now, guarding with single-minded devotion. Mahānāma replied:
"Great King!
If one does not sleep, there will be no faults.
Then Mahānāma spoke these verses:
"Indulgence in sleep is like drinking wine; Intoxicated, one enters the wilderness.
Faults then arise in its wake; Therefore, one must cease from sleep.
From the *Buddha-bhāṣita-saṃghabhedavastu-mahāsūtra*, Scroll Four.
The Sutra of the Great King Mahāsudarśana Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Dharma Xian, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, under Imperial Decree.
At that time, having spoken these verses, Mahānāma went to the northern gate and asked in a loud voice:
"Who is here, staying awake to provide guard?"
King Amṛtodana said,
"I shall remain here awake to guard him.
Mahānāman replied:
"If one does not sleep, one will guard against all faults.
Thus he spoke in verse:
"Fearful of sleep as of a treacherous mountain pass, And likewise as of drifting upon a river or sea;"
"With a single mind guard against danger; Ceasing sleep is likewise so.

When Mahānāma had spoken this verse, he immediately went out to wander through the markets and alleys everywhere, observing the people as they ceased their sleep to keep watch, and spoke these verses:
"Abide by the Dharma and leave what is contrary to the Dharma; Speak the truth and do not speak falsely."
"O King Śuddhodana, most excellent one, cease your sleep and remain vigilant.
When Mahānāma had spoken this verse, the night was nearly over; he approached King Śuddhodana and addressed him, saying:
"A day and night have passed, and both within and without all is peaceful and quiet, free from any demonic obstacles."

"I only pray that Your Majesty will further command the military forces to guard with diligent care for seven days and nights more, so that the Prince may certainly obtain the position of a Wheel-Turning King.
Thus they provided protection until the sixth day and night had passed.
At that time, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, observing that the Prince intended to proceed to the site of enlightenment, spoke these verses:
“Excellent, O Great Man!
Śākya Lion, the Muni;”
One must surely renounce the royal palace and seek the mountain wilds;
Fulfilling the six pāramitās, one achieves unsurpassed wisdom;
Delivering all living beings, one ultimately reaches the further shore.
At that time, while Prince Siddhārtha was enjoying himself with his palace ladies, he suddenly reflected: "Although I now have Yashodharā,
Utpalavarṇā, Mṛgajā, and these other queens, as well as sixty thousand court ladies, if I depart to practice the path without having sons or daughters,
everyone will say, 'Prince Siddhārtha is no true man.'"
After he had departed in seclusion, Yaśodharā immediately became pregnant.
Thereupon, the Prince spoke to the palace ladies: "Phenomena arise through conditions and exist as illusions;
within the cycle of birth and death, if one does not still the mind, there will be no end."
"If one shares a bed or seat with a woman, it is like stepping on fire that brings swift and great suffering; therefore, I now give rise to weary detachment.
While he was speaking these words, a courtesan spat foam from her mouth, her hands and feet flailed about, her hair became disheveled, and she fell to the ground in a swoon.
At that time, the palace women were struck with extraordinary terror; seeing this, the Prince felt deep compassion and lamented:
"How bitter! Why is there such an inauspicious sign of death?"
And he spoke in verse:
“In an instant it changes and decays, producing foul signs; The hands and feet flail about as saliva and froth flow forth.
Beholding this impermanent body of suffering and affliction, I now seek liberation.”

At that time, having spoken these verses, the Prince observed all sentient beings as lacking any substantial characteristic of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. He viewed them as entering a cemetery with nothing to love or delight in; as treading upon mud, only increasing foulness; as nurturing a venomous serpent, ultimately providing no benefit; and as being like lightning, a dream, foam, or a bubble—shrouded by fundamental ignorance and thus remaining unaware.
Having observed this, King Śuddhodana himself recounted his four dreams:
first, a dream of the full moon being eclipsed;
second, a dream of the sun rising and then setting in the east.
Third, he dreamed that a great multitude of noble beings came to pay him homage;
fourth, he dreamed that his own body laughed and then wept.
Yaśodharā also recounted eight dreams:
First, he dreamed that his noble lineage was scattered;
second, he dreamed that his auspicious throne was shattered;
third, he dreamed that his armlet fell and was damaged.
Fourth, he dreamed that his teeth fell out;
fifth, he dreamed that the hair on his topknot hung down in disarray;
sixth, he dreamed that auspicious clouds emerged from his palace.
Seventh, he dreamed that the full moon was eclipsed;
eighth, he dreamed that the sun, having risen but not yet high, set again in the east.
At that moment, the Prince further reflected upon five dreams he had previously experienced:
First, he dreamed that his bed and seat were like Mount Sumeru, upon which he sat and lay at ease;
second, he dreamed that with his two hands he supported the Eastern Sea on the left and the Western Sea on the right, while his two feet dangled into the Southern Sea;
third, he dreamed that flowers, fruits, trees, and various medicinal herbs grew as high as the celestial realms.

Fourth, he dreamed that a great multitude of large-bodied birds, their bodies white and heads black, as well as various small birds of many colors, came from the four directions and gathered before him; they all turned into a single color and prostrated at his feet.
Fifth, he dreamed that he was walking back and forth upon a great rocky mountain, looking around in all directions.
The Prince thought to himself:
"Since my dream was such as this, I shall certainly renounce the secular life and realize great Bodhi.
At that time, Yaśodharā, reflecting on her previous eight dreams, requested the Prince to interpret their auspicious or inauspicious significance.
The Crown Prince said:
"In the first dream, a noble clan was scattered; yet my own lineage remains united, never having been divided for even a moment.
In the second dream, the auspicious throne was broken; yet that throne remains as it was before."
Third, you dreamed that your armlet was broken and fell, yet it is seen upon your arm;
fourth, you dreamed that your teeth fell out, yet there are no teeth that have fallen;
fifth, you dreamed that your hair hung down in disarray—who has seen such hanging hair?
Sixth, she dreamed that auspicious clouds emerged from the palace; now I am the Auspicious One (*Śrī*), yet I am still within the palace.
Seventh, she dreamed that the moon was eclipsed; how could there be an eclipse now that it is in the heavens?
"In the eighth dream, the sun rose but before it had reached its height, it set again in the east; at that time it was midnight and the sun had not yet risen.
Since there is nothing inauspicious in these dreams, why do you harbor such anxiety and doubt?
The Prince reflected:
"These eight dreams must be omens of my renunciation," he thought,
and he immediately told Yaśodharā:
"I shall now go to those mountain regions for the sake of all sentient beings, seeking the Dharma of Nirvāṇa and liberation."
Yaśodharā said, "I shall follow wherever my husband intends to go.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and Brahmā, King of the Gods, addressed the Prince, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Quickly renounce the five desires and leave the palace at once; when the signs of dawn appear, you shall realize all-knowledge.
The Bodhisattva said:

“Kauśika! I am within the deep palace like a tiger entering a pit, surrounded by the fourfold army of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; the gates and doors of the palace are all locked and barred, with bells suspended everywhere to provide warning and guard—how can I depart?”
Śakra replied:
"Simply recollect the practices and vows you cultivated throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas of the past, for the purpose of severing all suffering and delivering the world."
When these words were spoken, the Four Great Kings and their retinues, through their majestic spiritual power, rendered those people unable to create obstacles.
Immediately, Śakra transformed a jeweled staircase and addressed the yakṣa lord Pañcika, saying:
"The Noble Bodhisattva is currently situated upon a high tower; you must welcome him at the front with this jeweled staircase."
Having heard this, the yakṣa followed the instructions and carried them out.
As soon as the Bodhisattva dismounted, he sought Candana to have him mount the horse-king. He then saw Candana fast asleep and spoke this verse:
"Excellent!"
"Canaka, rise quickly! Be mounted upon my horse-king Kāṃcana;
let us enter the mountain where all Buddhas practice, to seek the realization of the Unsurpassed Awakening of the Muni."
Having spoken this verse, Chandaka awoke from his sleep; he immediately rose, joined his palms, and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"There is no need for haste. Why do you urgently seek the King of Horses in the middle of the night, wishing to mount him and travel far away?"
"Moreover, within these palace precincts, there are currently no dangers from armies, no dangers from bandits, nor any dangers from water or fire;
why then do you act in such a manner? The Bodhisattva said, "Since time immemorial, you have always served me with diligent devotion; why then do you now fail to comply with me?"
Candaka replied, "It is now the middle of the night;
truth and falsehood are difficult to distinguish, and I fear some unforeseen mishap might bring about a great calamity.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva reflected in silence; fearing that others might perceive his intent, he went of his own accord to the inner stable.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, holding a torch in his hand, led the way forward; upon reaching the gate of the stable, he led forth the King of Horses, who immediately became terrified and stamped the ground with both hooves.

At that time, the Bodhisattva raised his hand—marked with the auspicious sign of ten thousand characters and possessing hundreds of thousands of majestic virtues—and forming the mudrā of fearlessness, he stroked the crown of the horse king’s head and said: “Kanthaka!

"You have a karmic affinity with me; if you can escort me to the places where the Buddhas practiced in the Snowy Mountains, so that I may realize the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi and let fall the great rain of Dharma to universally moisten the world, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, your merit will be immeasurable."
At that time, Kātyāyana immediately accepted the command, yet his body and feet remained unmoved.
Then there were four great deva-sons:
the first was named Kula;...
The second is named Upakula;
the third is named Parananda;
the fourth is named Paranashavati.
These four devaputras approached the Bodhisattva, joined their palms in reverence, and said to him:
"We now know that you have gone forth to cultivate the practice of bodhi; we, the four devas, wish to follow you."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Do you possess power?
The first heavenly son replied:
"The soil of the entire great earth can be carried away," said the second son.
"All the great oceans and rivers can be carried away," he said.
The third devaputra said,
"All mountains and peaks may be carried on one's back.
The fourth devaputra said:
"All the great earth, mountains, rivers, and oceans can be carried upon [his back] without fatigue.

Having heard this, the Bodhisattva immediately used his supernormal power to shift his feet and step upon the ground; the earth shook violently, and the four Great Heavenly Kings stood rooted to the spot, each struck with wonder:
"Who would have known that the Bodhisattva possessed such majestic power? How shall we, the Four Heavenly Kings, offer our apologies?"
At that time, when Chandaka beheld this supernatural power, he led the horse-king before the Bodhisattva.
Then, the devas of great majesty and the various nāgas and spirits, grieved by the sorrow of parting from their beloved, wept and shed tears from the sky above.
Cūḍapanthaka said,
"How can it rain from the sky when there are no clouds?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"This is not rain falling.
I am about to depart; the devas and nāgas, grieving at our parting, weep tears that fall like rain.
Cūḍapanthaka listened to these words, stood respectfully with palms joined.

The Bodhisattva immediately contemplated deeply the Buddha’s merits, majestic demeanor, and the dharmas that bring benefit and happiness; he further reflected upon the kindness of his parents in nurturing him with compassionate love and care, thinking that to depart without taking leave would be a failure in filial conduct.
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the palace and saw King Śuddhodana fast asleep. He circumambulated him once to the right, joined his palms, and addressed him, saying:

"At this time, I shall go into the Snowy Mountains to seek the unsurpassed path, in order to deliver the world from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and to enable all sentient beings to attain great liberation."
Having spoken thus, he took his leave.
At that time, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Mahānāma, who beheld the Prince and, filled with longing, distress, and grief, wept with tears streaming down his face, saying:
"Why, on account of karma, do you so lightly abandon the royal palace?"
The Prince replied,
"I seek the fruit of Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings. Mahānāma said:
"The King has commanded us to guard you for a long time, not allowing the Prince to leave the palace even for a moment.
The Prince replied, "In the past, I gave rise to the bodhicitta;

having passed through three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas and cultivated the myriad practices to seek unsurpassed enlightenment, desiring to deliver all sentient beings, this royal palace is no longer my dwelling place."
When Mahānāma heard these words, his distress and sorrow redoubled; weeping and wailing in grief, he uttered these harsh and pained words:
"Alas! Alas!"
"King Śuddhodana’s hopes have not been fulfilled; he has caused the Crown Prince to abandon the deep palace and set out on a distant journey.
When Yaśodharā heard these words, she was struck with alarm, doubt, and terror; she fainted and fell to the ground, regaining consciousness only after a long time.
He addressed the Prince, saying:
"For what reason do you abandon me today and depart?
Amṛtodgata, Mṛgarāja, and the various palace ladies proceeded forward with tears of sorrow and said to King Śuddhodana:

"The Crown Prince, for no apparent reason, wishes to leave the palace chambers and go to those mountain wilds; he is like one possessed by a malevolent spirit and cannot be restrained. Your Majesty alone must strictly admonish him not to go there in haste."

Having heard this, the King wished to issue his commands; however, Śakra, the King of the Devas, and Brahmā, together with the sons of the gods, came forth to welcome the Bodhisattva as he departed from the city.

To the Bodhisattva’s right stood the son of the gods from the Form Realm, Sudarśana, whose majestic deportment was sublime; to his left stood the son of the gods from the Desire Realm, holding banners and streamers. Countless celestial music preceded him as they led the way, while hundreds of thousands of sons of the gods rained down *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, white lotuses, and *mandārava* flowers from the midst of the void.
They further rained down aloeswood, powdered incense, sandalwood incense, and various kinds of exquisite, superior garments.

Furthermore, some sons of gods sang and danced, while others held the horse’s hooves in their hands; gazing up at the Bodhisattva, they followed him with single-minded devotion. Surrounded by and paid homage to by Kuvēra and countless other devas, in a mere moment they reached the Snowy Mountains, twelve yojanas from the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and Mahābrahmā, together with their retinues, joined their palms and said:

"We devas have aroused a mind of diligence and have followed and attended the Bodhisattva as he came to this mountain. When our Bodhisattva achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, we pray that you will graciously accept us and deliver us."
Standing to the right, he gazed up with single-minded devotion.
The Bodhisattva immediately spoke these verses for him:
"I have attained the supreme path, the sphere of action of all Buddhas."
"I shall deliver you all, as well as those other sentient beings.
Having spoken these words, he immediately removed his precious crown and exquisite garments, and said to Chandaka:
"Take my clothes and that horse-king back to offer to my father the king; unless I realize Bodhi, I vow never to return."
He further spoke in verse:
"Take the horse-king and the precious robes, and return quickly to your own land, Kapilavastu.
I shall remain on the Snowy Mountains to practice the holy life; I will not return until I have realized Bodhi."
When the Bodhisattva had finished speaking these verses, Cunda heard them and wept again in sorrow, saying:
"In this mountain there are many tigers, wolves, lions, and various other predatory beasts; how can the Bodhisattva remain alone here?"
"Furthermore, this mountain wilderness is filled with thickets, thorns, earth, stones, and barren soil; how can the Bodhisattva practice walking meditation here morning and evening?
The Bodhisattva said, "Cunda!"

How deluded and confused you are! The physical bodies of sentient beings are produced by the afflictions of karmic action; they are a confluence of the four great elements whose natures and characteristics are mutually opposed. When the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death arrive at the body, they do not discriminate between those of noble lineage and those of high birth, the wealthy and the poor, the beautiful and the ugly, the young and the old, or enemies and kin, self and others; all swiftly return to dissolution and decay, equally subject to impermanence.
"How does one practice so as to fear no perils? Cunda replied,
"The meaning of the Bodhisattva’s conduct is just like this."
"If the King should see me but not see the Prince, he will surely give rise to grief and distress, which may lead to a grave illness; what would such a matter be like?
The Bodhisattva said:

"I am now leaving the home life to practice the factors of enlightenment—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—and to achieve the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. How could I cause my parents to encounter anything inauspicious?"

Having spoken these words, he immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in homage, and with hands raised holding a sword like the petal of an *utpala* flower, he cut off his own hair and cast it into the midst of space.

Śakra, Lord of Devas, exercised his great supernormal power to catch the hair with his hand; together with the devaputras, he established it in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and made offerings to it according to the Dharma.
Later, faithful brahmins, elders, and householders erected a stūpa and temple upon this mountain site.
At that time, having cut off his topknot hair, the Bodhisattva asked Cunda:
"What is your intention?
Can you remain here and practice together with me?"
Channa said, "The will of the royal family does not permit me to remain here; how could I dare to stubbornly disobey?

The Bodhisattva then used his hand, marked with the auspicious sign of the *svastika* and endowed with hundreds of thousands of majestic virtues, to stroke the crown of the horse-king Kaṇṭhaka’s head and bestow upon him the prophecy of enlightenment, before sending Channa back to the city of Kapilavastu.

After traveling for seven days and nights, they arrived at a park outside the city at the beginning of the second watch. The King commanded his palace attendants and kinsmen to go to the park to receive him; however, they saw only the horse king and did not see the Prince.
At that time, the palace ladies and their attendants all went before the horse, embracing the neck of the horse-king and wailing aloud.
Hearing this sound of weeping, the horse Kāṇṭhaka thought of the Crown Prince; with tears of grief and deep sorrow, after a brief moment, he looked back to both sides and then passed away.

Due to past causes and conditions, he was born into a family of six-petaled *brāhmaṇas*; with sharp faculties and attenuated fetters, he was intelligent and possessed great wisdom. After the Prince attained Buddhahood, he went to the Buddha’s presence, heard the Dharma, realized the Way, and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected:
"I have now shaved my hair to assume the appearance of a śramaṇa; how shall I obtain a kāṣāya robe for my body?

Having thought thus, there was in the city of Anupama a householder whose kin and dependents were flourishing and whose wealth was immeasurable, like Vaiśravaṇa. He had ten sons, who were handsome in appearance, possessed of sharp wisdom, and all delighted in leaving the household life to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring. Because they observed that external objects are subject to constant change and flux, they became pratyekabuddhas.
After his father passed away, his aged mother became deeply devoted to the faith; she fashioned a *kāṣāya* robe and offered it as a gift to a *pratyekabuddha*.
The son said to his mother, "I shall soon enter into *nirvāṇa*."

"As for this kashaya robe, if I were to accept it, there would be no use for it. Not far from here dwells the son of King Śuddhodana named Siddhārtha; before long, he will attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Offer this kashaya to that Bodhisattva, so that I, an old woman, may obtain a great reward."

Having spoken these words, he exercised great supernatural power, manifesting clouds, thunder, lightning, wind, and rain in the midst of the sky; thereafter, he transformed his body into fire and entered the realm of parinirvāṇa.
At that time, as the old woman was about to pass away, she entrusted the robe she held to a daughter and instructed her to present it to the Bodhisattva.
Suddenly, this daughter fell ill; as the moment of her own death approached, she placed the robe upon a tree and addressed the tree deity, saying:
"Give this robe to me so that I may present it to Siddhārtha, the son of King Śuddhodana."

At that time, Śakra, having understood this matter, transformed his own body into that of a hunter; carrying a bow and sword in his hands and wearing the *kāṣāya*, he saw the Prince approaching and sat by the side of the road.
The Prince asked, "You are a hunter;
how is it that you have upon your person this exquisite Dharma robe of Kauśika silk? May you give it to me?"
The hunter replied, "I have no affection for this monastic robe; I wish to give it to you. However, as this garment is exquisite, I fear that others might seize it and take your life."
The Bodhisattva said, "All the world knows my power; you need only offer me the robe and harbor no anxiety.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately resumed his original form, prostrated himself at the Bodhisattva’s feet, and then offered the *kāṣāya* to him.
Having been given it, he immediately donned it, but it did not fit his body. When Śakra saw that the robe did not fit, doubt arose in his mind.
At the very moment he had this thought, through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, the kāṣāya robe became equal in size to his body.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven took refuge in it and made offerings; subsequently, brahmins and householders established a stūpa at that site, where bhikṣus constantly came and went to pay their respects.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, endowed with perfect deportment, was walking gradually when he saw a seer named Parigava, who rested his chin upon his hand with a displeased countenance.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What do you think? The rishi replied:

"I have a *tāla* tree in this dwelling of mine, its flowers and fruits were abundant, its flavor sweet and its fragrance fragrant; now it has suddenly withered and dried up, causing me great distress.

The Bodhisattva asked again, "The Rishi dwells here originally for the sake of spiritual cultivation; is it because the flowers and fruits have withered that you have fallen into such sorrow and vexation?"
Upon hearing this, the rishi’s mind suddenly awakened; seeing another bodhisattva of exquisite and majestic appearance, he gazed up at him with longing and asked again:
“Are you a renunciant bodhisattva?”
The Bodhisattva replied, "You have seen clearly.
Vārigava was immediately severed from his doubts and his Dharma-eye opened and purified; he invited the Bodhisattva to sit and made offerings of flowers and fruits according to the Dharma.
After a brief moment, the Bodhisattva asked again:
"How far is the city of Kapilavastu from here?
The seer replied:
"It is twelve yojanas from here to there.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"The city is not far away; if the Śākyas come, they will surely create obstacles for me."

He then took his leave of the rishi, crossed the Ganges River, and went to the city of Rājagṛha; there, using his own skillful craftsmanship, he fashioned alms bowls from tree leaves and entered the city carrying them.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, atop a high tower, saw from afar the Bodhisattva’s physical form, which was upright and majestic, and his deportment, which was tranquil. Seeing him wearing the Dharma robes upon his body and holding an alms-bowl in his hand as he went from door to door begging for food, the king uttered this sigh of admiration:
"Among all the people dwelling within the city of Rājagṛha, there is none with such dignified deportment and physical appearance."

This bhikṣu here is surely not of the commoner or low-born class; he must be one of royal lineage who has renounced his throne to leave the household life, extinguishing his sinful karma and practicing a pure livelihood.
At that time, the Bodhisattva took his bowl and left the city for a mountain. Placing his bowl on the ground, he sat upright and entered meditative absorption, reflecting:
"When King Bimbisāra sees my resolve, he will surely harbor a different intention."
While he was reflecting thus, the king said to his ministers:

"On the upper terrace, I saw a bhikṣu whose physical form was upright and dignified and whose deportment was harmonious and disciplined; he is certainly not born of the common folk or a lowly lineage."
"You must search for him and find out where he is now.
Immediately, the king dispatched a messenger to the mountains, who saw the bhikṣu sitting there with serene composure.
Once the king learned of this, he went in person to visit him; upon meeting and gazing upon him, his heart was filled with joy, and he addressed him, saying:

“Your physical appearance is most dignified and handsome; it would not be fitting for you to be a bhikṣu. I have palaces, towers, and pavilions, as well as consorts and beautiful women and the highest wealth and honor; enjoy these with me, and do not become a bhikṣu.”
"What is your family name?
To what lineage do you belong? Please tell me."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Near the Snowy Mountains there is the city of Kapilavastu; my father-king is of the Kṣatriya caste, named Śuddhodana, who currently governs this kingdom."
I must abandon my father and husband in order to seek Bodhi.
For one who is foolish and possessed by craving, even if the entire world and the four great oceans were filled with precious jewels, it would still not suffice;
just as a great fire burns dry wood, so too does craving consume the body and mind.
"Great King!
I regard these things as if they were enemies, or like venomous snakes—the very root of all sorrow, affliction, and fear.
Great King!"
Even if a great wind could blow and shake all the mountains, it could never move Mount Sumeru;

even if all the rare treasures and supreme wealth in the world—kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, servants, and attendants—could delude and distract the minds of all people, they could never move my mind. Only nirvana and liberation are the ultimate reality.
At that time, King Bimbisāra said,
"What do you seek here now?
The Bodhisattva replied:
“I seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The King said,
“If you attain enlightenment, I pray that you will grant me your acceptance.”
The Bodhisattva replied: "So it is! So it is!"
The king was filled with joy and returned to his own abode.
At that time, the Bodhisattva went to Vulture Peak Mountain; not far from the mountain’s side lived a seer who diligently practiced the holy life, able to stand upon one foot for an entire day.
Hearing of this, the Bodhisattva likewise stood upon one foot for two days.
The seer again stood for one day with his body scorched by the five heats;
the Bodhisattva then stood for two days.
At that time, those seers were struck with mutual wonder and, having been subdued, offered their praise:
"This is their practice; this is the Great Śramaṇa!
The Bodhisattva asked, "In what do you seek through your practice?"
One said, "I seek Śakra. Another said:
"I seek the state of a Brahma King," one said; another said,
"I seek the body of a Mara."
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflected to himself:
"The practices cultivated by this seer are all false paths; they are not what I rely upon."
I now seek neither Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor the realm of Māra here; rather, for the sake of my original vow to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings, I seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
"Since the Way is not the truth, you ought to abandon it.
The Sutra of the Mahāsudarśana Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
The Sutra of the Mahāsudarśana Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharma Xian, Grand Master of Illuminating Teaching (Mingjiao Dashi), Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Shaqing), and Imperially Ennobled Subject, during the Song Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva went to the place of Ārāḍa Kālāma to study the path of the Dharma. Upon arrival, he joined his palms and respectfully inquired after him with great earnestness.
“What is the meaning of the Dharma you practice?

Āḷāra Kālāma replied, “In the past, I diligently cultivated concentration and wisdom until I attained complete mastery of all the samādhi-gates up to the heaven of perception; why do you not know this?”
The Bodhisattva immediately reflected:
"The wisdom attained by Rāma, as well as the samādhi-gates of the Heaven of Perception, are truly real and not false."
Again, he thought to himself:
"Why have I not yet attained this Dharma?
In the space of a single kṣaṇa, his meditative concentration and wisdom were both fully realized, and he spoke these words:
"I have now attained the Dharma of your school's practice.

At that time, Ārāḍa Kālāma observed that the Dharma attained by the Bodhisattva was true and without error; he then respected and honored him as his own original teacher, making offerings with the utmost sincerity of the finest incense, flowers, and rare fruits.
The Bodhisattva further reflected:
"This current practice of the Dharma has not yet reached its ultimate goal; it is not the true path.
He then departed and went to the place of Udraka Rāmaputra to study the practice of the Dharma.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself, joined his palms, and asked:
"Regarding the Dharma you have attained, what is its meaning?
Then Udraka Rāmaputra replied:
"In the past, I diligently cultivated wisdom and attained long ago the samādhi-door of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; why do you not know this?"
Having heard this, the bodhisattva immediately observed that the wisdom cultivated by that person and their samādhi-door of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception were without error;
he then reflected to himself: "Why have I not yet attained these dharmas?"
When he had this thought, they both attained accomplishment simultaneously, whereupon [the Buddha] said:
"I have now also attained the Dharma-practice you possess.

At that time, Udraka Rāmaputra did not yet believe or accept this; however, after observing with a focused mind, he saw it was true and without error, and thus he revered and made offerings to him even more than to his own former teacher.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected to himself:
"This practice of the Dharma is not yet ultimate; it is not the path to true awakening. I must quickly abandon it and seek another clear path."
At that time, King Śuddhodana, presiding over the main hall, recollected the Crown Prince; not knowing his whereabouts, he was filled with anxiety and distress.
A close minister reported:
"He has departed from the city of Rājagṛha and gone to the place of Udraka Rāmaputra; standing alone and solitary, he diligently seeks the Way."
Having heard this, the king’s heart was filled with profound sorrow, and he immediately dispatched three hundred of his own attendants to serve as his retinue.
At that time, King Subhāṣitabuddha of Devaṅguli also sent two hundred men to serve as his retinue.
When these five hundred people arrived,
they prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and gazed up at him with reverence.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Having abandoned the royal palace to dwell in mountain seclusion, I have resolved to practice for the sake of seeking the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta*).

Now, these crowds of people, noisy and distracting day and night, obstruct the Noble Path; therefore, let only five—my paternal uncles and maternal uncles—remain, and send all others back to their own country."
