The Bodhisattva immediately took these five men and went to the village of the seer Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, to a nearby place for walking meditation, sightseeing, and practicing tranquility.
Along the Nairañjanā River, he saw a forest grove where the ground was level and even, and the trees were secluded and serene; it was as cool as the moon and was called a sacred site.
He addressed the five men, saying:
"Virtuous sons!
"If a person practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*) here, they will soon realize the unconditioned peace (*śānti*) that has not yet been realized;

I now rely upon this place to seek the unsurpassed path. Thereupon, he sat cross-legged beneath the tree, training in meditative observation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*). He clenched his teeth, pressed his tongue against the upper palate, and withdrew his mind and spirit as if grasping an object in his hand. After a long while, sweat broke out from his pores; with diligence unflagging and mindfulness and concentration in accord, he focused his mind one-pointedly, inducing the untainted state (*anāsrava*), though it did not yet manifest in active function.

Furthermore, he practiced a distinct meditation, sitting in the full lotus posture with his mouth closed, eyes shut, and tongue pressed against the upper palate. He held his breath so that it neither entered nor exited; after a long while, the suppressed air pressed upon the crown of his head with such extreme pain that it was as if needles were piercing his brain. Though he endured this great suffering, his mind remained free from inversion and undistracted. With firm and resolute diligence, mindfulness and concentration became manifest; focusing his mind one-pointedly, he induced the untainted state (*anāsrava*) though it did not yet manifest in active function.
As he thus gradually moved the breath, it descended from the crown of his head down to the openings of his two ears; the pain increased further, like the suffering of hell.

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind was neither inverted nor distracted; with fierce and intense diligence, mindfulness and concentration were present before him. He focused his mind one-pointedly, inducing the untainted state (*anāsrava*), though it had not yet become manifest.

Furthermore, he closes his breath and externally forgets all seeing and hearing; as the vital energy accumulates within the viscera and fills his entire body, the suffering reaches its ultimate limit, beyond any comparison. At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind is neither inverted nor distracted; he practices with firm perseverance, and mindfulness and concentration manifest before him. With single-minded focus, he brings forth the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, though it does not yet manifest in active operation.
Having practiced in this way, he further reflected to himself:
"From this day forward, I shall abstain from food and drink.
At that time, a son of heaven, having perceived this from afar, addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Within the pores of this physical body of mine, there are exquisite and sublime celestial foods fit for offering.
The Bodhisattva replied, "The food I consume is fundamentally not pungent or acrid; the food emerging from your body is likewise not pure. If I were to eat it, I would surely fall into hell."
"O Son of Heaven!
Whatever is available in each region—whether rice or beans—I permit you to offer according to your means, whether in abundance or scarcity; I shall accept it."
The devaputra followed his instructions and provided him with grain as food.

After the Bodhisattva had eaten, his body became emaciated and his countenance grew haggard; yet his mind was free from suffering and affliction, and he experienced no regression. He aroused the intent of diligence, brought mindfulness and concentration before him, and focused his mind with single-minded devotion. Although he induced the state of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), it did not yet manifest in active operation.

Furthermore, as he restricted his food, his body became increasingly emaciated and frail; his two eyes sank deep into their sockets like stars appearing in a well. At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mind was free from suffering and affliction, nor did he experience any regression. He aroused a spirit of diligence, brought mindfulness and concentration to the fore, and focused his mind with single-minded intent; thus he induced the untainted state (*anāsrava*), yet it did not yet manifest in active operation.

Furthermore, he reduced his food intake until it was extremely meager—perhaps a single bean, a single sesame seed, a single grain of rice, or a single grain of barley. Having eaten such things, his physical strength grew increasingly depleted; whether walking or stepping, he would rise up only to fall down again.

At that time, the Bodhisattva practiced with diligence without retreat; mindfulness and concentration were present before him, and he focused his mind single-pointedly. Although this induced the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), it did not yet manifest as active conduct.
He then reflected:
"This practice is not ultimate; it has not reached the final goal."

While he was reflecting thus, three sons of gods approached the Bodhisattva; seeing his physical form emaciated and transformed, they each described the Bodhisattva’s countenance differently—some saying it was black, others that it was purple-green.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva reflected again to himself:
"Though I have undergone such diligent austerities in this place, my complexion has changed and I have gained nothing at all.
If one seeks perfect enlightenment, why rely on restricting one's food?"
When one is endowed with right view and is able to forget both grasping and rejecting, this is true Bodhi; this is the ultimate reality.
It is like damp firewood: though its substance is moist, if it encounters fire, it will inevitably produce blazing flames.
Furthermore, just as a member of the brahmin caste may engage in sensual desire yet remain free from attachment in mind and thereby attain liberation, so too am I now:
if I act in accordance with the True Dharma without attachment, I shall certainly realize Bodhi.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, learning that the Prince was diligently practicing austerities in the mountains and wilds, subsisting on a daily diet of hemp and wheat in his quest for the Unsurpassed Way, wept with tears of sorrow and, filled with deep anguish, dispatched two hundred and fifty attendants each from himself and King Suprabuddha to serve and protect him.
At that time, Yaśodharā suddenly became pregnant; the King immediately issued a proclamation:
"From this day forward, none of the palace ladies or attendants shall speak of the Prince’s austerities in the mountains, for I fear it might cause her distress and harm the child in her womb."

At that time, the Bodhisattva went to the Śītavana forest and lay down on his right side, resting his head upon a corpse with his feet stacked one above the other, contemplating how conditioned phenomena in the world arise and perish, circling like ants in an endless cycle without end.
Having reflected thus, he sat down again and entered *samādhi*.

At that time, some boys and girls came to the foot of the forest and beheld the Bodhisattva sitting with his eyes closed and motionless; they took sticks in their hands and pierced through both sides of the Bodhisattva’s ears.
They all spoke these words:
"This dust-dwelling ghost must not be approached.
They then threw sand, gravel, and potsherds at the Bodhisattva’s body and each departed.
After a brief moment, he emerged from samādhi; right mindfulness was present before him, and his body and mind were unmoving. He further reflected:
"What I have just done is not the correct practice; it is not in accord with the unsurpassed path."

I recall that in the past, when I was a crown prince, I briefly left the royal palace and went beneath a Jambū tree to enter samādhi. That place was pure and far removed from the defilement of sin; free from all impurities and evils, it gave rise to roots of goodness, and there I practiced until the fruit of the Path was surely perfected.

Having formed this thought, he immediately attempted to rise and move forward with his whole body; however, his strength being weak and depleted, he was unable to do so. He then took the food and drink, as well as the medicinal decoctions, and consumed them in their proper sequence. Furthermore, he anointed his body with fragrant oil, bathed, and slept, thereby bringing peace and comfort to his body and mind and increasing his vital energy.
Then those five men said to one another:
"In the past, the Prince renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, left the city of Kapilavastu, and entered the mountains and wilds to practice asceticism for a long time here."

When the fruit of the Path is about to be attained, if one’s resolve is not firm, how could one expect that at this time one would indulge in food and drink, smear fragrant oils upon the body, bathe oneself, and sleep in ease?
To suffer such decline and loss—how can one hope for liberation?

"We have wasted our efforts here in vain. We have heard that in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī there is a Deer Park where a community of noble Arhats constantly resides; we should go to that place and each seek the path of illumination."

At that time, the Bodhisattva bathed in the waters of the Nairañjanā River; his body was emaciated and his strength was weak, so he found it difficult to take even a single step. He reached out and grasped a branch from a tree on the bank to pull himself out, and then proceeded toward the village of Senānī.
Within that village there were two young girls:
the first was named Nanda,
and the second was named Nandamāla.
Her physical form was upright and beautiful, and her mind was kind and compassionate.

She had recently heard that the Prince was dwelling at the abode of the seer Kapila by the banks of the Bhagirathī River at the foot of the Snowy Mountains, where he was training in and practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Possessing the thirty-two marks and adorned with merit and virtue, she felt deep admiration and longing for him, wishing to become his consort; thus, she practiced giving and cultivated merit in the hope of fulfilling her wish.

At that time, having heard that there was an ascetic seer by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, the young girl resolved with diligent sincerity to offer him milk porridge. She immediately divided a thousand cows into two herds;

she milked five hundred cows and fed their milk to another five hundred. She then divided those five hundred into two herds; she milked two hundred and fifty cows and fed their milk to another two hundred and fifty.

Continuing this process of division and feeding until she reached eight cows, she milked those eight cows for the most concentrated and rich milk. Using a crystal vessel, she cooked the milk into a porridge, upon which appeared the *śrīvatsa* mark and the sign of a thousand-spoked wheel.
At that time, a certain person, seeing this mark of the wheel, thought to himself:
"If a person obtains this food, they will swiftly realize the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
He then addressed the young girl:
"I am now hungry and thirsty; you should give me some gruel and rice as alms.
The young girl replied, "I have prepared this food to offer to an ascetic seer; it is not for you to take."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa and stood before the woman; the woman wished to give him the milk porridge as an offering.
The brāhmaṇa said, "I do not dare to accept it."
"There is a Great Being, a Lord of the World, who is worthy of being honored.
The young girl asked again,
"Who is this Lord of the World?"
The brahmin said,
"Not far from here dwells the Great Brahmā King.
Accepting these words, the young girl went to that place and offered him the rice gruel.
The Great Brahmā King said, "I do not dare to accept it.
There is a Devaputra named Pure Light (Vimalaprabha), who is most supreme and excellent; you should offer it to him."
The woman went to him again and offered him gruel as an act of charity.
The Devaputra Viśuddhaprabha said,
"I do not dare to accept it."

There was a bodhisattva bathing in the Nairañjanā River who, his body exhausted of strength, grasped a tree with his hand and emerged onto the riverbank; there he donned the kashaya robe, intending to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
"If one can make offerings, one shall obtain great benefit.
Upon hearing this, the young girl immediately hurried there and, filling her bowl with gruel, offered it with devout heart.
The Bodhisattva accepted her offering in silence.

Having finished eating, he cast his bowl into the Nairañjanā River. A nāga king approached to retrieve the bowl, but Śakra, having transformed himself into a garuḍa, caused the nāga to retreat in alarm. Śakra then recovered the bowl and placed it in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he erected a stūpa to make offerings to it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva asked the two maidens,
"In making this offering of milk-rice, what do you seek?
The maidens replied:

"I have heard that near the Snowy Mountains, on the banks of the river Bāhīkā, at the dwelling of the seer Kapila, there is a youth of King Śuddhodana whose physical marks are so dignified and handsome that he is destined to become a Wheel-Turning Monarch; I wish to seek him as my husband."
The Bodhisattva replied:
"That youth has long cultivated the pure conduct of celibacy and is free from desire; he is named Sarvārthasiddha. Before long, he shall attain enlightenment. How could he be your husband?"
Having heard this, the maiden stood silent.

The Bodhisattva raised his entire body and ascended a rocky mountain that was steep, solitary, and towering, where trees grew in great abundance; he sat there peacefully, and before even a single hour had passed, the mountain collapsed.
The Bodhisattva was struck with wonder, asking, "What karmic conditions have brought this about?

At that time, the Devaputra Pure Light addressed the Bodhisattva, saying, "The ten thousand practices are now perfected and the four wisdoms are about to be attained; yet this ground possesses meager merit and cannot sustain you."
"Not far from here is the Vajrāsana, the place where the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time attain perfect enlightenment.

The Bodhisattva then proceeded there; as celestial beings led him forward, lotuses sprang up beneath his feet, the ocean tides surged, and the great earth shook with a resonance like the striking of a bell.

The Bodhisattva walked slowly until he reached a great cave where a black dragon resided; the dragon had formerly been blind, but upon hearing the earth tremble and the ocean tide surge, it immediately emerged from its lair, its two eyes suddenly becoming clear. It beheld the Bodhisattva’s physical form, which was dignified and majestic, with a radiance surpassing that of a massed sun.
The dragon was filled with great joy; gazing up at him with longing and veneration, he spoke in verse:
"The earth quakes and the ocean tides roar together; Hearing this, I have swiftly left my palace.
Suddenly obtaining this radiance, I behold the Tathāgata; Gazing upon him with a single mind, I give rise to joy."
At that time, the Dragon King said to the Bodhisattva:
"I recall that in the past, when a Buddha appeared in the world, both my eyes attained clarity and I beheld that World-Honored One;
now it is likewise, for once again my eyes have opened and I behold the physical marks of the Buddha’s body."
He then spoke in verse:
“In the past, I relied upon the Buddha’s great majestic power, Which enabled me to behold his body of marks and signs;
I shall surely meet the Muni who has perfected the path of awakening, And seeing the Buddha’s sublime countenance shall be just like this.”

At that time, as the Bodhisattva was about to reach the Vajrāsana, he first raised his right foot and proceeded like a bull-king. His body was like a mountain of jewels, his *kāṣāya* robe remained motionless, and his mind was equal to space. His face was like the full moon, radiant with golden light, and he carried within him the great medicine of the Dharma. Auspicious birds and strange beasts circled him to the right; such were the ten kinds of auspicious omens.
The Bodhisattva thought:
"I shall spread kusha grass upon the Vajrāsana.

Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of Devas, immediately manifested a transformation body and went to Mount Gandhamādana to fetch the kusha grass; that grass was as soft as tūla-cotton, and he brought it before the Bodhi tree and laid it upon the Vajrāsana.
At that time, the Bodhisattva raised his body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, ascended the diamond throne, sat cross-legged, and made this vow:
"I shall not rise from this seat until all outflows are exhausted."
With right intention and focused mind, he entered samādhi.
At that time, there were two kinds of banners within the palace of Māra:
the first was named "Sign of Joy," and the second was named "Sign of Doubt."
Movement always signifies something.

At that time, the banner of the signs of doubt suddenly began to flutter; seeing this, Māra was struck with alarm and suspicion, fearing some inauspicious event. He immediately engaged in contemplation and realized that Prince Siddhārtha, son of King Śuddhodana, was seated upon the Vajrāsana seeking unsurpassed enlightenment.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas gave rise to a heart of jealousy; he transformed himself into a human being and forged a letter from King Śuddhodana, arriving before the Bodhisattva to pay his respects and inquire:
"Why do you remain here so long without returning?"
Devadatta entered the Prince’s palace, where he acted lawlessly at will and killed members of the Śākya clan.
Upon first hearing this, the Bodhisattva gave rise to three kinds of unwholesome thoughts:
he pondered upon lust, the slaughter of his kinsmen, and the arousal of anger.
Recognizing these as the deeds of Māra, he further accomplished three virtues:
first, detachment from desire; second, non-killing; and third, freedom from anger.
Māra questioned him again, saying:
“How is it that you sit beneath this Bodhi tree?
The Buddha said,
“I seek unsurpassed wisdom.”
The Māra said,
"How have you attained unsurpassed wisdom?
The Buddha replied:
“You are a person guilty of demonic transgressions; yet by providing a single offering to a brāhmaṇa, you still obtain such sovereign retribution.

I have passed through three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, relinquishing countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of heads, eyes, marrow, brains, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, gold, silver, and precious jewels, seeking unsurpassed wisdom for the benefit of sentient beings. How could I not attain it?”
The Māra said:
"I have established a Brahmin who has attained wealth, nobility, and sovereignty; you can serve as his witness.
But as for you, who throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas have sacrificed your head, eyes, marrow, and brain to benefit sentient beings and seek unsurpassed wisdom—who is your witness?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, while seated upon the diamond throne, extended his right hand—marked with the thousand-spoked wheel and webbed fingers—and formed the mudrā of fearlessness, touching the surface of the ground, saying:
"Bear witness for me."
At that time, the Earth Deity emerged from the ground and, joining her palms, proclaimed:

"O Māra! Our Buddha, in the past, throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, sacrificed countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of heads, eyes, marrow, brains, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, gold, silver, and precious jewels to benefit sentient beings and seek supreme wisdom. This is true and not false; you, Māra, need have no doubt."
Upon hearing this, the Māra was struck with terror and thought to himself:
"If the Bodhisattva attains enlightenment, he will invade my realm and seize my majestic splendor."
He immediately returned to his celestial palace and devised a demonic stratagem.

He transformed himself into three women, exquisite and majestic in appearance, who approached the Buddha; they moved with graceful and languid steps, feigning reverence while intending to bewitch him with their charms.

By his supernatural power, the Buddha transformed himself into an old woman with white hair, wrinkled face, and a haggard, emaciated appearance; when she looked into a mirror, she withdrew in shame. Upon seeing this, the Māra King regretted that his purpose had failed and felt intense mental anguish.

Immediately, he led thirty-six *koṭis* of ghostly and demonic generals, clad in armor and wielding various weapons such as spears, swords, bows, crossbows, and nooses. He further gathered venomous dragons, fierce beasts, elephants, horses, water buffaloes, tigers, wolves, jackals, and other creatures, who rushed together to join him. Moreover, he manifested clouds, thunder, lightning, thunderbolts, wind, and hail in the sky, assailing and harassing [the Buddha] from all four directions at once.

The Buddha gazed upon them with his Buddha-eye, taking pity on their ignorance and delusion, and entered the samādhi of loving-kindness. Immediately, the Pure Radiance Deva-son manifested a great parasol in the void of space that covered the entire sky, shielding against wind, hail, swords, spears, bows, arrows, and all manner of weapons, which were all transformed into celestial flowers—namely, *utpala* flowers, *padma* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *pāṇḍarīka* flowers—which circled the Vajrāsana as an offering to the Buddha.

Immediately, through the power of supernatural faculties within samādhi, he merged many into one and made one into many; he walked, stood, sat, and lay down in the midst of the void sky; water issued from the upper part of his body while fire issued from the lower part; and he walked upon water as if it were solid ground, and so forth.

Having performed these various miraculous transformations, he further observed the wrong views, doubts, greed, hatred, and delusion of that assembly of *puṇḍarīkas*, as well as those sentient beings who were free from desire or possessed of desire, those with perception or without perception, and those in the stages leading to the proximate deliverances—whether they were liberated or not—and thus he thoroughly and clearly understood all such phenomena.

By means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), he observes the past parents of sentient beings such as Māra—through one life, two lives, a hundred lives, a thousand lives, and even through eons of increase and decrease, and incalculable eons—including their worlds, lands, clans, lineages, and retinues; whether they were wealthy or poor, noble or lowly, long-lived or short-lived, and their deaths and rebirths—all these he knows and realizes without exception.

By means of the supernormal power of the divine eye, he clearly and thoroughly perceives the future destinies of sentient beings such as Māra, as well as their birth and death, the causes and effects of karma, and their wholesome and unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, including the excellence or inferiority of the retributions they receive.
Furthermore, he reflected:

"Regarding the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, as well as the characteristics of the four truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—whether defiled or pure, whether conceptual or innate, there are the primary afflictions and their secondary derivatives."

Having reflected thus, his untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) swiftly manifested before him; seeing that the two paths of vision and cultivation were to be abandoned simultaneously and would no longer arise, he attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that moment, the hosts of Māra immediately retreated and dispersed. He then addressed King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Prince Siddhārtha has attained impermanence upon the Vajra Seat."
Having heard this, the King, together with his retinue, wept and lamented in grief and distress, fainting and falling to the ground.
At that time, a celestial being addressed King Śuddhodana:
"The Prince has already attained unsurpassed Bodhi."
Upon hearing these words, the king was greatly delighted in his heart.
It was further reported to him that King Amṛtodana had fathered a son.
Yaśodharā also gave birth to a son.
All the King’s kinsmen and attendants were filled with great joy.
At that time, King Śuddhodana commanded his ministers and officials:

"Have the streets, lanes, and alleys swept clean and sprinkled with water; burn various exquisite incenses and erect banners and streamers; and at the four gates of the city, gather gold, silver, precious gems, and all kinds of wealth to bestow as gifts upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and followers of other paths, as well as upon the poor and beggars, thereby creating merit and blessings."
"When King Amṛtodana gave birth to a son, his kinsmen were filled with joy and named him Ānanda.
When Yaśodharā gave birth to a son, there was an eclipse of the moon, so he was named Rāhula."
At that time, King Śuddhodana said,
"Yaśodharā’s son is not of the Buddha's lineage.
Having heard this, Yaśodharā constantly harbored grief and distress.
On a rock by the shore of a pond in the rear garden of the royal palace, known as the Bodhisattva Rock, Rāhula was sitting and playing.
His mother suddenly saw him and made a vow:
"If he is of the Buddha’s lineage, may he not be drowned; if he is not of the Buddha’s lineage, let him sink beneath the water."
Having made this vow, he pushed the rock with his hand; the boy also fell along with it, yet the rock floated upon the surface of the water while the boy continued to play.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue, came to the shore and, seeing his son in such a state, was filled with great joy and praised him, saying:
“Excellent!”
"It is truly rare!

At that moment, the great earth shook, and the Buddha’s light shone universally upon all dark places; all sentient beings were able to see one another and took refuge, prostrating themselves in worship.
The Sūtra of the Great King Mahāsudarśana Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six;
The Sūtra of the Great King Mahāsudarśana Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafa, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor and Great Master Dharma-bhadra, by Imperial Decree:
At that time, there were two sons of Brahmā who, dwelling in their own Brahma realm, had this thought:

"Now, in Jambudvīpa in the south, there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has attained equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River beside the Uruvilvā pool."
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, sat cross-legged beneath a tree and entered the realm of fire for seven days and nights.
At that time, the two Brahmā deities said to one another:
"We gods and humans also possess great power; we could reach that place in the time it takes to extend an arm. We should now go there quickly and offer praise and entreaty with sublime verses."

Thereupon, the two devas departed swiftly from that Brahma realm and arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling. After circumambulating him, gazing upon him, and completing their respectful salutations, they stood before the Buddha.
Then, one of the sons of heaven first praised and entreated him with a verse, saying:
“May the Buddha arise from beneath the Bodhi tree To rescue and deliver the realms of sentient beings!”
To preach the supreme Dharma, so that they may attain the jewel of the Dharma of wisdom.
The second son of heaven also spoke a verse, praising and entreating him, saying:
“The Buddha’s face is like the full moon; his mind is pure and afflictions removed.”
"May you preach the Dharma of ambrosia, which brings peace and happiness to the world.
Having spoken these verses in praise and made this request to the Buddha, the two Brahma sons vanished from sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from that meditative concentration, surveyed the world, and spoke these verses:
"All the sensual pleasures found in the world, Even all the pleasures found in the heavens—
Compared to the great bliss of severing craving, They do not equal even one-sixteenth part."
He further spoke in verse:
"Bearing the heavy burden of worldly suffering, One is deluded by suffering and does not relinquish it;
If one relinquishes this heavy burden of suffering, One is able to bear the supreme bliss."
He further spoke in verse:
“One who can sever all craving in the world And cause all afflictions to naturally subside—
Knowing the nature of afflictions, such a one escapes saṃsāra And shall attain the bliss of liberation.”
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged for seven days and nights, entering into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

During this interval, there was no one who brought food as an offering. Just after he had spoken these verses, a merchant leader named Poṣadhavāraka suddenly appeared, leading five hundred wagons laden with various precious goods, intending to travel to another country and passing through the vicinity.
At that time, Puṣpavālika, by the power of his roots of merit from previous lives, constantly gave rise to this thought:
"How may I obtain virtuous friends and an excellent retinue?"
Suddenly he heard someone say,
"The World-Honored One has entered meditative concentration for seven days, neither drinking nor eating.
Upon hearing this, he thought to himself:

"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is at the foot of the Bodhi tree by the side of the Nairañjanā River near Lake Uruvilvā; having gone without drink or food for seven days and nights, he has entered meditative concentration, attained the bliss of liberation, and realized perfect enlightenment."
"This is my virtuous friend; he shall surely bring me benefit.
I should now go to him quickly and offer food as the highest act of worship.

Having formed this thought, a certain deva, through his supernormal power of divine hearing, became aware that Puṣyavarman had conceived such an intention. He then surveyed Puṣyavarman and all the chariots and vehicles he was leading, and first addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Now the caravan leader Puṣpabali, having heard that the Buddha is here and has attained the bliss of liberation, having realized perfect enlightenment and sat cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree, entering into meditative concentration for seven days and nights without drinking or eating—he will surely come to offer food as an act of worship, seeking the fruit of his merit and desiring great peace, happiness, and benefit."
Having spoken these words, he vanished from sight.

Thereupon, Puṣpavaliyaka, together with his companions and friends, prepared various kinds of food and drink with their own hands; once they had completed these exquisite, fragrant, and pure delicacies, he focused his mind with devotion and offered them to the Buddha.
Before reaching the Buddha’s dwelling, they again formed this thought:
“We now present this food as the supreme offering; the Tathāgata will surely expound the supreme Dharma, so that by the cause of our offering food, we may obtain the fruit of celestial bliss.”

Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was and prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata. Having paid homage, he stood up and remained there gazing up at him.
Then, Poṣapālaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I have prepared various kinds of food and drink with my friends and relatives to come and offer as alms; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will deign to accept them.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent but did not yet receive them.
For what reason?
When the Buddha first attained the Way, there were no alms bowls.
He reflected thus:
"If I were not to accept this offering with my alms-bowl, those externalists and Māras would surely give rise to slander, saying:
'How could it be that the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past accepted such offerings for the sake of benefiting sentient beings?'"
When the Buddha had this thought, that Brahmā son addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past all carried alms bowls to receive offerings of food and drink from donors.”

Thereupon, as the World-Honored One contemplated the need for alms-bowls, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, immediately perceiving the Buddha’s intention, each commanded skilled artisans within their own respective heavens to select precious gems. In a short time, they fashioned the bowls, which were pure, translucent, and of incomparable excellence.
When the Four Heavenly Kings had completed the bowls, each took one and came together to offer them.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they immediately prostrated themselves with their heads at the World-Honored One’s feet; having paid homage, they gazed up at him and stood to one side.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings addressed the World-Honored One with one voice:
"We have each fashioned an alms bowl from precious gems and have come together to offer them to you."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will,
out of compassion, graciously accept [this offering].
Having spoken these words, he waited expectantly for the Buddha’s instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One further reflected to himself:
"Now these four kings each offer a bowl; if I accept only one, three of them will be displeased;
if I accept three, one king will feel resentment."
"I shall now equally accept the bowls of the four devas.
Having accepted the bowls, he further reflected:
"If only one vessel is used, which of the four bowls should come first?"
Thereupon, by means of his supernatural power, he joined the four bowls into one; although the four vessels were joined, their rims remained distinct and layered.
Then, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the World-Honored One took this bowl to the place of Puṣpabhārika and accepted the alms-food offered there.
Having accepted [the teachings], he then said to Puṣyavarman:
"I shall now expound for you the Three Refuges; you should receive them with careful attention.
At that time, Puṣyavarman remained there, respectfully following the instruction.
The World-Honored One said:
"Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha of the future.
These are the Three Refuges; for as long as your life lasts, you must not violate or regret them."
Then Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the future Saṃgha; for as long as this life lasts, I shall not dare to violate or regret [this vow].”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa Śailaka, saying:

"The fruit of rejoicing in giving is never in vain; you have personally practiced generosity and will certainly obtain happiness. Whatever blessings and rewards you seek shall all be attained according to your vows, and you shall likewise realize the supreme tranquility."
Pūrṇa! If one practices giving, the merit and benefit produced therein cannot be confounded by humans, devas, or Māras; this extends even to meditative concentration and wisdom.
If one can practice them all to the full, one can exhaust the source of suffering and realize the state of an Arya before one's very eyes.
At that time, having heard these words, Posālapurika felt his heart rejoice and he leaped for joy, saying:
"May I, in future ages, remember, uphold, and never forget this."
Having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.

At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the food offered by the merchant leader Puṣpabharika; he then took it and went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River, where he spread grass upon the shore and sat down to eat the food he had received.
When the meal was finished and he had once again washed and rinsed his mouth, at that moment he suddenly felt a wind-disorder arise within his body.
Why was this? The Buddha appeared in the world and manifested this as a condition in order to cause sentient beings to know that the body is like an illusion.

At that time, the celestial Māra feared that the Buddha would appear in the world to teach and transform sentient beings so that they might escape the three realms, thereby leaving his own domain empty; he constantly watched for an opportunity to come and cause confusion and disorder.
Suddenly learning that the Buddha was ill, he quickly departed from the celestial realm and came to where the Buddha was, saying: "Sugata!
You are now unwell, and the time for your parinirvāṇa has arrived; I now entreat the Buddha to enter great parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that this Māra had come with the intent to disturb his mind, addressed Māra, saying: "My parinirvāṇa has not yet arrived.

I shall now simply wait until my śrāvaka disciples have mastered the divisions of the Buddha-dharma, possess clear and penetrating wisdom, and fully understand the root of the teachings; until they extensively expound the characteristics of the Dharma; and until bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās practice the holy life (brahmacarya), and many people throughout the great earth, as well as those among devas and humans, all realize liberation. Only at such a time will I enter parinirvāṇa."
When that celestial Māra heard the Buddha’s words and realized he would not enter parinirvāṇa, his heart was filled with distress; thus, the celestial Māra withdrew in shame.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived from afar that the World-Honored One was afflicted by a wind-related ailment. Descending from the heavens to Jambudvīpa, he went to a grove of large *harītakī* trees located neither too near nor too far from the Bodhi tree and stayed therein.
Having gathered some excellent *harītakī* fruits from within this grove, he quickly proceeded to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head to the ground, paying homage at the World-Honored One’s feet. Having paid homage, he gazed up at him and stood to one side, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

"I know that Your Holy Body has a slight wind ailment; in this Jambudvīpa there is the harītakī fruit, which is exquisite in color and fragrant in scent, and can cure this malady. I have now brought it here to offer to the World-Honored One; I pray only that, out of great compassion, you will accept and partake of it."
The World-Honored One accepted it and immediately partook of it; his wind ailment was instantly cured, and his body became as comfortable as before.
The World-Honored One comforted him, and Śakra then withdrew and returned to his celestial palace.
At that time, the World-Honored One again departed from the Bodhi tree and went to the palace of the Naga King Mucilinda.
Having arrived at that palace, he sat cross-legged beneath a tree and entered into meditative concentration.

At that time, it rained heavily for seven days and seven nights. Then the Naga King Mucilinda, perceiving that the Buddha was in meditative absorption while the rain was falling, feared that the wind and rain might disturb the Buddha’s body, and further feared that mosquitoes, gnats, gadflies, and flies might vex his holy form. He therefore coiled his own body around [the Buddha] seven times and raised his head to cover him above, like the shape of a parasol;
for seven days and nights, he remained without moving or shaking.
As the Buddha was about to emerge from meditative absorption, the nāga withdrew its body.
The nāga king returned to his palace, again adorned his body with various flower garlands and fragrant ointments, and came to where the Buddha was; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he said:
“World-Honored One!”
"During these past seven days, has there been any disturbance from wind, rain, mosquitoes, or gadflies?
How is your holy body?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Observing all sentient beings in the world,
If one attains freedom from harm, One rejoices and is filled with happiness.
This bliss of renouncing desire and severing afflictions Is beyond comparison."
"If ignorance is subdued, this is the supreme bliss.

At that time, having spoken these verses in response to the Dragon King, the World-Honored One departed from that place and returned to beneath the Bodhi tree. There he sat cross-legged for seven days and nights, entering meditative concentration to observe the twelve links of dependent origination: how do they arise, with what as their root and what as their cause?

That is to say: conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arise; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises;
conditioned by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise. Through such causes, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being.
When the root does not arise, then everything attains cessation; that is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;

with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. Understanding such cessation, one attains the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.

At that time, the World-Honored One remained in meditative concentration for seven days and nights; having thus observed the twelvefold dependent origination, he emerged from *samādhi* and spoke these verses:
"When one observes the nature of suffering through pure conduct, One knows that every single phenomenon has its cause.
If one knows that the nature of suffering does not arise, Then all that is cherished will naturally be severed."
When one observes with pure conduct the cessation of feeling, one knows that the dharma of the cessation of feeling is inexhaustible;
if one knows that the cessation of feeling is non-arising, then all that is cherished will naturally be severed.
When one observes dependent origination through pure conduct, one then knows that dependently originated phenomena are inexhaustible;
if one knows that what is dependently originated is unborn, all that is cherished will naturally cease.
When one observes the outflows with pure conduct, one then knows that the phenomena of outflow are inexhaustible;
if one knows that the phenomena of outflow do not arise, all that is cherished will naturally be severed.
Observing such dharmas with pure conduct, one knows that all such dharmas are without arising;
like the sun illuminating the world, they move through space without obstruction.
Purifying one's conduct, one observes the characteristic of suffering, Knowing that each and every suffering is ultimately unarisen;
Destroying afflictions until none remain, Just as the Buddha subdued the armies of Māra.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, he further said:
"If there are sentient beings who have severed the cycle of saṃsāra, who know the profound Dharma, and who are able to fully comprehend subtle and wondrous expressions—such persons are the wise.
For such people I speak; for such people I cause to know. Thus, I now dwell alone in the forest and wilderness, relying on the practice of yoga and seeing the joy of the Dharma."
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he moved and dwelt with sovereign ease, free from all attachments; he neither spoke of the Dharma nor gave rise to any thought.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, perceiving that the World-Honored One neither spoke of the Dharma nor gave rise to any thought, formed this thought:
"If it is thus, the world will perish."
Why is this? A Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world as rarely as the udumbara flower, appearing only once in a great while.

Now, if he were not to preach the Dharma and instead take delight in the Dharma for himself alone, all those possessed by desire and those who delight in false teachings would remain unaware and unenlightened.
"How can the world not perish?
I shall now go there to extend my exhortation.

At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, departed from that Brahma realm and arrived at the Buddha's dwelling in the time it takes to stretch out one's arm; standing before the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
“Having appeared in the kingdom of Magadha, the past Dharma is stainless;
you have opened the gates of ambrosia for all, expounding the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
The World-Honored One replied:
“My Dharma is profound, difficult to see and difficult to understand; if I were to speak of it hastily, it would quickly lead to my destruction. Why is this?
Because all those in the world who delight in false dharmas and those possessed by desire do not take pleasure in hearing or receiving it, nor are they able to awaken to it.”
"Why is this? Because those who possess craving are shrouded and obstructed by darkness.
Brahmā replied:
“World-Honored One!

Sentient beings are born in the world and age in the world; there are those with sharp faculties, dull faculties, and middling faculties, even including various ordinary persons who possess the marks and signs of excellence and are easily transformed, whose defilements and impurities are slight.”
"World-Honored One!

It is just as, for example, blue lotuses or white lotuses and the like grow in water, mature in water, and decay in water; among them, some emerge from the water while others do not, and it is likewise so."
"Bhagavān!
If you do not preach various sublime dharmas for the sake of all ordinary beings, they will all fall into ruin.
We only pray, Sugata!"
Bestow upon us the treasure of the Dharma;
we pray only that the Sugata will let fall the nectar of immortality!
At that time, having received the Brahma King’s earnest entreaty, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.

He then, with the Buddha-eye, scrutinized the sentient beings of the world—their births in the world and their aging in the world; those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties, even those of middling and inferior capacities; those of handsome or ugly countenances; those easy to transform and those difficult to transform; those with few defilements and those with extremely few defilements. Regarding such beings as these, he thought:
"If I do not preach various sublime Dharmas for them, they will not know the root of all sufferings and will all fall into ruin."
Having thus observed and known this, the World-Honored One gave rise to great compassion and, about to expound the wondrous Dharma, first spoke these verses:
"I now let fall the rain of the nectar of Dharma, To moisten those who delight in hearing it and all beings;
From this, people in the world shall obtain the causes for the Dharma— But if they see the evil Māra, I shall not speak extensively."

At that time, having heard these verses, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, knew with certainty that the World-Honored One was expounding the sublime Dharma. His body and mind were filled with bliss, and his joy was beyond measure; he immediately prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and vanished from sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected to himself:
"Who shall be the first to hear the Dharma?
Thereupon, he recalled:
"In the past, the sages such as Āḷāra Kālāma were worthy to hear the Dharma first. Why is this?
Because in the past, I went to their dwellings, accepted their sublime offerings, and received their entrustment; therefore, I shall now preach the Dharma to them first."
While he was reflecting thus, a deva came to inform the Buddha, saying:
"Ārāḍa Kālāma and the others have all passed away; it has now been seven days."
The World-Honored One knew it silently and, hearing the proclamation of the devas, sighed and said:
"Is the world not startled by this great matter of impermanence?
He further reflected:
“Alāra Kālāma and the others were so unfortunate as not to have heard the True Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One further reflected:
“Who should be the first to hear the Dharma?”
"That son of the Rudraka Kālāma also once made offerings to me and once entrusted himself to me.
As he was thinking this, a deva named Rata addressed the Buddha, saying:
"That son of the Rudraka Kālāma has also passed away."
The World-Honored One knew this silently and further heard the proclamation of the devas; the World-Honored One then sighed and said:
"The True Dharma is difficult to hear, yet those with meager merit are such as these.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought of the five men.
"I have left the royal palace and entered the mountains to practice austerities; these people have followed me to serve me, so I ought to preach the Dharma to them first.
Thereupon, with his purified divine eye, he observed where they were.
Seeing those five persons in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, the World-Honored One then departed from the Bodhi tree for the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī.
At that time, by the side of the road, there was a seer named Upaga who was coming toward them.

Suddenly, on the road, that seer beheld the World-Honored One; seeing his body sixteen feet tall, with a golden hue radiating brilliantly, his marks and signs upright and majestic, extraordinary and surpassing the world, he marveled for a long while and then spoke these words:
"Gautama!..."
"Gautama! Beholding your marks and signs, which are serene, pure, and like the color of gold— unrivaled by anything in the world—
for what reason have you left the household life?"
In what dharma do you take refuge? Who is your teacher?
And where are you going now?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a verse in response to the seer, saying:
"I have no teacher now; Abiding in the world alone without peer, I have awakened to Perfect Enlightenment, And am the Supreme Teacher of Gods and Humans."
"Knowing all phenomena of the world, neither stained nor severed;
possessing the power of all-knowledge, you shall subdue the armies of Māra.
Thus spoke the seer Upagā.
"Gautama! It is truly as you say; this is undoubtedly the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Having realized this and attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), and having subdued sinful karma, he is therefore called a Buddha.
Then the seer Upaga asked again: “Gautama!
"Where are you going now?

The Buddha replied, "I am going to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to beat the great Dharma drum and turn the great wheel of Dharma. I shall preach that which has never been preached in the world, and I shall also proclaim the injunctions of the Buddhas of the past, so that the world may know the Dharma and become free from desire."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the ṛṣi Upaga prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and departed along the road.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded on his own to the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

There, five men—named Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahānāman, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, and Mahāprajāpatī’s son Yaśas—had just bathed and anointed their bodies with fragrant oils; they were seated in a row, having spread out a wide array of food and drink, in the midst of their meal.
When those five men saw the World-Honored One from afar, they recognized that it was no other than him; filled with great astonishment, they consulted one another, saying:
"This Prince, who dwelt in the mountains practicing austerities desiring to attain the Way of the Buddha, has now retreated from his resolve and comes back to seek us out.
Let us remain seated as we are and do not go out to welcome or attend to him."
The World-Honored One, knowing this from afar, proceeded in silence.
The Buddha’s body was majestic, like a mountain of gold; he was noble and auspicious, fully endowed with the marks and signs of excellence, possessing great majesty and virtue beyond compare.

At that time, when the five men saw the Buddha approaching nearby, his majestic virtue overwhelming them, they were unable to remain seated; they all rose to welcome and attend him, whereupon the five men all said:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"Please, be seated.

At that time, among the five men, some spread out a seat for the Buddha, some drew water to wash his feet, some offered him fine robes, and some took his hands to assist him; thus, the five men served the Buddha just as they had done in the past.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat down calmly and spoke with composure, addressing the five men:
"When you first saw me, all five of you made a secret agreement that you wished to treat me with contempt."
"You are all very foolish; you are all of my own kin, and you should practice my precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the five men, saying: "You!..."
Do not give rise to contempt for the Tathāgata. Why is this? You all!
"If one gives rise to contempt for the Tathāgata, one will gain no benefit and shall later undergo great suffering for a long night.
The five men replied,
"Regarding all the past dignified conducts of the Buddha— the most supreme worldly dharmas and sublime matters— "
"Later, while practicing asceticism, he attained the most holy, pure, and unsurpassed wisdom, and thoroughly penetrated the subtle Dharma that he had originally touched and practiced.
Where is he now? The Buddha said:

“Śāṭyāyanīputra, Māhākaulika, Māhāra, Jīvaprabha, and Hara-viśrānta: if you see beings making vast offerings and vast gifts—exquisite food and drink with the flavors of ghee and milk; having finished eating, bathing, and anointing their bodies with fragrant oils; with their faculties purified, adorned with exquisite beauty, looking back and forth with a joyful countenance—if you see me in such a way, you do not see me.”
Sāṃkṛtyāyana and the others said: “So it is! So it is!”

At that time, those five men were constantly engaged in begging for alms; when the World-Honored One arrived, sometimes three would go begging while two attended upon him, or sometimes two would go begging while three attended upon him, serving one another with diligence and without weariness.
The Buddha, because of this, established a rule, saying:
"There are two matters that a practitioner must not engage in.
What are these two matters?"
To give rise to craving for form and desire is the root of saṃsāra, not the dharma of superior persons.

If there is one who can rectify their own mind and practice asceticism, remaining without delusion or attachment toward these dharmas—the five aggregates and the three poisons—observing them with the eye of wisdom, severing that saṃsāra, and departing from both suffering and pleasure to walk the Middle Way;

and further, extensively cultivating the eightfold path of right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, thereby attaining supernormal powers and realizing nirvāṇa, this is called the Middle Way, and such a person shall proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"In this matter, I have accomplished everything without remainder.
When the World-Honored One had spoken thus, he further perceived that the five men were capable of receiving the Dharma, and he addressed them again, saying:
"This is suffering; you must know it."

Thereupon the five men reflected; observing this Dharma with the eye of wisdom, they recalled what they had previously heard and studied in past lives, whereby bodhicitta arose and they attained realization.
He spoke again, saying:
"This is suffering; you should bring it to an end.

Thereupon, the five men reflected upon this teaching and, observing with the eye of wisdom, realized and understood it through the awakening that had arisen from what they had previously heard in past lives.
Again he said to them:
"This is cessation; you should realize it.

Thereupon the five men reflected again, and observing this Dharma with the eye of wisdom, they realized that they had heard and listened to it in the past, and thus awakening arose and they attained full understanding.
He spoke again, saying:
"This is the path; you should cultivate it.

Thereupon, the five men reflected once more and observed this Dharma with the eye of wisdom; they realized that they had heard and listened to this very teaching in past lives, and thus the awakening (bodhi) arose within them once again.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the five men, saying:

"The dharma of suffering I have known; the dharma of its origin I have abandoned; the dharma of its cessation I have realized; the dharma of the path I have cultivated. By means of these dharmas, I have attained the Way of the Buddha."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the five men, saying: "You!
You should learn from me: know suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and cultivate the Path."

"You! If you are able to attain full awakening to this true path of the Four Noble Truths, you will naturally know that there is no accumulation, no cessation, no ignorance, no wisdom, no enlightenment, and no non-arising; furthermore, even the Brahma realm, the Mara realm, the various devas, worldly people, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas have no place of abiding for you. Free from inverted perceptions, with a joyful and tranquil mind, you shall decisively realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the future."
At that time, the World-Honored One thus turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Then, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and others were cleansed of dust and grime, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye; likewise, eighty thousand devas and humans attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, once the five men had realized the Way, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to leave the household life within the Buddha’s Dharma; we pray that you will grant us your permission.
At that time, the Tathāgata said to the five men:
"Welcome, Bhikṣus! Thereupon,
the hair and beards of the five men fell away of their own accord, saffron robes appeared upon their bodies, and they took on the form of śramaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kātyāyana and the others, saying:
"Is form permanent or impermanent?
Is it suffering or not suffering?"
Is this emptiness or is it non-emptiness?
Is there a self or is there no-self?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
Is this suffering or is it not suffering?
Is this empty or is it not empty?
Does this have a self or is it without a self?
Kauṇḍinya replied:
“World-Honored One!
I contemplate form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as all being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.”
At that time, when the five bhikṣus heard the Buddha teach this Dharma of the five aggregates, they attained the exhaustion of outflows and realized the state of no-more-learning.
Then the Buddha addressed them, saying: "You all!"
"What was to be done has been accomplished; the holy life has been established; birth has been extinguished; and the cycle of rebirth is forever severed.
You and I, six in all, shall be the foremost field of merit for the world; the names of the Triple Gem are now complete."
At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, there was a yakṣa named Puma who cried out in a loud voice:

"Today, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, the World-Honored One has turned the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths in its three phases and twelve aspects for the sake of compassionately benefiting the world and the supramundane—namely, the Brahmās, Māras, devas, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas."

When the yakṣa Pāñcika had uttered this proclamation, the Cāturmahārājika devas, the Trāyastriṃśa devas, and all those other gods announced it to one another. In an instant, even as far as the Brahma realm, all the Brahmā devas came to know and hear that the World-Honored One was at the Abode of the Sages in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, where he had turned the Wheel of Dharma three times; thus the Three Jewels appeared, bringing benefit, peace, and joy to humans, devas, and all sentient beings.

At that moment, the earth shook violently and the heavens became brilliantly illuminated. Thereupon, Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas each took up precious banners, pennants, and canopies and came to where the Buddha was. They rained down exquisite celestial flowers, performed divine music, sang hymns of praise, and made various offerings; filled with joy and exultation, they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
The Mahāsudarśana Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Seven.
The Mahāsudarśana Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor, Minister Faxian, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had first turned the Wheel of Dharma and delivered the five bhikṣus, he took the bhikṣus and went to the banks of the Varakā River, where they stayed for a short while.

At that time, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a son of the elder Kūlika named Yaśas. His family was immensely wealthy and possessed vast treasures; his maternal kin and relatives were all prominent clans of the country. He maintained many male and female servants, with whom he vied in mutual displays of power and prosperity. These servants were all young, intelligent, and skilled in many arts; moreover, they were adept at singing and music, and constantly attended upon him.

At that time, Yaśas, the son of the elder, suddenly one day within his own home, ordered his female musicians to adorn themselves in beautiful attire and perform music; together with his kinsmen and retinue, he indulged in pleasure from dawn until night before finally ceasing.
At that time, the courtesans each returned to their respective quarters; being exhausted and overcome by deep sleep, they were entirely unconscious.

Then, during the latter part of the night, Yaśas, the son of the elder, went on patrol through the various chambers and inspected the treasuries. He saw that the doors of the courtesans' rooms were not closed and that they lacked restraint: some had their hair disheveled, others had their clothes fallen from their bodies, and they lay prostrate or supine in all directions, their bodies exposed like corpses with no difference whatsoever.

At that time, Yaśas, the son of the elder, whose causes and conditions had reached maturity and whose time for renunciation had arrived, beheld these signs and was suddenly struck with world-weariness, as if he had gone mad.

Because Yaśas was so wealthy, he possessed as many as a thousand pairs of sandals adorned with mani jewels; thus, wearing these jewel-encrusted sandals, he went to the royal palace at night and said to the gatekeeper:
"I am suffering!"
"I am suffering!
Please report this to the King.
But the gatekeeper was unwilling to report it.
He went again to the rear gate and said to the gatekeeper:
"I am suffering! I am suffering!"
"Please report this to the King.
Yet the gatekeeper would not listen.
At that time, from the latter part of the night until the break of dawn, Yaśas walked back and forth beyond the city gates to the banks of the Varaka River, speaking only these words:
"I am suffering! I am suffering!
At that time, the World-Honored One was on the opposite shore, walking in meditation at dawn.
Thereupon, Yaśas saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s majestic virtue and dignified appearance were peerless; knowing him to be no ordinary man, he addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!"
"I am suffering,
Noble One!
I am suffering!"
At that time, the World-Honored One comforted and called out to him with gentle words:
"Good son! Come here;
I am now in this place, peaceful and free from trouble."

At that time, having heard the compassionate voice of the World-Honored One calling out to him with gentle words, Yaśas immediately removed his jeweled sandals and set them aside on the bank; he then crossed the Varā River, approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One returned with Yaśas to his place of residence; having spread out a seat and sat down, he preached the Dharma to Yaśas as was appropriate for him.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Yaśas:

"Generosity and the observance of precepts are the causes for rebirth in the heavens; yet, although one may exercise mastery over the five desires, the cycle of saṃsāra remains unbroken. Do not give rise to joy or pleasure on account of celestial blessings."

If you now wish to sever the afflictions, remove the hindrances, and attain liberation, you should apply yourself to the cultivation of the Noble Path; thus you may realize the tracks of the path and realize Nirvana.
He spoke again:
"Yasa! I now ask you: Is form permanent or impermanent?"
Is this suffering or not suffering?
Is it empty or not empty?
Is there a self or no self?
Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
Are they suffering or not suffering?
Are they empty or not empty?
"Is there a self, or is there no self?

When those members of the assembly of the Jains heard the World-Honored One preach such a Dharma, they were like white cloth that is easily dyed; they were freed from dust and defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One further expounded for him at length the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that moment, Yaśas attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows and realized the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

He then spoke these words in response to the World-Honored One: "As the Buddha has taught, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are indeed impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."

The World-Honored One, knowing that Yaśas had indeed realized the liberation of the exhaustion of outflows, yet still wore the jeweled ornaments and garments of a householder, spoke these verses for him:
"If one has attained the Right Path, yet still yearns for adornment;
Though practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), he is not yet called one whose mind is stilled."
"If one can subdue [the self], / Carrying a staff yet remaining ever vigilant;
/ Though a Brahmin by birth, / Such a one is a true Śramaṇa.
At that time, Yaśas, who possessed innate wisdom and had already realized the state of no-more-learning, reflected within himself as soon as he heard the Buddha recite these sublime verses:
“The Blessed One has spoken this precisely because I am still wearing the jeweled ornaments and garments of a householder.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I now wish to become a śramaṇa within the Buddha’s Dharma; may the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, grant me permission.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
His beard and hair fell away naturally, the *kāṣāya* robe appeared upon his body, and he took on the form of a śramaṇa, complete with the proper deportment and characteristics.
At that time, when it was just beginning to dawn, the elder Kūṭadanta saw those around him hurriedly reporting:
"The elder’s son Yaśas has departed from the house before the break of day; he has not returned, and we do not know where he has gone."
When the elder Kūṭadanta heard these words, he was struck with extraordinary alarm and thought to himself:
"My son has gone out at night; could it be that some unrighteous person has enticed him?"
He further asked his attendant:
"Is the manner of my son's walking and the style of his clothing constant or inconstant?
The attendant replied:
"The fine garments and precious sandals he usually wears are not in their usual place; they must have been put on his person.
At that time, the elder Kuṭika further reflected:
"Since my son Yaśas is wearing his jewel-encrusted sandals and exquisite robes, there can be no evil matter; I should now quickly search for him everywhere."
Thereupon, he ordered his servants to search in all directions while he himself went out through the city gate to the banks of the Varaka River to inquire and seek him out.

Suddenly, by the riverbank, he saw the jeweled sandals his son was wearing; furthermore, he heard that on the opposite shore there was a Buddha who, together with his disciples, was staying and dwelling there.
He thought to himself, "My son must certainly be residing there."

Then the elder Kūṭadanta immediately took off his sandals and crossed the river to search for him; as he was about to reach the Buddha’s dwelling, the Buddha saw him from afar and knew that he had come seeking his son.
Having arrived before the Buddha, he beheld the Buddha’s radiance and observed other extraordinary signs; not yet having had time to speak of his son, he could only exclaim in wonder and admiration.
The World-Honored One, through skillful means, recognized his aspiration and first addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, householder!"
"Are you not fatigued?
Please be seated for a moment; I shall speak with you now.

At that time, as the elder Kuṭika first beheld the World-Honored One’s majestic radiance and excellent physical marks, and was further comforted by the Buddha’s gentle words, his veneration increased so much that he completely forgot about searching for his son.
The World-Honored One said, "I have a sublime Dharma; would you like to hear it?
The elder Kūṭadanta replied:
“May the Buddha, out of compassion, deign to reveal this to us.
The Buddha said:

“Generosity and the observance of precepts are the causes for rebirth in the heavens; however, the karmic fruits of such heavenly rebirth are not ultimate. If one cuts off the afflictions (*kleśa*), one may proceed upon the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).”
"Householder Kūṭadanta!
I now ask you: Is form permanent or impermanent?
Is it suffering or not suffering?"
"Is this emptiness not emptiness?
Is there a self or no self?
He asked again:
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
Are they suffering or not suffering?
Are they empty or not empty?"
"Is there a self, or is there no self?
At that time, the World-Honored One explained extensively for him:
"You should observe this and report to me with truthful words."
Then the elder Kulika said:
"I now truly know that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are indeed phenomena that are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self."

At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths in detail for him. Thereupon, the elder Kulika, by means of this, removed the dust and defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; his body and mind were at ease and joyful, and his gladness was immeasurable.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the householder’s mind was opened and his attachment had faded so that he would surely feel no sorrow or suffering upon seeing his son in the guise of a śramaṇa, asked him: “Kulika!”
"For what reason have you come here?
The elder Kūṭadanta related all that had occurred to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha called out:
“Bhikṣu! Yaśas then emerged.
At that time, seeing Yaśas had gone forth in the form of a śramaṇa and knowing further that his outflows were exhausted and he had realized the fruit of arhatship, the elder spoke these words:
"My son is truly blessed!

He is now able to benefit both himself and others. That I have been able to hear this sublime Dharma, that I am far removed from dust and defilement, and that my Dharma-eye has become pure—all these marvelous benefits have been obtained through my son."
Thereupon, Kulika spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"I now dwell as a householder; I pray that the Buddha will bestow the precepts upon me.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
I shall now receive you into the Three Refuges; you should receive them with full attention.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Kulika! You take refuge in the Buddha, you take refuge in the Dharma, and you take refuge in the Saṃgha; for as long as life lasts, you must not violate or regret this.
Kulika replied:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said, "Kulika!"
"Now that you have received the Three Refuges from me, you shall become the foremost upāsaka in the world.
At that time, Kuṭika, having been taught various dharmas by the Buddha, attained freedom from dust and defilement, and his Dharma-eye became pure.
Furthermore, having received the Three Refuges, his mind was at ease and his joy was immeasurable; he then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I shall prepare a vegetarian feast in my own residence tomorrow; I only pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of noble ones will, out of compassion and pity, deign to grant me your presence."
The Buddha remained silent.
Then, Kūṭadanta, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage to him, and withdrew.
Once Kuṭika had invited the Buddha, he quickly returned home and informed his wife, children, and all his kinsmen:
"Yasa went out at night and crossed the Varāka River; he has gone forth under the Buddha and become a śramaṇa, and furthermore, he has already realized the fruit of arhatship."

I sought Yaśas and likewise arrived there, whereupon I was granted the Dharma teaching by the World-Honored One. Having attained freedom from dust and defilement, I gained the pure Dharma-eye; furthermore, he conferred upon me the Three Refuges.

I have invited the Buddha to receive my offerings on the morrow, and the Buddha, together with the assembly of noble ones, will surely descend to attend. You, my kinsmen, should now quickly purify the house for me, sprinkle it with scented water so that no dust remains, and swiftly prepare various foods and drinks, as well as incense, flowers, and all requisites for offering. If you apply yourselves with single-minded devotion, you too shall obtain great benefit.

When the following morning arrived and the dawn light had appeared, all preparations within the house were completed. The elder Kuṭika then stood at the edge of the courtyard, holding an incense burner and burning incense, and addressed the World-Honored One from afar:
"The food and drink are prepared; we pray that the Buddha will deign to descend."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya:
"All you Arhats, you may go together to attend the invitation of Kūlika.
He then addressed Yaśas, saying:

“Your appearance and attire upon returning to your own home will not be as they were before; your mother and kinsmen will surely be grieved at heart. Now that you have left the household life and attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), you should employ skillful means to transform them and cause them to rejoice.”

After the Buddha had finished his exhortation, he proceeded with them to the house to receive food. At that time, the elder Kuṭika stood at the entrance of the gate, gazing expectantly for the Buddha’s arrival. When the Buddha reached the gate, the elder Kuṭika prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, burned incense, and led him through to the second gate.

Then Yaśas’s mother, her wet nurse, and their attendants all came out to welcome him. Upon first beholding the World-Honored One, they saw that his physical marks were dignified and majestic, and his radiant splendor was extraordinary. They also saw Yaśas and the various Arhats, their bodies adorned in dharma robes, their deportment composed and deliberate; in every movement and gesture, they possessed a sublime and transcendent manner. Surrounding him and gazing up in reverence, they rejoiced beyond measure.

The elder Kūṭadanta invited the Buddha to take his seat, and the various arhats likewise took their seats. At that time, the elder and his retinue prostrated at the feet of the Buddha in succession; having completed their salutations, they gazed upon him with reverence and each withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for Yaśas’s mother and her retinue according to their needs, causing them to rejoice and inspiring them to resolve upon Bodhicitta. He then addressed them, saying:

"Through generosity and the observance of precepts, one attains birth in the heavens; yet though such states are joyful, they do not transcend saṃsāra. To transcend saṃsāra, one must sever the afflictions and thoroughly understand the nature of arising and ceasing."
"Listen attentively and reflect deeply; I shall now analyze and explain this in detail for you.
The Buddha said:
"Form is impermanent, it is suffering, it is empty, and it is a dharma that is without self."
He further said:
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self phenomena.
Do you understand this?"
Thus the World-Honored One explained in detail.

At that time, Yaśas’s mother, his wet nurse, and the others had all previously planted roots of goodness; now encountering the World-Honored One as he preached the sublime Dharma for them, they were like clean white cloth taking on various colors—becoming bright and exquisite according to the dye applied—and Yaśas’s mother and the others were likewise so transformed.

The World-Honored One extensively expounded for them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Yaśas’s mother and the others, without rising from their seats, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; they severed craving and abandoned all doubt, gaining unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena. Thereupon, they rose from their seats, stood before the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"The five aggregates, the three poisons, and the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impermanence—I have already known them as they truly are.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately received his triple refuge.
Having completed the threefold refuge, he leaped for joy and bowed in gratitude to the Buddha, further saying,
"The time for the meal has arrived.
The Buddha remained silent.
