Thereupon, the elder and Yaśas’s mother took all the various kinds of exquisite, fragrant, and delicious food they had prepared and personally offered them with their own hands to the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones.

When the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones had finished eating and completed their ritual ablutions, the householder and Yaśas’s mother sat upon low seats before the Buddha and requested him to teach the Dharma;
the Buddha then transformed and benefited them, causing their hearts to rejoice.
Then the elder Kūṭadanta, together with Yaśas’s mother and the others, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We have a slight doubt that we wish to set forth for inquiry; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us and sever our doubts.”

"Now, for what cause and by what condition has my son Yaśas obtained this fruit—that he suddenly conceived such a mind while at home, encountered the World-Honored One who preached the sublime Dharma for him, and having donned the dharma-robes to adorn his body, attained the exhaustion of all outflows and realized the fruit of Arhatship?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elders and others, saying:

"In a past age, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a rishi living at a place neither near nor far from the city. Possessing a heart of compassion, he sought to benefit sentient beings and would regularly enter the city with his alms bowl to beg for food."

At that time, on one occasion, that seer saw a dead insect at a crossroads; observing its decay and putrefaction, as well as its foul stench, such that passersby could not even approach it, the seer suddenly gave rise to this reflection:
"My own body is impermanent; it is no different from this."
Thereupon, he conceived a sense of weary detachment toward saṃsāra.
At that time, there was also a young boy who saw the dead insect and, like that rishi, grew weary of the suffering of saṃsāra.
That seer and that youth, having become weary of saṃsāra, subsequently applied themselves diligently to practicing the right path to liberation.
That seer was none other than myself; that youth was none other than Yaśas.
"Therefore, Yaśas has now encountered me and, having heard the sublime Dharma, realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Upon hearing these words from the Buddha, the elder Kulika and his retinue rejoiced, accepted them with faith, paid their respects, and withdrew.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, leading the assembly of noble ones, returned to the Deer Park, the abode of the rishis.
At that time, Kulika had four sons:
the first was named Pūrṇa;...
The second is named Vimala;
the third is named Ghaṇṭapati;
the fourth is named Somahuk.
Seeing Yaśas having renounced the world to follow the Buddha and realized the fruit of arhatship, they all thought to themselves:
"Why do we still cling to craving and desire instead of seeking liberation?"
Again, they reflected:
"If there were no Supreme Awakening in this world today, who else would be able to proclaim the Supreme Dharma?

We have been unable to sever the cycle of saṃsāra; now that we have encountered the Buddha’s teaching, we should give rise to right faith. We ought to renounce our homes together, just as Yaśas did, in order to seek liberation."

Thereupon, the four brothers, including Pūrṇa, departed from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī together and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“We are the sons of Kūlika and the younger brothers of Yaśas. We have now come to take refuge in the Buddha and wish to become śramaṇas; we only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant us permission.”
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately ordered his disciples to shave [his] hair and beard and don the kashaya robes.
Once he had become a śramaṇa, the Buddha further preached the Dharma to him, saying:

“Purāṇa! Since you have become a śramaṇa, you should practice austerities to restrain the mind from distraction, seek the True Dharma so that the mind is free from self, and attain definitive knowledge of all phenomena. Thus, exhaust the source of birth and death, forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, and proceed toward liberation.”

When Pūraṇa and the others had heard this Dharma taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, their right faith became firm and they practiced with diligent application. They attained the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava-kṣaya), achieved liberation of mind (ceto-vimukti), and realized the fruit of Arhatship: what was to be done had been done, the holy life (brahmacarya) was established, birth had come to an end, and the cycle of saṃsāra was forever severed.

At that time, there were ten great Arhats. Then, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there were fifty sons of prominent clans and elders who had long been friends with the son of Kūlika. Suddenly hearing that Kūlika’s son Yaśas, Pūrṇa, and the others had followed the Buddha into homelessness and realized the fruits of the Path, they all thought to themselves:

"Those sons of elders, Yaśas, Pūrṇa, and the rest, belong to a noble and eminent lineage with wealth beyond compare; their wisdom surpasses that of men and their comeliness is rarely matched. Yet, though they constantly enjoyed pleasure and were free from all suffering, they were still able to renounce their homes and study the Way to seek liberation. How can we still harbor such attachment?"

After the sons of the elders had formed this thought, they departed from the city of Vārāṇasī and went together to where the Buddha was. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated at his feet and stood to one side.

The sons of the elders spoke thus to the Buddha in unison: "We, the sons of the elders, are exactly fifty in number; we now wish to go forth in the Buddha’s Dharma to become śramaṇas. We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion and pity, will grant us permission."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! You,
son of a householder, have now reached the very time to leave home and take up the path."
He immediately ordered his disciples to shave [the youth's] hair and beard, clothe him in the kashaya robes, and ordain him as a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One further preached the Dharma for him, leading him to seek the supreme fruit.
The Buddha said:
"O son of a householder!

Those who each renounce their homes to become śramaṇas must practice asceticism with their own bodies, collect their minds without distraction to seek the Dharma of True Reality, and cause the mind to be free of self. Thus, they shall definitively understand all dharmas, exhaust the source of birth and death, forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, and proceed toward liberation."

Having heard the World-Honored One teach this Dharma, the sons of the elders attained firm and decisive right faith and practiced with diligent application. They realized the exhaustion of all outflows and attained liberation of mind; having done what was to be done and established the holy life, their births were extinguished and they forever severed the cycle of saṃsāra, all fully realizing the fruit of arhatship.
Thereupon, there first appeared in the world sixty great arhats. At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed his disciples and addressed them, saying:

"For immeasurable kalpas I have practiced with diligent perseverance, and only today have I attained perfect enlightenment. It is precisely for the sake of all sentient beings that I have untied their various fetters. Today you have all heard the True Dharma from me; your outflows are exhausted and you are liberated. You are fully endowed with the three insights and the six supernormal powers. Having escaped the bonds of both heaven and humanity, you may serve as the supreme field of merit for sentient beings; you should now practice compassion and bring benefit and joy according to conditions."
Before he had finished speaking, the sinful Māra, named Maṇava, immediately perceived from afar:
"Today, the śramaṇa Gautama is deliberating with his disciples in the Deer Park, saying:
'You have attained liberation from the bonds of the heavens and the human world; you should each go forth according to conditions to bring benefit and happiness.'"
"If I do not now cause him to become deluded and confused, he will surely transform and exhaust all sentient beings in the world.

Then that sinful Māra Maṇava transformed his body to appear like an ordinary person; in the time it takes to extend one's arm, he arrived at the Buddha’s location and stood before the Buddha, reciting a verse:
"Your mark of liberation is not liberation; having attained this liberation, you are no śramaṇa."
"You are now yourself bound by great fetters; whom do you intend to liberate?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that this sinful Māra Maṇava had come to cause confusion and distraction, realized that he was merely creating karma for himself and could never destroy him. He then spoke a verse in response to the sinful Māra:
"In the heavens and among humans, I have already attained liberation from all fetters."
"Even unto those who are beyond training and free from all fetters, you, O sinful Māra, shall not be able to break them.
When the Māra Maṇava heard these words, he reflected to himself:
"This Śramaṇa Gautama knows the thoughts of others; I certainly cannot disturb him."
Thus, they withdrew in distress and concealment.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I have already told you:..."
"You have already been freed from all bonds in the heavens and among humans; you should compassionately regard sentient beings and proceed to guide them.
Go forth with haste!"
Then the Arhats, having received the Buddha’s instruction, paid their respects and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the Arhats, left the delightful site of the Deer Park; the Buddha then proceeded alone to the village of Kṣāntivādin, where he went to the Karṇapāśa grove by the side of the Uruvilvā pond to walk and sit in meditation.
At that time, there were sixty virtuous men in a certain village who, in Vārāṇasī, took various courtesans and musicians with them, performing music every day without ceasing.
Suddenly, one woman felt a sense of weary detachment toward this pleasure; she abandoned the group and fled, her destination unknown.

At that time, the sixty virtuous ones, whose roots of goodness had matured, sought out this woman and entered the Karavīra forest. Suddenly, beneath a tree, they beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Struck with extraordinary wonder, they said to one another:
"This śramaṇa now has a body like a mountain of gold, radiating brilliant light; his countenance is upright and his marks are complete; he is auspicious, noble, and beyond compare."
Unable to cease his lamentation, he immediately went forward to approach him and asked:
"Sramaṇa! Did you see a woman pass by while you were staying here?"
The Buddha said,
"Worthy assembly!
This place is tranquil and is not a resort for women."
"You have now come here seeking a woman; why do you not seek your own bodies?
At that time, when the group of virtuous ones heard what the Buddha said, they immediately attained realization and understood their former error, replying to the Buddha:
"That we previously sought a woman was truly a fault."
"Now we seek it within ourselves; we pray that you will grant us instruction.
The Buddha said, "O virtuous assembly!"
"Since you are thus, sit down for a moment; I shall now proclaim the essential points of the Dharma for you.
Thereupon, the group of virtuous ones prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha said:
"Worthy assembly!

Generosity and the observance of precepts are causes for rebirth in the heavens; though they bring happiness, they are not ultimate. If you seek liberation, you must sever the afflictions and likewise discern the phenomena of arising and ceasing."
When those virtuous ones heard these words, their obscurations were immediately removed, and they reflected within their minds with immeasurable joy.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, then extensively expounded for them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Just as clean white cloth easily takes on various colors, becoming bright and beautiful according to whatever dye it encounters, so too did that assembly of noble ones, while seated upon their thrones, realize the subtle principles of the Four Noble Truths. Having attained knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, their craving was extinguished and their doubts forever severed; they then realized the four fearlessnesses within the Buddha-dharma. Rising from their seats, they bared their right shoulders, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One..."

Out of compassion and discernment, I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha. From this day forward, I shall never again take life; for the rest of my life, I shall uphold the precepts of an upāsaka.
At that time, the sixty virtuous ones, having heard the Dharma from the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew with joy.
*The Sūtra of the Great Auspiciousness Spoken by the Buddha*, Scroll Eight.
*The Sūtra of the Great Auspiciousness Spoken by the Buddha*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmabhadra, Imperial Censor of the Third Order, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master Mingjiao, under Imperial Decree.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had delivered those sixty virtuous ones, he further reflected upon who else might first be ready for conversion. He then recalled that within the village of Vaniya, Nanda and his eldest daughter, along with their kinsmen, were fit to be converted first.
He recollected:

"In the past, when I was departing after my ascetic practices, I passed by that house; at that time, Nanda, his eldest daughter, and their kinsmen together brought milk porridge, ghee, honey, and other offerings to present to me."
"Now, observing that their faculties and conditions have matured, they are fit to be converted.

Having formed this thought, on the following day at the time for alms, the World-Honored One took his bowl and entered the village of Siṃsapā, proceeding from house to house for alms until he reached the house of Nanda.
At that time, Nanda and his eldest daughter, seeing the Buddha arrive at their gate, leaped for joy and said to him:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
Is your holy body at ease?"
"The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; please deign to visit my home for a moment.
The Buddha then entered the gate, and Nanda and his daughter prepared a seat for the Buddha.

When the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Nanda, his daughter, and their entire retinue prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet. Having each paid their respects, they withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for him.
The Buddha said: “Nanda!
Listen attentively!

Generosity and the observance of precepts are the causes for rebirth in the heavens; yet, although they induce sensual pleasures, one will ultimately fall away from them. You should sever all afflictions in order to seek liberation.
Furthermore, the Buddha extensively analyzed the phenomena of arising and ceasing for them, causing them to understand.

When the Buddha spoke these words, the faculties and conditions of Nanda and the others reached maturity, their hindrances were immediately removed, and they contemplated with deep reflection and immeasurable joy.
The Buddha then further expounded for them at length the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

At that time, Nanda, along with his wife and retinue, attained the knowledge and vision of the Dharma while still seated; they realized the principle of the Four Truths, severed all doubts, and, having forever eliminated craving, placed their sole trust in the Buddha. They rose from their seats, joined their palms in prostration, and said:
"World-Honored One!"

I have truly known and seen the various dharmas as taught by the Blessed One; I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha. May you accept me as a lay follower who shall never again take life.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The time for the meal has arrived; we pray that the Buddha, out of great compassion, will accept our offering.
The Buddha remained silent.

Then Nanda and his retinue, seeing that the Buddha remained silent and understood that he had accepted their invitation, took various kinds of incense, flowers, food, and drink, and personally offered them with their own hands.

When the World-Honored One had finished his meal and completed his washing and rinsing, Nanda and his retinue again took their seats in a humble position, desiring to hear the Dharma. The Buddha then employed skillful means to preach the Dharma in various ways; Nanda and his retinue, having heard the Dharma once more, were filled with joy and exultation, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished converting Nanda and others in the village of Vṛji, he again reflected and desired to travel to the kingdom of Magadha to benefit and bring happiness to beings according to their conditions.

At that time, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was the skilled physiognomist Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, three hundred years of age, who claimed to have already attained the path of an Arhat. He resided on the banks of the Nairañjanā River with five hundred disciples and followers;
the King of Magadha, his ministers, and all the common people respected and made offerings to him beyond compare.

"In that kingdom of Magadha, there are immeasurable multitudes of people who are like those shrouded in blind darkness; they constantly rely upon Ulūka as their guide, and though these multitudes receive his instruction, they have no means of escaping [saṃsāra]."
"I shall now transform that Ulūka Kāśyapa and his followers, causing them to see the True Path.
Having thus reflected, he proceeded to the dwelling of Ulūka Kāśyapa on the banks of the Nairañjanā River in the kingdom of Magadha.

At that time, when Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa suddenly saw the World-Honored One arrive at his dwelling, and further beheld him endowed with the marks and signs of perfection and possessed of extraordinary majesty, he immediately went forward to welcome him and paid him further reverence, saying to the Buddha:
"Welcome, Great Śramaṇa!"
"Where did you previously dwell,
that you have suddenly arrived here now?
He then prepared a seat for the World-Honored One and invited him to sit.

When the World-Honored One had taken his seat, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa also sat down; he then greeted the World-Honored One with various words of inquiry, and the World-Honored One likewise instructed and transformed him through various skillful means.
Before their conversation had concluded, the sun had already set in the west, and the Buddha addressed him, saying:
"Now that evening has fallen, I wish to stay one night at a quiet place in your house."
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa said: "Great Śramaṇa!
Among my various dwellings, my kinsmen reside within; there is only one secluded place suitable for a śramaṇa to stay."
"However, there is a venomous dragon within this place of tranquility; though I do not begrudge it to you, I fear it may cause you harm.
Please consider this for yourself.
Thus the Buddha spoke to Uruvilvā Kāśyapa.
"I only wish to borrow it; I promise there will be no harm done.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa replied, "If that is so, you may do as you please."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to the nāga’s dwelling.
Having washed his feet outside the dwelling, he entered the nāga’s abode, spread pure grass for a seat, sat down cross-legged, and immediately entered *samādhi*.

At that time, when the venomous dragon suddenly saw the World-Honored One sitting within the house, he immediately gave rise to wrath and produced smoke and mist that pervaded both the interior and exterior of the dwelling. Thereupon, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, also manifested smoke and mist.

The venomous dragon became even more enraged and set fire to the interior of the house; the Buddha, through his spiritual power, likewise manifested fire. The two fires of the Buddha and the venomous dragon both blazed intensely, until the entire house, inside and out, became a great mass of flames, with tongues of fire surging upward and illuminating everything far and near.
At that time, Kāśyapa was regularly observing the constellations during the night when he again saw the dragon's dwelling had become a great mass of fire, whereupon he lamented:
"Alas! How bitter!"
Alas! That handsome śramaṇa did not heed my words; the dragon-fire blazes a hundred times more fiercely than usual. How tragic that this śramaṇa will surely be harmed!
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his followers all beheld the signs of a great, blazing fire.
Then that venomous dragon, knowing that the World-Honored One could not be harmed, and being himself greatly exhausted, ceased its malicious poison and the flames were extinguished;
the World-Honored One then withdrew his supernormal power, and having subdued the venomous dragon, he placed it within his alms-bowl.
After dawn had broken, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa and his retinue went to the dragon’s abode to observe the śramaṇa.
Having arrived at the dragon’s abode, they saw the Buddha sitting upright and addressed him, saying:
“O Great Śramaṇa!
"Have you been well during the night?
The Buddha said,
"I am well."
“Great Śramaṇa, what is in your bowl?
The Buddha said,
“This is the nāga of this house.”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"You say that this house contains a venomous dragon such that no one dares to dwell there;
I shall now subdue it and place it within my alms bowl, so that you may examine it closely and know the truth for yourself."

Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, considering himself senior in years, eminent in virtue, and preeminent in ascetic practice and learning—such that among all he had seen or known there was none who surpassed him—beheld the World-Honored One unharmed by the dragon-fire and having even subdued it and placed it within his alms-bowl; thereupon, he praised him, saying:
"How marvelous!"
"Śramaṇa!
You possess great power; this is a rare thing that I have seen and heard. This great śramaṇa is a mahāpuruṣa, and he is also an arhat."

At that time, having subdued the venomous dragon, on the second day the World-Honored One went to a place not far from the dwelling of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; there, beneath a tree, he practiced walking meditation and sat in quietude. That very night, the Four Great Heavenly Kings descended to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, Kāśyapa went out at night to observe the stars and constellations, whereupon he saw four great masses of fire before the Buddha.
Kāśyapa then said to his disciples,
"That great śramaṇa also practices fire-worship."
The disciples asked,
"By what means did the Master know this?
Kāśyapa replied:
"I observed the stars at night and saw four great masses of fire before the Great Śramaṇa; I know that this śramaṇa undoubtedly worships fire.
Then, as soon as dawn broke, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went quickly to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"O Great Śramaṇa!..."
"Do you also serve fire?
The Buddha replied,
"I do not serve fire."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Last night I observed the stars and saw four masses of fire before the śramaṇa;
if he does not serve the fire, for what purpose are these used?"
The Buddha then replied, "This is not fire;
it is the four Great Heavenly Kings who have descended to listen to the Dharma. It is merely the radiance from the bodies of those four devas!"
Kāśyapa said in astonishment:
"How marvelous!
O Śramaṇa!"
"This is indeed the case.
This Great Śramaṇa possesses such majestic power that he has moved the Heavenly Kings to come together and listen to the Dharma; is he also an Arhat?"

On the third day, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side, whereupon the Buddha preached the Dharma to Śakra as was appropriate for him.
Having heard the Dharma, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, returned to his celestial palace with great joy and exultation.

At that time, Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was observing the constellations at night when he saw before the World-Honored One beneath the tree a mass of fire, exceedingly vast and blazing, its radiance shining like the rising sun.
Then Kāśyapa said to his disciples,
"This śramaṇa is certainly attending to the fire.
When dawn had broken, he went quickly with his disciples to the place where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
“O Great Śramaṇa!

Last night I went out to observe the stars and constellations, and I saw a mass of fire blazing before your seat; the flames soared upward like the rising sun. I now know for certain that you, Śramaṇa, worship fire.”
The Buddha replied:
"I do not tend the sacrificial fire;
it was the radiance of Śakra’s body that illuminated this place last night as he descended to listen to the Dharma."
Kāśyapa sighed in admiration and said:
"How marvelous!
O Śramaṇa!"
"He possesses such great majesty and virtue; this is truly rare!
I now know for certain that he has also attained the fruit of Arhatship.
On the fourth day, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa went out to observe the stars and again beheld before the seat of the Śramaṇa a great mass of fire, its radiance shining like the sun at its zenith.
At that time, Kāśyapa returned and told his disciples:

"Tonight, as I again observed the constellations, I saw once more a fire before the śramaṇa’s seat, its radiance shining even more intensely than before, equal to the midday sun without any difference. Examining these signs closely, it is certain he is tending a sacrificial fire."
When dawn had broken, he went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"Last night I observed the stars and saw a fire before the seat of the śramaṇa; I knew for certain that this śramaṇa worships fire."
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!
I have nothing to seek; what use would I have for fire?"
"During the night last night, Mahābrahmā, the lord of that Sahā world, descended to listen to the Dharma and sat before me; what you saw was the radiance of his body."
Then Kāśyapa again sighed in praise, saying:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses such great power of majestic virtue that he can move the Brahmā King to descend and listen to the Dharma; this is truly rare!
I am certain that I too shall realize the fruit of Arhatship."

On the fifth day, the five hundred followers of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa, such as Mañjuṣaka and others, all served three fires; each had three hearths, and thus there were one thousand five hundred hearths in total.
At that time, the World-Honored One was beneath that tree, and it happened that the assembly there was performing a fire sacrifice to the heavens.

According to their usual custom, those five hundred men attempted to kindle the fire, but it would not ignite. The disciples immediately informed their teacher, who went to where Uruvilvā was and said to him:
"Teacher, do you know what has happened?"
"We have lit the fire, yet the fire will not ignite.
We do not know what cause has made it thus today.
Thus did Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa reflect upon this matter.
"Since that śramaṇa resides nearby, we fear he may exercise some restrictive power through his majesty.
Thereupon, together with his disciples, he went to the Buddha's dwelling and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Great Śramaṇa!..."
"My disciple Maṇavaka, along with his assembly of five hundred followers, habitually uses fire for fire-sacrifices; yet this morning, though they have kindled the fire, it will not catch."
"I suspect that this matter is surely governed by the supernatural power of the śramaṇa.
The Buddha then replied,
"Do you wish for fire to burn?"
Kāśyapa replied,
“I wish to light it.
The Buddha said:
"Go; the fire shall kindle itself naturally.
Kāśyapa returned home, and the fire was already burning.
Then Kāśyapa and his disciples all exclaimed in praise:
"This great śramaṇa possesses such power; he must surely have also attained the fruit of arhatship.
Having completed the fire sacrifice, he wished to extinguish the flames, but the fire would not be extinguished; despite exhausting all his strength, he was ultimately unable to put it out.
The young disciples, the māṇavakas, went quickly to where Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was and said to him:
"Does our teacher know?
Although the fire has been kindled, it cannot now be extinguished."
Kāśyapa replied,
"This must surely be the doing of that śramaṇa again.
Kāśyapa then went back to where the World-Honored One was and said to him:
“Śramaṇa! Although the fire has been kindled, it cannot now be extinguished.
Could it be that you, Śramaṇa, have once again suppressed it?”
The Buddha replied,
"Do you wish to extinguish it?
Kāśyapa answered:
"I wish to extinguish the fire.
The Buddha said, "You need only return; it will surely extinguish itself."
Kāśyapa returned, and the fire had already been extinguished.
He sighed again, saying, "This Great Śramaṇa possesses such supernatural power; he too is an Arhat."

On the sixth day, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa himself intended to perform a fire sacrifice to the Fire God (Agni), yet the fire would not ignite. He then entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) intending to cause the fire to burn, but the fire still would not ignite.
He came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"When I used fire previously, it would always ignite according to custom;
yet now it will not ignite. Could this be due to the power of the śramaṇa’s restraint?"
The Buddha said,
"Kāśyapa, do you wish for the fire to ignite?"
He replied, "I wish to do so.
The Buddha said:
"Simply go away; the fire will surely ignite by itself.
Kāśyapa returned, and the fire was already burning.

When he had finished using the fire and wished to extinguish it, the fire would not go out. He entered meditative concentration again, wishing to cause the fire to be extinguished, yet the fire still would not be extinguished.
Unable to avoid the situation, he came and said to the Buddha:
"Although the fire was lit, it will not go out now.
This must surely be due to the power of the śramaṇa's restraint."
The Buddha asked,
"Do you wish to extinguish it?
Kāśyapa replied:
"I wish for the fire to be extinguished.
The Buddha said, "Simply go; the fire will surely extinguish itself."
When they returned home, the fire had already been extinguished.
After the fire was out, they gathered the remaining embers in one place.

Some time later, the embers spontaneously ignited again; although he and his disciples together tried to extinguish the fire, they were ultimately unable to do so, despite exhausting all their strength.
He came again and said to the Buddha:
"O Great Śramaṇa!
The fire had just been extinguished, but now it has spontaneously blazed up again, twice as fierce as usual; I am unable to extinguish it."
"This must be due to the power of a śramaṇa who has restrained it.
The Buddha asked,
"Is the fire burning again?"
He replied,
“The fire is burning.
“Are you unable to extinguish it?”
He replied,
“I am unable to extinguish it.
The Buddha then said to him:
"Simply turn back, and the fire will extinguish itself.
Kāśyapa immediately turned back, and the fire had already extinguished itself.
Kāśyapa exclaimed:
"How marvelous!
O Śramaṇa!
You possess such power!"
When I wished to kindle a fire, the fire would not ignite, yet he told me it had ignited;
when I wished to extinguish a fire, the fire would not go out, yet he told me it had been extinguished.
"Now that the fire has been rekindled, it cannot be extinguished again;
yet that the fire could now be extinguished was also due to his power.
This great śramaṇa possesses such great majesty and virtue; this is truly extraordinary, and he must surely also be an arhat."
When that day had passed, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa prepared a seven-day assembly according to the rites of the non-Buddhist outsiders; this was heard and known by the king of Magadha and all his subjects.
Kāśyapa reflected:
"The Great Śramaṇa now dwells nearby; he was able to suppress all the fire-sacrifices performed previously—could it be that he will now suppress the rite I am performing?"
"If that śramaṇa does not come for seven days, my doctrine will surely be established;
but if he should return, I fear he might impose restrictions upon me.
He further thought thus:

“That great śramaṇa possesses the marks and signs of excellence and is endowed with preeminent majesty; if the officials and commoners of the kingdom see his superiority, they may fear he will abandon us to serve him.”
Because of this matter, he reflected upon it again and again.

The Buddha immediately perceived his thoughts; for seven days, the Buddha traveled elsewhere to teach and transform beings. Although he was dwelling nearby, Kāśyapa and the assembly did not see the World-Honored One during those seven days.
At that time, Kāśyapa performed the seven-day rite; the officials and commoners of the kingdom all brought incense, flowers, and precious treasures to make extensive offerings.
When the ritual was completed and the assembly concluded, he thought to himself:
"I have not seen that great śramaṇa for seven days, yet my current assembly has many leftovers; if the śramaṇa were to come now, there would be much for him to offer."
Having formed this thought, the Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately proceeded to the dwelling place of Kāśyapa.
As soon as Kāśyapa saw him, his heart was filled with joy:
"This great śramaṇa has come to me just as I had thought."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Has a śramaṇa come?
The Buddha said:
"I have come!
he said. Then he asked again, "Why did you not come for seven days?"
The Buddha said, "You had this thought:
'I am convening a seven-day Dharma assembly; if that śramaṇa comes, I fear the Dharma will not be accomplished.'"
"I knew your intention, and for that reason I did not come.
Now you think to yourself:
'The ritual has been completed; if the śramaṇa were to come, there would be great offerings.'"
"I also know this, and that is why I have come.
Kāśyapa reflected:
"This Great Śramaṇa is a Great Sage; he knows my thoughts entirely. He must certainly also be an Arhat."
After the Buddha had finished his discourse with Kāśyapa, he returned to his dwelling.

Later, with a heart of devout purity, Kāśyapa prepared various foods and drinks, making them exceptionally fragrant and delicious, far surpassing his usual fare. When the next day arrived, he went in person to the Buddha’s location and said:
"O Śramaṇa!..."
"I have prepared the meal with single-minded devotion; I pray that you will pass by my house to accept this offering.
Having accepted the invitation, the Buddha told him:
"You may go on ahead; I shall follow shortly."

After Kāśyapa had departed, the World-Honored One entered samādhi; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he took jambu fruits from the jambu tree within the realm of Jambudvīpa, filled his alms bowl, and returned. Arriving first at Kāśyapa’s dwelling, he sat cross-legged.
Kāśyapa arrived later and, seeing that the Buddha had already arrived, was startled and said,
"Has the śramaṇa come?
The Buddha replied:
"I have been here for a long time," Kāśyapa replied,
"By which path did you come?"
The Buddha replied,
"I went from my dwelling to the realm of Jambudvīpa to fetch the fruit of the Jambu tree,
and have now returned here. Kāśyapa said:
“The Great Śramaṇa possesses such swift supernatural powers that he was able to go there, take the fruit, and return within a short time; this Great Śramaṇa must also be an Arhat.”
The Buddha then showed him the fruit, saying:
"Kāśyapa! Have you ever seen this before?"
Kāśyapa said,
“I have never seen such a thing.
The Buddha said:
"Do you like to eat?
He replied,
"I like to eat."
The Buddha said,
"As you wish.
Kāśyapa ate the fruit and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
When the meal of fruits was finished, he personally offered with his own hands the various kinds of food and drink he had prepared.
After the Buddha had eaten and completed his ritual rinsing, he spoke a verse for Kāśyapa; having finished the benediction, he immediately returned to the foot of the tree.

On the second day, he again invited the Buddha to receive offerings. The Buddha, as before, entered into samādhi and went to Pūrvavideha to fetch āmalaka fruits, arriving first at the dwelling place of Kāśyapa.

Furthermore, on the third day, he invited the Buddha to receive offerings. The Buddha entered samādhi, went to the continent of Aparagoyānī to obtain the bilva fruit (kavita), and returned, arriving first at the dwelling place of Kāśyapa.

On the fourth day, he invited the Buddha to receive an offering. The Buddha immediately entered *samādhi* and, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, went to Uttarakuru to take naturally grown rice from the fields and brought it back in his alms bowl. He arrived first at Kāśyapa’s dwelling and sat down; only after a long while did Kāśyapa arrive.
Kāśyapa asked again:
"From which path have you come?
The Buddha replied:
“Kāśyapa! I have just gone to that continent of Uttarakuru, taken naturally produced rice, and brought it here.
Kāśyapa exclaimed:
"This great śramaṇa possesses such supernormal powers; he must have also attained the fruit of arhatship.
The Buddha then asked him, "Do you enjoy eating the food from the Northern Continent?"
He replied,
“I enjoy eating.
The Buddha said:
"As you wish.
After Kāśyapa had eaten, he marveled at what he had never before experienced; he then offered the various foods he had prepared to the Buddha.
When the Buddha had finished eating and completed his ritual rinsing of the mouth, he spoke a verse for Kāśyapa’s benefit and, having made his aspiration, returned to the foot of the tree.

On the following day, the World-Honored One personally took his alms bowl and went to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, proceeding as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to take celestial ambrosia, returning to the tree where he resided to eat it.
When the meal was finished, he thought of water for washing and rinsing.
Knowing that the Buddha was thinking of water, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, arrived at the Buddha’s location in the time it takes to extend one's arm and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Do you desire water to use?"
The Buddha said, "I desire water.
Śakra immediately observed a dried-up pond nearby; pointing his finger toward it, water instantly welled up, pure, fragrant, and clean beyond compare.
The Buddha then washed his mouth and used the items as he pleased.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, returned to his celestial palace.
When Kāśyapa suddenly saw this, he was struck with extraordinary wonder and astonishment:
"This dried-up pond has been without water for a long time; now it is full again, yet I do not know where it has come from.
He quickly went to the Buddha's dwelling and said to the Buddha, "Great Śramaṇa!..."
"This pond has been dry for a long time; by what cause does there now appear water?
The Buddha replied, "Today, after finishing my meal, I had no water for washing or rinsing. Śakra, knowing this from afar, descended from heaven to provide water for me."
Kāśyapa marveled, saying,
"How extraordinary!
To obtain food from the heavens and cause water to emerge from the heavens— to be able to manifest such power, he must surely have also attained arhatship."
Kāśyapa then established a name for the pool, calling it Paṇikhāta.

Later, when the Buddha entered the pool to bathe, there was a large tree on the bank named Ajiraṇa; the Buddha hung his *kāṣāya* robe upon this tree. When Kāśyapa arrived and saw the Buddha’s *kāṣāya* hanging on the tree, he knew the Buddha had been bathing and came to behold him.

When the Buddha had finished bathing, he emerged from the water onto the bank and extended his hand, intending to grasp a tree branch; at that moment, the branch of the *ajira* tree bent down of its own accord.
Kāśyapa saw this and again exclaimed in praise:
"This Great Śramaṇa is truly inconceivable; he has moved even an insentient thing to bend naturally. This Śramaṇa must have attained Arhatship."
Later, the World-Honored One thought of washing his robes and considered,
"How can I obtain stones for this purpose? Śakra,
knowing this from afar, immediately went to where the Buddha was and said:
“World-Honored One!
Does the Buddha wish to wash his robes using a stone?
The Buddha said:
"I require stone.

Śakra then commanded a yakṣa to go into the great mountain and fetch a single block of stone, which he had him fashion until it was level and smooth, and then polish it until it was radiant, before placing it beside the pond.
The Buddha then washed his robes; having finished washing them, he wished to dry them.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, again commanded a yakṣa to fetch a separate stone and place it on the bank of the pond. Once the Buddha had finished washing his robes, he went to the stone to dry them.
When Kāśyapa arrived, he again saw that there was suddenly a stone on the bank of the pond; he was struck with wonder and said to himself:
"This was not here before on the bank of the pond; from where has it come?"
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa!
From where did these stones on the bank of the pond originate?"
The Buddha replied, "I wished to wash my robes, but as there was no stone, I immediately gave rise to a thought; Śakra descended and provided one for me.
Again, I thought that there was no place to dry the robes, and that Lord Śakra again installed a stone."
"The two stones came from Śakra.
Kāśyapa marveled greatly:
"This great śramaṇa performs deeds that do not exist in the world; he must have already realized arhatship."
"However, that which you have realized should not surpass mine.

Kāśyapa’s mind seemed to undergo a moment of awakening; the World-Honored One, employing further skillful means, manifested another extraordinary sign to instruct Kāśyapa and lead him onto the Right Path.

The Buddha then miraculously caused the waters of the Nairañjanā River to suddenly overflow; many people living on its banks were swept away and drowned, while dried-up ponds and pools everywhere became filled. The place where the Buddha was staying happened to be right in the midst of this, yet by his supernatural power he caused the water to swirl around it, standing like a wall on all four sides with dust rising from its center.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw that the river was overflowing more than usual and thought to himself, "Will that Great Śramaṇa not be swept away?
Thereupon, he boarded a boat and hurried to the Buddha's location.

He saw the World-Honored One walking back and forth beneath a tree, with dust rising at every step; furthermore, because the surrounding water rose so high as to stand like a wall, he was unable to disembark from his boat. His sense of wonder was redoubled beyond the ordinary, and from afar he offered words of consolation, saying:
“Is the śramaṇa well?
Is he free from sorrow and affliction?
The Buddha said:
"I have no grief or distress; do not trouble yourself by trying to persuade me.
He then thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers himself; why does he not depart from here?"
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Do you wish to board a boat and depart from here?
The Buddha said:
"I wish to leave this place.
Kāśyapa replied,
"If you wish to leave, you should board the ship yourself."
By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha was already seated cross-legged within the boat in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
When Kāśyapa saw that the Buddha was already seated, he could not perceive where [the Buddha] had come from or how he had entered.
Kāśyapa praised him, saying:
"This śramaṇa is a great man of great majestic power; he possesses such supernatural faculties as this.
Kāśyapa then said:
“I myself have also attained the fruit of arhatship, yet it does not equal the path realized by this śramaṇa.
Knowing that Kāśyapa’s mind was firmly resolved to turn toward the Dharma, the Buddha immediately said to him:
“As for your claim that you have realized arhatship, it is not a true realization!”
When Kāśyapa suddenly heard the World-Honored One utter such words, the hair on his body stood on end, and he reproached himself, thinking:
"This Great Śramaṇa knows all my various affairs; it is now fitting that I take him as my teacher to advance in the Way."
Having thus resolved his thoughts, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa! Please be aware of my intention;

I now wish to go forth within the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa to become a member of the Saṃgha, receiving and following your instructions to practice the holy life (brahmacarya). I only pray that you will compassionately grant me your permission."
The Buddha, knowing that the time had come for Kāśyapa to realize the Way, and wishing to convert his followers through skillful means, said to Kāśyapa:
"If you wish to leave the household life within my Dharma to study the Path as a śramaṇa, have you already informed all your disciples of this?"
Kāśyapa replied,
“The disciple does not yet know.
The Buddha said:
"As you are a teacher of men, you must not act with such rashness.
You should return for now and deliberate with your disciples; if they agree, you may come again, and even then it will not be too late."
Kāśyapa, having received these instructions, returned to his residence. There, he gathered together with his five hundred disciples, including the Maṇava-kas, at one place and addressed them, saying:

"That Great Śramaṇa possesses extraordinary marks and signs, and his supernormal powers are difficult to equal. Whatever he does, the devas know from afar; sometimes they come before his seat to listen to his Dharma, and whenever he has any need, they are able to provide it for him. Having witnessed his miraculous transformations repeatedly, I am truly not his equal."
Now I wish to take him as my teacher, leave the household life, and advance upon the Way.
I have already reached this decision; what do you intend to do?
Deliberate carefully within yourselves and report the truth to me.
The māṇavaka said to Kāśyapa:
"That fire-dragon was the first of the violent and wicked ones to be subdued; his supernatural powers and his knowledge of others' minds were witnessed by all with their own eyes."
All that we practice has been transmitted from our own teacher; since the teacher himself has not yet attained [enlightenment], what can his disciples say?
If the teacher resolves his will, we shall all follow him;

if the teacher reaches the source of that school, we also pray that he grant us deliverance. We have already made this decision with one mind as a community; now, if it may be done, let there be no delay.

Thereupon, Kāśyapa, knowing the sincere aspiration of the assembly, ordered his disciples to take up their fire-worship implements—such as the *homa* ladle and various other vessels—as well as items such as deerskin robes, bark garments, water-pots, staffs, and leather sandals, and cast them all into the Nairañjanā River to demonstrate his resolve not to turn back. Master and disciples then proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa,
"Have you come again?
Kāśyapa replied:
"Now I have come together with my disciples, wishing to leave the household life and practice within the Dharma of the Great Śramaṇa.
The Buddha, having already known this beforehand, asked again for confirmation:
"Is it with sincere hearts that you and your disciples have come?"
Kāśyapa replied, "I and my disciples are all of sincere heart; we only pray that you will compassionately grant us all deliverance.
The Buddha then silently consented to ordain them as śramaṇas, and further addressed him, saying:
"You all have this morning truly gone forth; you are truly practicing the holy life (brahmacarya); having donned the saṃghāṭī robes, you are indeed śramaṇas.
At that time, Uruvilvākāśyapa, wearing the saṃghāṭī robes and having assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa, further heard the Buddha say:
"You have now truly gone forth; you are truly practicing the holy life."
I rejoiced within myself, for my [doubting] mind was completely extinguished.
Furthermore, I reflected:
"In the past, the Great Seer spoke of this matter:"

"It is rare in this world for a Buddha to appear; having attained unsurpassed enlightenment and possessing all-encompassing wisdom, this Great Sage is able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings in both the heavens and the human realm."

"In the past, when I went out at night to observe the stars, I saw a great mass of fire; thinking it was someone who worshipped fire and shared my own lineage, I realized it was actually Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings who had come to one another to listen to the Dharma."
"Now, regarding this matter, who else but a Great Sage could have done this? If he were not a Great Sage, who then would be a sage?
Thereupon, Kāśyapa changed his address from "Śramaṇa" and called the Buddha "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān).
The Sutra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Nine.
The Sutra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Subject Dharma-bhadra, the Great Master Mingjiao, by imperial decree.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa had two younger brothers:
one was named Nadī-Kāśyapa; [the other was named Gayā-Kāśyapa].
The second was named Gayākāśyapa.

Each of these two Kāśyapas had two hundred and fifty disciples, all of whom lived on the banks of the lower reaches of the Nairañjanā River, diligently practicing and training within their respective teachers' doctrines.

One day, while the two Kāśyapa brothers were by the Nairañjanā River, they suddenly saw the fire-offering implements of Uruvilvā Kāśyapa—such as the *homa* ladle and other utensils—as well as his deer skin, bark garments, and even his water flask, staff, and leather sandals, all floating down the river. They were struck with wonder and thought:
"Could it be that my elder brother Kāśyapa has met with royal peril?"
Have you encountered no difficulties from thieves?
Or even difficulties such as those caused by water or fire?
Is it because of such difficulties that you have regressed and lost your practice?
If it were not so, why would the various implements for fire-sacrifices be cast into the water to flow away by themselves?
One can know with certainty that a difference will surely be seen today.

Thereupon, the two younger brothers deliberated together repeatedly and set out to seek their elder brother, intending to ascertain the truth of the matter. Upon arriving at their brother’s dwelling, they did not see Kāśyapa or his disciples; there remained only the empty stillness of the place where they had lived.
At that time, the two Kāśyapas were overcome with even greater sorrow; they immediately went to their neighbors to inquire about the reason.
The neighbors replied, "Uruvilvā has abandoned the path of the sages and, taking his disciples with him, has gone to join the Śramaṇa."
"We do not know the matter; we request that you go there yourself to inquire into its cause.

When the two Kāśyapas heard this, they said to one another, "We have also heard that a śramaṇa has recently arrived here, whose every movement and gesture is extraordinary compared to ordinary people."
"If it should be true that my elder brother and his disciples have indeed become so, it would be an exceedingly rare occurrence.
We should now go there ourselves to observe whether it is real or not.

The two men went together to the Buddha's dwelling, where they finally saw their elder brother Uruvilvā and his disciples wearing saṃghāṭī robes and assuming the appearance of śramaṇas, all sitting before the Buddha, gazing up at him and listening to the Dharma.
At that time, the two Kāśyapas witnessed these events and thereby came to know the truth; their hearts were struck with alarm and their hair stood on end, so that they could not advance.
Seeing Nadi-Kāśyapa coming in search of his elder brother and standing before the assembly unable to proceed, the Buddha immediately sent Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa to rise and welcome him.

When the two Kāśyapas saw their elder brother leave his seat to welcome them, they immediately hastened forward to prostrate at his feet and inquire after his well-being. The two Kāśyapas said, "Our elder brother is advanced in years and possessed of virtue;

he has long practiced the path, and his vast learning and comprehensive mastery are peerless in this world. The King of Magadha, as well as his ministers and all the commoners, believe our brother has realized the state of an Arhat. They constantly bring various kinds of incense, flowers, food, drink, exquisite garments, and precious jewels to make offerings to him, and there is no one who does not faithfully believe whatever he says."
How is it that today you have suddenly abandoned your own path to follow another teaching?

We originally practiced according to your instructions, and even among the disciples, none followed a different course. Now that you yourself have abandoned what you originally cultivated, how can we continue to advance with firm resolve?
"Entangled in a great web of doubt, I pray that you will grant me an explanation.
Having spoken thus, he stood respectfully to one side.
Then, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa addressed Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, saying:

"In past ages when there was no Buddha, it was like a dark night; people lacked the eye of wisdom and did not know they were sinking and falling. During this time, I practiced with rigorous austerity, taking the service of fire as my merit and constantly praying for the realization of the Holy One.
Furthermore, I have used this path to instruct you all. No other person is able to surpass my way, and thus I claimed for myself that I had realized Arhatship."

There is a great śramaṇa called the Buddha, the World-Honored One; his body is sixteen feet tall and of a radiant golden hue, endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, and possessed of exceptionally sublime majesty and virtue. Out of compassion for me, he has come to dwell nearby.
All his movements and stillnesses were known by the heavens from afar;
the Four Great Heavenly Kings, up to Brahmā and Śakra, all came to listen to the Dharma;

furthermore, I witnessed his supernormal powers as he traveled back and forth among the four continents and even the heavens in a single kṣaṇa, bringing back the essence of sudhā, which he showed to me in its entirety.
Furthermore, he realized that I had not yet truly attained the path of an Arhat.

For this reason, he felt my way was inferior; out of self-reflection, he first felt sincere shame and regret, and subsequently went forth into homelessness with his disciples, casting himself in sincere devotion.
"Out of compassion for me, you have granted me deliverance, allowing me to don the dharma robes and enter the Saṃgha.
It was my fault that I did not inform you beforehand.

At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa, their faculties and conditions having already matured, gave rise to faith and devotion; hearing these words, they were overcome with a mixture of sorrow and joy, and spoke to their elder brother:
"I originally practiced because of my elder brother's instruction; now that you have abandoned me, I too wish to follow.
He further said:
"Were no Buddha to appear in the world, how could one ever hear the True Dharma? Though I am old and decrepit, I still hope for liberation."
Uruvilvā replied: "Excellent, excellent!
Now is precisely the right time."
Nadī-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa then went before the Buddha; having prostrated with their heads at his feet in salutation, they withdrew to stand to one side and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"My elder brother Uruvilvā was formerly my teacher;
having now gone forth as a śramaṇa, I too wish to go forth. I pray that you will grant me deliverance."
Although the Buddha silently consented, he nevertheless directed his disciples toward them and asked:
"Have you disciples all understood yet?
The two Kāśyapas replied:
“I do not yet know.
The Buddha said, “You may let him know; he will return to deliver you.”
Then the two Kāśyapas, having received the Buddha’s instruction, returned to their respective dwellings and gathered their disciples, addressing them, saying:
"Māṇavakas! Do you know yet?"

There is a great śramaṇa named Buddha who has come to dwell near our teacher Kāśyapa; he repeatedly manifests extraordinary signs through his supernormal powers, all of which our teacher has witnessed with his own eyes.

Furthermore, by means of his spiritual power, he has restrained [Kāśyapa’s] magical feats; thus our teacher, having attained realization and recognized that his own dharma was inferior, has led his assembly of disciples to join him and renounce the world.
Because I saw the articles of use he had discarded flowing down with the current, I went in person to investigate the circumstances of the matter.

Upon arriving there, I saw my teacher Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples, all wearing *kāṣāya* robes and appearing as śramaṇas, sitting together in the assembly listening to his preaching of the Dharma.
When I saw this, I was initially struck with great wonder and alarm and could not proceed further. My teacher Kāśyapa rose from his seat to welcome me, and I related the preceding events in detail.
Upon hearing of such an extraordinary excellence, he also wished to renounce the household life; however, remembering you all, I have returned to inform you.
"This is my intention; you all should reflect upon it and each report back to me with a heart of faith and sincerity.
After those two Kāśyapas had spoken these words, the assembly of Maṇava disciples said to Kāśyapa:
"We have practiced and studied according to what we received from our teacher; as for the teacher's discernment of the superior and the inferior, how could the disciples possibly know it?"
"Our teacher has already renounced the world to follow him; how can we continue to hold fast to our former ways?
If he is indeed resolved upon this, we too wish to follow him.

Thereupon, Nadī-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa each led their disciples to the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the assembly, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"Have you two come?
Then the two Kāśyapas replied:
"We have come," they said, and further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We have each brought our own disciples to seek refuge in the Buddha. We pray to go forth from home within the True Dharma, to receive and uphold the precepts (*śīla*), and to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
"I pray that the Buddha, out of great compassion and pity, will grant me permission.
The Buddha immediately accepted him and ordained him as a śramaṇa.
The Buddha further replied:
"Today, you have truly gone forth; today, you have truly entered the holy life.

When Kāśyapa and the others heard these words, they were filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. Each of them prostrated before the Buddha and circumambulated him; having finished, they stood gazing up at him in reverence.

At that time, having ordained the thousand bhikṣus including Kāśyapa and his followers, the World-Honored One departed from the site of Śītavana and, taking the elder Kāśyapa and the other thousand bhikṣus with him, proceeded to the stūpa on the summit of Mount Gayā to practice walking meditation.
Having arrived at Gayā, the Buddha manifested three kinds of deeds for the bhikṣus and others:
first, supernormal powers;
second, preaching the Dharma.
Third is subduing.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One entered samādhi and manifested signs of supernatural power; he vanished from his original seat and appeared in the void of the eastern sky, displaying the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;
furthermore, from his body he emitted five-colored rays of light, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson.

Furthermore, water issued from the upper part of his body and fire from the lower part; fire issued from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part; and he manifested these same signs even in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Having witnessed this miraculous manifestation, he returned to his original seat in an instant.
At that time, the World-Honored One again preached the Dharma to the bhikṣus, saying:

"Regarding all phenomena such as mind, mentation, and consciousness—whether you have doubt or no doubt, mindfulness or no mindfulness, or whether they are to be extinguished or not—you should practice with certainty within these phenomena."
He further addressed them, saying:
"You should know this!

With eye-consciousness as a condition, one craves various forms; because of contact with form, internal mental states arise—namely, suffering, pleasure, or that which is neither suffering nor pleasure. This is likewise true for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
"O Bhikṣus!
Just as it is with the fire of greed, so it is with hatred and delusion;
through these, one undergoes the cycle of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair."
"O Bhikṣus!

These three fires blaze fiercely with 'I' as their root. If you wish to extinguish these three fires, you must sever this root of 'I. Once the root of 'I' is severed, the three fires will naturally subside, and all the sufferings of saṃsāra within the three realms will spontaneously be cut off."

At that time, the three Kāśyapas and their thousand bhikṣus, having further received from the World-Honored One the manifestation of miraculous powers and the exposition of the True Dharma, attained the exhaustion of all outflows and the liberation of mind. Having accomplished what was to be done and laid down the heavy burden, they rightly attained their own benefit, forever severed the cycle of saṃsāra, and all fully realized the path of arhatship.
At that time, on the summit of Mount Gayā, the World-Honored One had led the three Kāśyapas and their thousand disciples to attain the path of Arhatship.

Then King Bimbisāra, along with his ministers, high officials, and even the commoners and citizens, all learned that the World-Honored One was on the summit of Mount Gayā, accompanied by a community of disciples numbering a full one thousand.
A certain high minister addressed the king, saying:

"I have heard recent talk among the people that a young boy has been born into the Śākya clan. At the time of his birth, there was a Brahmin skilled in physiognomy at the banks of the Sāṅgalika River near the Snowy Mountains—the former dwelling place of the sage Kapila—who examined him and declared:

'This boy is endowed with the marks of excellence and is perfected in merit and wisdom; he will certainly become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents under the great ocean, governing all within its bounds, administering the world through the True Dharma, and leading the people to practice the ten virtuous deeds.'"

Furthermore, there appeared naturally and followed him constantly the wheel-treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the general-treasure, the steward-treasure, the elephant-treasure, and the horse-treasure;
he also had a thousand sons of supreme physical beauty, endowed with great valor who could defeat enemies, and whose majesty caused all four continents to submit in fear.
"However, should he renounce the world, shave his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and practice with a rectified mind, he will surely attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Having related all these matters in detail to the king, he requested that the king act promptly so as not to cause future regret, saying, "If you can kill him, the kingdom will be preserved and you will enjoy ultimate good fortune."
At that time, King Bimbisāra sat alone upon the main throne, contemplating and constantly mindful of five matters:

first, he always prayed that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, would appear in the world;
second, that he might go there early to behold, pay homage to, and rejoice in [the Buddha].
Third, having arrived, one immediately hears the Dharma;
fourth, one is able to fully comprehend the Dharma as it is taught;
fifth, one receives the precepts for my sake, and having received them, upholds and practices them.
While he was reflecting on this matter, he suddenly heard the words of the ministers' deliberation; sighing in sorrow for a long time, he replied, saying:
"You are truly fools, wishing to give rise to such extreme malice toward the Tathāgata; this is great delusion."
"You may depart at once; do not speak further.
When the minister heard these words, knowing he was not permitted to comply, he withdrew in shame and fear.
At that time, King Bimbisāra looked toward his attendants and addressed a senior minister of noble appearance and perfect fortune who possessed great wisdom, saying:
"Go to the World-Honored One at the summit of Mount Gayā and, on my behalf, respectfully invite the World-Honored One.
Speak these words for me:

'King Bimbisāra bows his head to the World-Honored One’s feet with boundless reverence and inquires after the World-Honored One’s health, asking if he is free from illness and affliction, if his daily life is light and easy, and if he dwells in peace and happiness.'"
"I now entreat the World-Honored One to descend upon the palace city to graciously accept our offerings, so that I and the people there may obtain great benefit and happiness.

I pray that the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of noble elders and great virtuous ones, will all deign to come. For the remainder of this life, I shall provide food and drink, medicinal decoctions, bedding, robes such as the saṃghāṭī, and all other necessities, ensuring nothing is lacking. I pray that out of great compassion, you will not decline on account of the toil."
Having spoken thus, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and waited expectantly for the Sage’s instruction.
The Buddha remained silent.
Then the messenger, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, paid homage, circumambulated him, took his leave, and returned.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the messenger had returned, quickly proceeded to the front hall to receive the envoy’s audience.
Once the rites between sovereign and minister were concluded, he immediately asked:
"Has the World-Honored One come?"
He sent a messenger forward to report to the King, saying:
"I have received Your Majesty’s command and traveled to Mount Gayā to invite the Buddha and his assembly; I have conveyed Your Majesty’s instructions in full to the World-Honored One."
"The Buddha has already given his silent assent; he will surely come to attend.

At that time, the King issued an edict to his ministers and officials, commanding them to strictly purify the palace and the city walls, and to ensure that even the four main thoroughfares were entirely clean. Furthermore, they were to prepare various kinds of famous incenses and exquisite flowers to welcome him.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the elder Kāśyapa and a thousand arhats, departed from Mount Gayā and proceeded toward the royal city. Not far from the city was the Staff Grove Stūpa; the Buddha and the great assembly arrived at the stūpa and stayed there.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, having heard that the World-Honored One and the assembly of noble ones had arrived at the Staff Grove Stūpa and were settled there, immediately ordered his officials to prepare the royal carriage with attendants leading and following in front and behind. Together with his own kinsmen and various ministers, he wished to depart from the city and proceed to the site of the Staff Grove Stūpa.

Not long after they had left the palace, a pit suddenly appeared in the ground where the king’s chariot was traveling, causing the wheels to sink and the vehicle to stall. The king thought to himself:
"I must have committed unwholesome deeds in the past, resulting in such an event as this today."
No sooner had this thought arisen than he heard a voice in the air proclaiming:
"In the past, you committed no unwholesome karma; however, it is because there are currently many imprisoned within the various prisons that you have fallen into this wheel-trap."

Upon hearing these words of emptiness, the King was certain that they were those of a sage; having received such instruction, his heart was moved with profound gratitude. He immediately dispatched messengers to all the prisons to grant amnesty according to the degrees of the offenses, from light to heavy.
As the royal carriage proceeded forward to the city gate, the king’s precious crown suddenly broke once more. He reflected again, saying:
"I must have surely committed unwholesome deeds in the past, for today such ill omens occur one after another."
When the King gave rise to this thought, the worthies and sages in the air spoke to him again, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!

You have no unwholesome karma from the past; however, it is because of those prisoners you previously confined—those who were light offenses having already been released, while those with heavy offenses, though alive, remain bound in separate locations—that this omen of the crown breaking has occurred."
When the king heard the words of the sages from the sky, he immediately dispatched messengers to summon them from all quarters; once they had all arrived before his chariot, he pardoned them all.
Having escaped their punishment, the criminals leaped for joy and praised the king’s virtue.

At that time, the king’s retinue and various kinsmen had twelve thousand chariots; furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of chariots belonging to the brahmins, elders, and common people of the kingdom, all of whom departed through the city gate together to visit the World-Honored One.

At that time, the king went to the Kāśyapa Stūpa at Yaṣṭivana; there, within a nearby grove, he gathered five *karkārava* flowers, which he held in his own hands as he proceeded to the Buddha’s location. Not far from the Buddha, he alighted from his carriage and walked on foot, setting aside his parasol, sword, staff, and other such items, while ordering his attendants to follow him.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and three times declared:
“I am King Bimbisāra. The Buddha likewise confirmed this three times:

"So it is! So it is! The king then offered five flowers to the Buddha, thereafter prostrated himself with his head to the ground at the Buddha's feet, and further extended his praise with various words of commendation.
The Buddha replied, “Please, Your Majesty, take your seat.

Once the king had ascended his throne, the king’s retinue, along with the brahmins, elders, commoners, and citizens, took their places in order, prostrating before the Buddha with joyful exultation. Each of them praised the World-Honored One with verses; having finished their hymns of praise, they withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa—who had previously been revered by the king, the ministers, and all the officials and commoners of the land—was now standing in attendance beside the Buddha as a śramaṇa. The king and the people could not help but feel suspicion and wonder, and they all thought to themselves:

"The elder Kāśyapa has long practiced the asceticism of serving the sacrificial fire; his wisdom and moral virtue have always surpassed those of others. Yet now, he stands among this assembly, giving rise to our doubts."
"Is it that the Tathāgata is following Kāśyapa’s instruction,
or is it that Kāśyapa is following the Tathāgata’s instruction?
As he was thinking this, the Buddha perceived it through his profound insight and said to Kāśyapa:
"You know the time yourself.

Accepting the Buddha’s holy command, Kāśyapa did not rise from his seat but entered *samādhi*. He vanished from his original place and appeared in the eastern direction, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
Furthermore, his body emitted light of five colors—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson—which were intermingled like crystal.

Furthermore, water issued from the upper part of his body and fire from the lower part; fire issued from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part. This was likewise the case in the south, the west, and even the north.
Having manifested these supernatural transformations, he suddenly returned to the assembly, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"In the past, I practiced the way of fire-worship, Serving it for many years; my efforts were in vain."
In his mind he constantly thought, "I have already realized arhatship," yet clinging to the mark of a self, he was unable to attain liberation.
Out of great compassion, the Buddha came to deliver him.
He regulates the fire so that it does not burn, yet causes it not to go out.
At first he thought we were like him, also serving the fire;
but when I said there was nothing to be sought, he asked, "What is the use of serving the fire?"
In the heavens above and the world below, there is nothing to which I am attached.
I have established this Dharma assembly solely for the sake of seeking gain and offerings;
whether you wish to come or not, may you all understand my intention.
Furthermore, from the four continents and even from those celestial realms,
he gathered fruits and rice and gave them all to me to eat.
I served the sacrificial fire, yet I was deluded regarding the correct practice.
They are like the blind and like the dead;
lacking vision and knowledge, they are certain to fall.
The Mahāmuni is like a great dragon.
Spreading clouds of diligence, he showers the rain of nectar,
benefiting all beings, both sentient and insentient.
Desiring liberation, I seek to become a śramaṇa.
Relying on the Great Compassion of the Buddha, you have preached the Dharma of purity;
through these supreme words, you have caused us to attain awakening.
I have now truly realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The Buddha is my teacher, and I am his disciple;
may all people know this and harbor no doubts.
These are words of truth, which you should faithfully believe.
When Kāśyapa had finished speaking these verses, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his original seat.
At that time, the great assembly, including the king and the people, truly knew that Kāśyapa was a disciple of the Buddha.
Knowing that the doubts of the assembly had been stilled, the Buddha said to the king:
"I shall now expound for you the essential points of the Dharma; you should listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
The king and the assembled multitude received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"Great King!

You should now know this: just as the physical form of the king is subject to arising and ceasing, you must carefully examine these two characteristics of arising and ceasing until you understand them truly;
furthermore, observe that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise identical to form.
"Good son!
If one can thus understand, as it truly is, that these are subject to arising and ceasing, one should further observe that they are not subject to arising and ceasing.
If one can understand that form is not subject to arising and ceasing, then one knows that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not subject to arising and ceasing."
Good son!

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing; they have no going and no coming. If one can understand them as they truly are—fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, with no going and no coming—one likewise does not abide in that which is neither arising nor ceasing, nor in that which has no going and no coming.
"Great King!
If one understands these dharmas as they truly are, one will immediately attain countless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) dharmas of quiescence.
At that time, among all the brahmins, elders, and commoners in the assembly, there were some who conceived doubts:

“World-Honored One, since you now teach that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are fundamentally non-existent, how can there be the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, the mark of a life-span, the mark of a *puṇḍarīka*, the mark of a *māṇavaka*, or marks such as a sovereign or one who performs service?”

If these marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, and so forth are also truly non-existent, how can one know that those sentient beings perform two kinds of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—and having abandoned these aggregates, proceed again toward other aggregates?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts that had arisen within that assembly, addressed Kāśyapa and the others, saying: "O Bhikṣus!

All views concerning a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span belong to foolish, ordinary worldlings; if one holds such views, one shall experience suffering. If one knows the arising of suffering, one should seek the cessation of suffering."
"O Bhikṣus!

Because the various conditioned phenomena of cause and effect arise from the transformation of the tranquil seed, I have known this for myself; desiring to cause sentient beings to likewise know the phenomena of arising and ceasing as I do, I have taught it."
"O Bhikṣus!

The Buddha’s eye is pure, surpassing that of the devas and others. Regarding all sentient beings—their auspicious signs and inauspicious signs, their noble birth and lowly birth, their virtuous aspirations and evil aspirations—I now know each and every one of them as they truly are, according to the karma of those beings. I know that the bodily actions of sentient beings are endowed with such qualities, their verbal actions are endowed with such qualities, and their mental actions are endowed with such qualities."

Briefly stated, sentient beings give rise to wrong actions through their false views, or they produce slander toward the Buddha-dharma; because of such karma, after the end of their lives, they fall into the evil realms and undergo all manner of suffering.
"O Bhikṣus!
