If there are sentient beings who perform various wholesome deeds of body and speech, possessing right view, right conduct, and right action, and who always rejoice in and praise the Buddha-dharma, by virtue of these wholesome roots, after the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the Heaven of the Well-Gone (Sugata)."
"O Bhikṣus!

I possess such knowledge and vision that it is not the case that I am unable to know the mark of a self (*ātman*), the mark of a person (*pudgala*), the mark of a sentient being (*sattva*), the mark of a life-span (*jīva*), the mark of a *buddhagra* (individual soul), the mark of a *manava* (young man), or even the marks of a sovereign or a servant; nor do I fail to know the various causes and effects of good and evil actions, or how, having abandoned these aggregates, one proceeds toward other aggregates—such matters as these also do not exist [as inherently real]."
I have already explained previously that the various conditioned phenomena of cause and effect arise from causes and cease because of causes, namely:

with ignorance as cause, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair arise. Through these causal conditions, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being.

"O Bhikṣus! If its causes are extinguished, everything is extinguished. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;

with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases."
"O Bhikṣus!
Because the accumulation of causes is extinguished, suffering naturally ceases; if suffering is brought to rest, one attains the bliss of Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, when the mark of self is forever severed and correctly extinguished without recurrence, one realizes that suffering does not exist—how could there be anything to extinguish? This is the attainment of cessation, this is the attainment of coolness; free from all conceptual formulations, this is Nirvāṇa."
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha, the Mahāsudarśana, Scroll Ten.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha, the Mahāsudarśana, Scroll Eleven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, Your Minister Dharmaśrī, respectfully translated by imperial decree:
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"Do you regard form as permanent or impermanent?"
The King said,
"It is not permanent.
The Buddha said:
"Is this suffering or not?
He replied, "It is suffering."
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
He replied:
"It is impermanent.
He asked again,
"Is it suffering or is it not suffering?"
He replied, "It is suffering.
The Buddha said:
“Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent, suffering, subject to inversion, and entirely without self.
The Buddha further addressed him, saying:
“Great King!

One should observe its reality with right knowledge and right wisdom: do those aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness exist in the past, the present, or the future?
“Are there internal and external, coarse and subtle, noble and base, distant and near?
He replied, “Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither past, nor present, nor future.”
"Nor is it internal or external, coarse or subtle, noble or base, distant or near.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Great King!"

If one can understand these five aggregates as they truly are—knowing them to be impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—and further perceives their reality with right wisdom, knowing them to belong neither to the past, present, nor future, and even extending to the internal and external, the coarse and the subtle, the noble and the base, the distant and the near, and is furthermore able to neither cling to nor reject them, this is true liberation.
"Great King!

One who attains this liberation possesses the liberation of wisdom; the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, birth has been exhausted, and one shall never again enter the path of saṃsāra."

At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, King Bimbasāra and eighty thousand devas and humans were distanced from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; likewise, a multitude of one hundred thousand people, including brahmins, elders, and commoners, were also distanced from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

Thereupon, King Bimbasāra, having attained the vision and knowledge of the Dharma, became firm in the Dharma, severed his craving and attachment, removed all doubt, and with unshakable right faith, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
My mind is supple and compliant; I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and I observe the precepts of a lay follower, forever abstaining from taking life.

I now entreat the World-Honored One to dwell permanently in my kingdom, and I vow to offer robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for as long as I live, never lacking anything, and to provide offerings to the entire assembly of noble ones throughout their lifetimes.
The Buddha remained silent.

Seeing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately prostrated himself, placing his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and then took his leave and withdrew.

At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus saw King Bimbisāra, having been taught the sublime Dharma by the Blessed One, attain the pure Dharma-eye—free from dust and free from defilement—without rising from his seat; they all felt doubt in their minds:
"How is it that this king, upon meeting the Blessed One, immediately heard the Dharma and realized the purity of the Dharma-eye, thereby removing the dust and defilements?"
Having formed this thought, the Buddha knew it intuitively and addressed them, saying:

"O Bhikṣus! This King Bimbisāra performed great wholesome deeds in the past; what he did was certain and its retribution is unfailing. Now, as a human king, he possesses great merit and virtue; such is the fruit he has experienced due to causes from his previous lives."
"O Bhikṣus!

When the external elements of earth, water, fire, and wind undergo transformation, all things—whether beautiful or ugly—within the aggregates, the elements, and the six sense faculties, will unfailingly receive their retribution in accordance with the virtuous or non-virtuous karma they have committed."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Whatever beings have done—whether good or evil—even across a hundred kalpas, cannot be destroyed by karma;
its retribution will surely be received by oneself."
“O Bhikṣus! In times past, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Araṇābhi, who was fully endowed with the ten titles and served as a teacher for gods and humans.
At that time, the World-Honored Buddha taught various dharmas to all sentient beings; having completed his work of transformation and benefit, he immediately entered nirvāṇa.”
His disciples collected his relics and, selecting a pure site, erected a magnificent stupa, constantly making offerings of various incenses and flowers.

After a long period of years had passed since then, a wheel-turning monarch appeared in the world named Kalkī; at that time, he possessed an army of eighteen koṭis, which he constantly led through the air on inspection tours, with the seven treasures always preceding him.
Later, on one day as he was passing over a stūpa, a spirit of the void seized his precious wheel and held it in mid-air so that it would not proceed.
At that time, King Kṛkī reflected upon this matter:
"Now as I travel, the precious wheel has stopped of its own accord; I fear this is a manifestation of my merit being exhausted."
The spirit of space then addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
It is not that your merit is exhausted; rather, below lies a stupa containing the relics of the Buddha Arāḍa. Your precious wheel-treasure cannot proceed directly because of this."

At that time, King Kṛkī, together with eighteen koṭis of flying troops, descended simultaneously to the site of the stūpa. The king and his retinue each used exquisite garments to wipe the Buddha’s stūpa; once it was purified, they scattered various wonderful flowers, burned precious incense, and performed all kinds of music as offerings. Prostrating themselves with their heads at the ground, they made this vow:
"By virtue of the various merits of the offerings I have now presented to the Buddha as my teacher, may the retribution thereof not be in vain, and may I obtain its fruits in the future."
"O Bhikṣus! What do you think?
That Cakravartin King Kṛkī and his retinue were none other than King Bimbisāra and his retinue."
"O Bhikṣus!

By virtue of the various merits of having made offerings to the stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One Araṇābhi, they shall experience the most supreme happiness among gods and humans for countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas. Through the power of their original vows, they now encounter me and again perform offerings; the merit thus obtained is equal and no different from that of the Perfectly Awakened One Araṇābhi."
"O Bhikṣus!
All sentient beings who perform black karma continue with black karma; those who perform white karma do not sever white karma; and it is likewise for those who perform mixed karma."
“O Bhikṣus!
All karmic fruits obtained arise from causes and actions; you should know this and explain it extensively for others.

At that time, within the assembly, the community of bhikṣus—having seen King Bimbisāra see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, thereby becoming free from dust and defilement, and having heard the account of his past lives—conceived doubts regarding Uruvilvā.

"How is it that the World-Honored One manifests supernatural powers and employs various means of instruction before they can turn their hearts? Since Nandika and Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa have been transformed by his words, and since the Buddha possesses great compassion and all-encompassing wisdom, he will surely be able to sever our doubts."
Having formed this thought, he was about to pose his question when the Buddha addressed him, saying:
"The ripening of results from cultivated causes is certainly not in vain."
"O Bhikṣus!

In a past kalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. That Buddha also performed great buddha-work in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī; having completed his work of transforming and benefiting others, he entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, there was a king named Kṛkin who constantly venerated and made offerings to that Buddha.

After the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, the king cremated the World-Honored One with various kinds of fragrant wood and extinguished the remaining embers by sprinkling milk. He then collected the relics and stored them in four precious jars, and further selected an auspicious site to erect a great jeweled stūpa.
That stūpa rose to a height of one yojana, and the king and the people constantly made offerings to it.

At that time, there was an elder in that country whose family wealth equaled that of Vaiśravaṇa; he had many kinsmen and enjoyed sovereign happiness. Previously, he had been a friend to an elder of another clan, and he regularly made extensive offerings at the Buddha’s stūpa.
Later, he married into that family as an alliance, and after many years had passed, three sons were born to him.

Subsequently, the eldest son reached old age and fell ill; though he took medicine, it did not cure him, and he gradually became emaciated and exhausted until he met his end. The three sons then buried him according to ritual in the charnel ground.
At that time, the three sons, recollecting their father’s instructions, wept morning and evening; moreover, mindful of their family’s wealth, they deliberated together on how to cultivate merit.
The eldest brother, being stingy and previously ignorant of goodness, was initially hesitant upon hearing of the desire to give alms, but with filial piety at heart, he soon gave his consent.
The eldest brother said, "Apart from what is given in alms, the remaining portion shall serve for our personal enjoyment.
The two younger brothers assented, and immediately taking gold, silver, and various kinds of wealth, they went to the stupa and performed the most supreme offerings.
Having thus given these gifts, they together made this vow:

"By the fruit of the merit produced by these roots of goodness, may we, in a future life, have the name Kāśyapa—just as the present Perfectly Enlightened One is named—as our family name; may we likewise encounter a Buddha appearing in the world, and upon hearing the Dharma, may we believe and understand it, realizing Bodhi."
Having made this vow, he prostrated, circumambulated me, and returned home with joy.
For this reason, Kāśyapa has now obtained this clan name; he encountered me and became a śramaṇa, and further, having heard the True Dharma, he realized the fruit of arhatship.
"O Bhikṣus!

As for Uruvilvā, who was initially difficult to convert, it was because in his past lives he harbored hesitation when wishing to practice giving; therefore, I had to manifest various supernatural transformations before he could attain realization.
As for Nadī-Gayā, who was easily converted, this was also because in the past, at the time of practicing giving, his mind was fundamentally pure and remained unchanged from beginning to end."
"O Bhikṣus!

Therefore, Uruvilvā and Nadi-gaya, who were brothers and bore the Kāśyapa clan name, further encountered me, heard the Dharma, and realized the Path. You should believe these events of the past with true conviction."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had related this account of Kāśyapa’s past lives, he departed from the Staff Grove Stūpa and stayed beneath a tree not far from the city of Rājagṛha, surrounded by a community of one thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, because the Buddha was dwelling nearby, desired to establish a vihāra to provide a place for the Buddha and the Saṅgha to reside permanently.

When King Bimbisāra was still a crown prince, he used to go outside the city to enjoy himself. Not far from the city there was a park with lush, verdant trees and clear springs and ponds; though the flowers and bamboos flourished constantly through all four seasons, the prince took a liking to it and wished to purchase it.

The elder who owned the park, relying on his own advanced age as well as his great wealth, refused to comply with the prince’s demand to take it by force. He spoke insolent words to the prince, saying: [The text continues with the elder's refusal and the subsequent events.]
"I would rather leave this kingdom than abandon this garden.
Having heard this, the Prince said to his attendants, "Now these elders have spoken most insolently; if I succeed to the throne, I shall not forget this."
Later, after his father King Mahāpadma had passed away, he was consecrated and invested with the title of king.
Once King Bimbisāra had ascended the throne, he recalled the previous events and issued an order to the relevant authorities to dispatch envoys to seize [the kingdom].
At that time, the elder suddenly suffered a heart ailment and passed away.

Following his death, because of his accumulated resentment and malevolent malice, he was reborn within the garden in the realm of snakes; harboring venom, he waited for an opportunity to avenge his former grievance.
Later, on a certain day during the spring festival, the king took his consorts and attendants to that garden to enjoy themselves to the utmost and indulge their desires.
While the king was resting there, exhausted from his revelry, a venomous snake, perceiving its opportunity, quickly emerged from its burrow, intending to sting the king.
At that time, the ladies of the court were wandering about for recreation;

the king had one close attendant who carried a sword to guard against any unforeseen danger. There was a bird named Kalandaka that frequented the garden, drinking and feeding as it soared about. Suddenly, seeing a snake emerge, the birds called out to one another with a clamor. Upon seeing the snake appear, the attendant carrying the sword immediately took its life.
The flock of birds became extremely noisy, and the king also woke up in alarm.
He asked his sword-bearer, "For what reason is there such a commotion? The sword-bearer replied:
"A venomous serpent was about to come and bite Your Majesty when the peacocks called out to one another in alarm; having witnessed this with my own eyes, I have already taken the life of that snake.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s heart was struck with terror and his hair stood on end. He summoned the crown prince and the various ministers to deliberate upon this matter:
"If a Kṣatriya anointed Great King of antiquity were to face a threat to his very life, and someone were to rescue him through loyal effort, what reward should be granted?"
The minister replied,
"Whoever can deliver one from this peril to life and limb shall be rewarded with half the kingdom.
The king then granted his consent and bestowed half the kingdom upon Kalandaka to reward him for his service.
The minister replied, "That Kalandaka is but a species of bird; what use would it have for the kingdom's territory?
The king said to the minister:
"What should be done about this?
The minister replied,
"One should plant many bamboos and trees near its nest so that it may fulfill its natural inclinations, and ensure that no harm comes to it."
"This is acceptable; nothing else can be done.
Upon hearing this, the king said, "Excellent!"

He then followed this proposal; he selected a separate location outside the grove, planted bamboo and trees extensively, established the Kalandakas there, and ordered men to guard them so that they would not be harmed.

The king had a maternal uncle who originally followed the path of the sages; constantly seeking a pure place to advance his practice, the king temporarily granted him the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, as it was free from all impurities, to dwell therein.
When he saw that the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, was resting in the open air beneath a tree near the city, he thought of abandoning that [previous plan] to construct a vihāra.
The King then prepared his carriage and went in person to the Buddha’s location; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the king, employing various skillful means to transform him and bring him joy; he further exhorted him to be diligent and to seek the supreme peace and happiness.

At that time, having heard the Dharma, the king was filled with joy and received it upon the crown of his head. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in prostration, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I now invite the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones to partake of a meal within my palace at dawn tomorrow. I only pray that you will compassionately and mercifully grant me your permission."
The Buddha remained silent.
At that time, the Great King, seeing the Buddha’s silence, knew that his invitation had been accepted; he rejoiced and leaped for joy, prostrated himself, and returned home.

He then issued orders to the relevant officials to quickly prepare various kinds of food and drink, as well as incense and flowers, making them all twice as exquisite, beautiful, and pure as usual. Furthermore, he commanded that the interior and exterior of the palace city, even down to the four-way intersections and alleys, be made entirely magnificent and clean.
As soon as dawn broke, he dispatched a messenger to inform the World-Honored One:
"The meal is prepared; we pray that the Buddha will deign to descend.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with a thousand arhats, donned their robes and took up their alms bowls, proceeding toward the royal palace surrounded by his attendants before and behind.

At the entrance of the gate, the king held an incense burner and burned incense, awaiting the arrival of the World-Honored One. Once the Buddha had arrived, he welcomed him inside and invited him to take his seat; the assembly of noble disciples likewise each took their seats. After the king and his retinue had completed their prostrations and veneration, they presented food and drink, burning incense and scattering flowers as offerings with great joy.

When the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones had finished their meal and washed their hands, the king and his retinue, desiring to hear the Dharma, listened as the Buddha preached it; each listened attentively with joy and received it with faith.
The King rose again from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"I now wish to offer this Karṇakagvha Bamboo Grove as a vihāra for the Buddha; I pray that the Buddha will graciously accept it."
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had granted his permission, the king immediately took a golden pitcher and poured water over the Buddha’s hand.

Having completed the offering, he said, "May the Buddha dwell as he pleases," and then he extensively prepared magnificent decorations for the World-Honored One; the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones resided there according to their pleasure.
The Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery was established because of this.

At a later time, for the sake of their benefit and happiness, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of noble ones, departed from the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery and went to the Śītavana forest to practice walking meditation and sit in quietude.

At that time, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha who invited the Buddha and his assembly for a meal offering on the following morning; thus, during that night, he, together with his kinsmen, servants, and attendants, prepared the food, drink, incense, flowers, and other necessary items.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having business to attend to, arrived at Rājagṛha and passed by that house; encountering the night, he stayed there for the evening and saw that all the elders and children in the housekeeper’s home were not sleeping, but were busy preparing various kinds of food and delicacies.
Finding this strange, he asked:
"In your household, both the elderly and the young are sleepless as they prepare food and drink; what purpose does this serve?
Are you inviting the King?"
"Is it because you have invited a high minister?
Or is there a gathering for the sake of marriage relations?
The householder replied:
"I did not invite the King or his ministers, nor was there any gathering of kinsmen.

However, because a Buddha has now appeared in the world and is traveling through this country with a thousand holy disciples, the King, his retinue, the ministers, and the common people have all turned toward him and are making offerings in succession."
"I have prepared a meal for that Buddha and his holy assembly for tomorrow morning; therefore, I shall not sleep.
Having heard these words, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada marveled at this extraordinary matter and asked again:
"What is meant by the term 'Buddha'?"

He replied, "In that Śākya clan there is a king named Śuddhodana who has fathered a son called Siddhārtha. He possesses the marks of a universal monarch (cakravartin), yet he renounced the world and practiced asceticism; having attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), he is indeed a Buddha."
Again he asked:
"What is the noble assembly? He replied:

"There are those from the Kṣatriya caste or the Brāhmaṇa caste, and even from the Vaiśya or Śūdra castes—such sons of noble family who have gone forth from home into homelessness under the Buddha, shaving off their hair and beards and donning the kāṣāya robes; with right faith they practice, hearing the Dharma and attaining realization, and all have fully realized the path of Arhatship."
"These are the one thousand noble disciples who follow the Buddha; it is precisely for them that I am making this offering.
Upon hearing these words, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s body hair stood on end with joy and he leaped for gladness, asking again:
"How may I come to see that Buddha and his noble assembly?"
He replied, "Come all together to my house tomorrow morning to receive food.
Although the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard these words, he was as if driven by madness; without waiting for the break of dawn, he desired to go to the Buddha’s dwelling.

At that time, it was the middle of the night, and the moon was bright and clear; he immediately went out his door and proceeded toward the Śītavana forest. Before he had reached the halfway point, the moon was suddenly obscured by clouds. Upon arriving at another gate, he did not dare advance further. Because the sky was overcast and dark, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada became terrified and stood still, reflecting:
"Could it be that some non-human beings have come here to harass me?"
His heart desired to turn back and his feet would not move forward.
At that time, a celestial being raised his voice and proclaimed:
"Householder, simply go; do not harbor a mind of retreat. There is only auspiciousness; there will certainly be no affliction or disturbance."
What do you think?

For example, suppose there were a hundred chariots and a hundred horses, variously adorned and decorated, such that all who see them would find them delightful; yet the merit of giving such a gift does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the merit of taking a single step forward toward the Buddha.
He spoke again, saying:
"Householder, simply go; do not let your mind turn back. There will be only auspiciousness and no disturbances.
What do you think?"

For example, even if one were to give as an act of charity a hundred golden elephants adorned with various jewels, the merit of taking a single step forward toward the Buddha would be sixteen times greater than that.
"O Householder!

Even if one were to give as alms a hundred young maidens, their bodies adorned with pearls, necklaces, and various jewels, this merit would still not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of taking a single step toward the Buddha."
At that time, the celestial being emitted light from his body that illuminated the path, shining from that gate all the way to the Śītavana forest, no different from the full brilliance of the moon.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada then asked the deva,
"Which noble being is capable of performing such a deed?
The deva replied:
"In the past, I was the mother of Śāriputra, named Nāgarāya.
After my life ended, I was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings; I am now known as Mātusajñātamānavaka, and I stand here guarding this gate."
"Do not harbor any doubts; you may go, O Elder, and you shall surely obtain auspiciousness.
Having heard these words, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍika praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"How rare is this matter! I shall now certainly go to see the Buddha;
of this there is no doubt. Anāthapiṇḍada further reflected:
"If a Perfectly Awakened One did not appear in the world, there would be no way to hear the most supreme and wondrous Dharma."
Thereupon, the elder obtained unobstructed light and proceeded directly to the World-Honored One’s dwelling in the Śītavana cemetery.

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking back and forth outside the Śītavana cemetery. When the elder saw the Buddha’s majestic virtue and his marks and signs, which were extraordinary compared to those of ordinary people, he immediately joined his palms and asked:
"Is this the World-Honored One?"
The Buddha replied,
“It is so. The elder’s body and mind were filled with immeasurable joy.
Again, he asked:
"Who in this world can sleep in peace?
The Buddha answered him with these verses:
"If a person's mind is tranquil, they shall sleep in peace;
if a person is bound by defiled desire, their feverish affliction will not cease.
When the feverish affliction of defiled desire is removed, one is liberated and free from all bonds."
"When the mind has been tamed, one attains rest and sleeps in peace.
Having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One entered the grove together with the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.

The Buddha returned to his original seat; the elder immediately stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side, desiring to hear the Dharma. The Buddha then exhorted him, causing his heart to rejoice.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder, saying:
"Through giving and observing the precepts, one may be reborn in the heavens; yet though one may exercise mastery over the five desires there, it is not the ultimate goal.
To escape the cycle of saṃsāra, one must sever the afflictions and extensively discern between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas."

At that time, having heard this Dharma, the elder contemplated it deeply through the power of his past roots of goodness; his obscurations were immediately removed, and his mind was filled with immeasurable joy.
Knowing this, the Buddha then extensively expounded for him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that time, the elder did not rise from his seat to realize the principle of the Four Noble Truths; like a clean white cloth easily dyed, whatever color it was dyed with became supremely exquisite.

Having attained the vision of the Dharma and forever severed his doubts, the householder’s faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha became firm and steadfast. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage, prostrated himself, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; I shall observe the precepts of a lay follower and never again take life.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the elder, "What is your name?"

The householder replied, "In this kingdom, I possess some small measure of wealth; whenever there are those who are poor, destitute, or solitary and come to beg from me, I provide them with food, drink, and their necessary requisites. Therefore, the people of the kingdom call me 'Giver of the Solitary' (Anāthapiṇḍada)."
"What is the name of your country?
He replied, "Śrāvastī."

I pray that the Buddha and the assembly will deign to descend to my kingdom; I shall offer them clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities for their use, providing them throughout my entire life.
The Buddha said, "Householder!
I and my bhikṣus number more than a thousand; without a vihāra, how could we dwell?"
The elder replied, "If the Buddha would deign to descend, we shall quickly erect it; I only pray that your great compassion will not refuse my request.
The Buddha remained silent.

Seeing that the Buddha remained silent, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika knew that his invitation had been accepted. Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and withdrew.

Thereupon, the householder entered the city of Rājagṛha; having completed the construction work, as he was about to return home, he went once more to the Śītavana forest to invite the Buddha and the assembly, saying, "Do not worry about the vihāra; I pray that you will deign to descend there at your earliest convenience."
Having spoken thus, he returned home.

From that day forward, all other activities were suspended as he searched throughout the city of Śrāvastī, both inside and out, for an exceptionally sublime and pure site where he might construct a vihāra to provide a dwelling for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
"Only the garden of Prince Jeta is most excellent. Why is this?

This prince’s garden has vast grounds free from all impurities; its bamboo and trees are lush, and its springs and ponds are pure. Neither cold winds nor summer heat can invade it, nor are there mosquitoes, gadflies, or venomous insects; there are only auspicious birds and beasts."
Furthermore, it is neither too far from nor too near the royal city; those who do not seek the Dharma cannot reach this place, and if a vihāra were built here, it would be most excellent.
Having finished his reflections, he went at once to Jeta, the son of the garden owner, and said to him:
“Young man, do not be alarmed; I have a matter of great importance that I wish to report to you.”
"If you, young man, will allow it, I shall venture to speak. The youth replied,
"If there is something to be said, please speak."
The elder rose and said to the youth,
"I wish to purchase this grove in order to construct a vihāra for the World-Honored One and his thousand holy followers, and to invite them to dwell therein."
"Venerable sir, if you will grant me your consent, I shall immediately pay the price.
Jeta the youth said to the elder,
"Everything may be yours, but do not speak of the garden."
The elder spoke again:
"I have heard the Buddha say:
'All things are impermanent and have no master; one should exchange non-durable dharmas for that which is durable.'"
The youth replied, "This is not within my knowledge; do not speak of it further.
The elder spoke again:
“A Buddha is difficult to encounter, yet a garden is easy to find; if you hesitate now, it will be too late for offerings later.
Although Prince Jeta heard these words, his heart was still unable to relinquish the land, so he constrained the elder with a challenge:
“If you can cover the ground entirely with gold, I shall give it to you, and you may do as you please.”
The elder, knowing that [the boy] might not yet be sincere and trustworthy, replied, saying:
"Young man, if it is so, you may inform the market official; he shall ensure that the two parties' feelings remain firm and without reversal."
As the youth and the official looked up and down together and consulted one another, the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing this matter from afar, thought:

"A Buddha has now appeared in the world; in the city of Śrāvastī, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada is purchasing Prince Jeta’s garden to establish a vihāra, and these two are consulting each other to seek the decision of the market official."
"I shall now transform my body to bring this matter to completion.
Having transformed his body into that of a market official, the Heavenly King went to the marketplace and waited expectantly for Anāthapiṇḍada and the boy to arrive.
When the two men had arrived, Anāthapiṇḍika spoke first:

"I wish to purchase that grove to build a vihāra; let it be covered entirely with gold coins spread over the ground, and if you can do so, I shall give it to you. I have come now to finalize the agreement."
"What is this price?
The market official said,
"Have the two of you reached an agreement on whether it is acceptable or not?"
He replied, "It has been settled.
The market official said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Let the youth take back the gold, and let the elder receive the park.
The youth remained silent, without further objection or regret.

On that very day, the elder quickly mobilized his carriages, vehicles, elephants, horses, and even his servants to transport the gold, distributing it everywhere until only a small portion remained before him, which had not yet been fully covered.
The elder deliberated:
"Which treasury of gold should I take to cover this entire ground?
At that moment, the youth said:
"You have already changed your mind; you may now take the gold.
The elder replied, "My mind has not changed.
I was merely considering where to store the gold so that it would cover this entire ground; for this reason, I reflected for a short while."
The youth reflected:
"How marvelous!
This elder is able to relinquish such vast wealth to construct a vihāra for the Buddha and the Saṅgha."
He further reflected:
"I have heard it said:
'If a Perfectly Awakened One does not appear in the world, all sentient beings do not hear the True Dharma.'"
"This may assist our act of giving, and in principle, it must be mutually compatible.
He then said to the elder, "Do not take the gold further;
I wish to turn this site over for me to build a gate. It would be excellent to accomplish this together, and the merit will be complete."
The elder replied, "It is not that I lack gold; young man, such as you are, this is truly most excellent.
Just as he had finished laying out the gold and was about to command the artisans, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), having learned of it all, arrived swiftly to cause confusion and said to the elder:

“The śramaṇa Gautama is currently residing in Rājagṛha, the capital of the kingdom of Magadha. This city of Śrāvastī is noble in its location and renowned for its prestige; it is not his place of residence. Do not build a vihāra here, and do not invite him.”
The householder immediately became angry and replied to the non-Buddhist practitioners, saying, "This city of Śrāvastī does not belong to you; what business is it of yours?

When the non-Buddhists heard this, they knew their wishes would not be granted. They went again to the king, but the king also did not grant their request. The various non-Buddhist practitioners were ashamed before his face, their complexions turning pale, and their minds were filled with extreme distress.
He went again to the elder and said to him:
"What I previously stated was not regarding the garden itself, but simply because those people are not my fellow practitioners.
Elder, if you are so resolute today, I shall inform them of this; please do not oppose me."
"I have heard that Gautama has a great disciple who has already arrived here; we may debate with him to determine who is superior or inferior.
If he prevails, a vihāra may be built for him; if he does not prevail, what is the use of inviting him?"
"What do you think of this that I have said?
The elder replied,
"This teaching is most excellent."
"If their meditative concentrations are distinguished by superiority or inferiority, they will suffice for mutual reliance;
clarity and turbidity must be separated, and truth and falsehood shall be discerned.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-saṃghabhedavastu-mahāsūtra*, Fascicle Eleven. The *Buddhabhāṣita-saṃghabhedavastu-mahāsūtra*, Fascicle Twelve.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmabhadra, Imperial Censor of the Third Rank, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master Mingjiao, under Imperial Edict.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at the Śītavana (Cold Forest) Grove, having accepted the invitation of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada. He foresaw that within the kingdom of Śrāvastī there were various non-Buddhist practitioners who were both diligent in asceticism and possessed of great intelligence; yet, despite their earnest cultivation, they had not attained liberation. It was at this moment that their roots and conditions for transformation had fully ripened.
The World-Honored One further considered who might go there;
seeing that only Śāriputra possessed the necessary karmic affinity from past lives, he realized that if he were to go first, it would surely bring great benefit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One summoned Śāriputra and ordered him to go first to the great city of Śrāvastī to assist Anāthapiṇḍada in establishing the vihāra.
The Venerable One accepted the command and went to Śrāvastī, where he visited the householder and discussed all matters with him.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having learned the intention of the non-Buddhists, came to inform the Venerable One:
"They wish to debate on doctrine; what do you think of this from the perspective of principle?"
He further said, "The people of this country have never before known the Buddha; it is fitting that you proclaim the excellence of the Dharma.
Śāriputra replied:
“Excellent, excellent!
These words are indeed true.
Thereupon, the Venerable One entered meditative concentration to observe: for how long will it take for the roots and conditions of these non-Buddhists and the people of Śrāvastī to reach maturity?
Seeing that the assembly of people had only seven days remaining,
the Venerable One emerged from meditative absorption and said to the householder:
"Please tell the non-Buddhists that they may come to debate after the seven days have passed."
The householder related the matter in full.
The non-Buddhists reflected:
"Setting a limit of seven days involves two possibilities:"
"First, knowing myself to be no match for him, I shall devise a plan to escape privately;
second, I may seek out my former friends to come and deliberate together.
Having thought thus, he considered: "Why should I not now seek companions?"
Thus, having personally searched through various places, he found a man named the Brahmin Red-Eyed and addressed him, saying:
"That śramaṇa Gautama has a great disciple who seeks to debate with me; you, O Brahmin, ought to assist me."
"Why is this? If we ourselves obtain superior gain and honor while they still remain, where shall we go when they become superior? He then asked:
"When will the debate take place? He replied,
"Seven days from now."
"When the time comes, we shall inform you, and you may surely come to assist us.
However, the Brahmin was deeply distressed by the prospect of defeat; his mind was filled with great anxiety, and he dispatched messengers everywhere to appeal to his allies.

When the seven days had passed, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada established a temporary site for debate in a spacious and tranquil place; he then prepared a lion throne for the Venerable Śāriputra and a high seat for the opposing non-Buddhist teachers.

Once the seating was completed, people from near and far gathered together—whether public officials or private citizens, young or old—numbering hundreds of thousands at that site of debate; there were also non-Buddhist practitioners and Brahmins from other countries who came to the assembly.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, holding a censer and burning exquisite incense, accompanied by his retinue as attendants, welcomed Śāriputra onto the lion throne;
once the Venerable One was seated, all gazed upon him in reverence, and beholding his majestic countenance, they all offered praise.
At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioner, accompanied by his followers, also ascended the high seat.
Once he was seated and settled, the Venerable One addressed him, saying:
"What do you intend to do?"
The non-Buddhist said, “I shall manifest supernatural powers; once I have manifested them, you too should manifest yours.
The Venerable One replied:
"What I have accomplished is something that neither gods nor humans can accomplish; how can you say that you are able to do as I do?
The Venerable One spoke again:
"Red-Eyed Brahmin!"
"Whatever you create, I am able to destroy it all.
The Brahmin Red-Eye manifested a flowering tree with such genuine, fragrant, and exquisite blossoms that they moved the multitude.
Through his supernormal power, the Venerable One produced a slight breeze, which blew the flowers, roots, and sprouts away to different places.
Furthermore, he manifested a pond filled with water, clear and serene, where lotus flowers bloomed everywhere to the admiration of all as being extraordinary;
the Venerable One then conjured a great elephant with a perfectly formed body, which entered the pond and trampled it until, in an instant, it was left in utter disorder.
The non-Buddhist practitioner further manifested a seven-headed dragon that bared its scales, glared with eyes of wrath, and lashed out fiercely at the sky;
the Venerable One manifested as a king of golden-winged garuḍas, swooping down from the air and sitting upon the heads of the dragons, whereupon the dragons submitted of their own accord.

Then that non-Buddhist practitioner, having finally transformed into the body of a rākṣasa, stood before the assembly; his appearance was so exceptionally hideous that anyone who saw him was struck with terror.

The Venerable One, through the supernatural power of his mantra, bound him; the rākṣasa, in his agony, instead gave rise to fierce anger. The non-Buddhist was seized with such dread that the hair on his body stood on end; fearing he would harm himself, he cried out for help and addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"I now take refuge; I pray you grant me protection."
The Venerable One dispelled the spell, and the rākṣasa’s anger subsided.
At that time, the Brahmin Red-Eye was delivered from the perilous fear of the rākṣasa; furthermore, he realized that what he had previously practiced was not the correct path.
He said to Śāriputra, “I wish to leave the household life and become a śramaṇa within the Venerable One’s True Dharma; may the Venerable One, out of great compassion and pity, grant me permission.”
Śāriputra immediately accepted him and ordained him as a śramaṇa. Thereafter, he cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Although he remained within the three realms (*tridhātu*), he was free from the poison of greed; his mind was as equanimous as space. He viewed gold as if it were soil, without making any distinction between them. Later, through cultivation, he attained the three knowledges (*traividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), realizing the fruit of arhatship. Consequently, Śakra and the various devas came to make offerings to him.
At that time, the great assembly was struck with wonder; their eyes were fixed and their minds concentrated as they praised Śāriputra with one voice:
"This master of dialectics is invincible by anyone, like a bull-king standing amidst the herd."
Everyone gazed upon him with insatiable devotion.

At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the mental dispositions and spiritual natures of the assembly, extensively expounded for them the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

In this great assembly, there were those who gave rise to the mind of taking the Three Refuges; those who gave rise to the mind of the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; those who gave rise to the mind of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; and those who gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.

Furthermore, there were those who left the household life and realized the fruit of srotāpanna, those who realized the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, those who realized the fruit of anāgāmin, and those who realized the fruit of arhat.

When the debate had concluded, the assembly dispersed. Among the non-Buddhists were those of stubborn disposition who, having been humiliated by their defeat in the debate, secretly consulted together to plot an unlawful act, saying:
"We should seek employment with the householder as laborers; then, when we find an opportunity, we may kill that venerable one."
The plan having been finalized, he addressed the elder, saying:

"You have already cut off all my means of livelihood; now I have nowhere else to turn. I pray that you will take pity on me and employ me as a laborer, or, considering my humble state, allow me to remain as a local resident; if you do not grant this, we shall each depart for other lands."
He pleaded thus three times with such sorrow that those nearby could not bear to hear it.
The elder then related the man's intention in detail to Śāriputra, saying:
"Virtuous one, you should consider and examine what is appropriate according to principle."
Śāriputra immediately entered samādhi and observed that, given the person’s faculties and conditions, the realization of the Way was not far off;
he then remarked, "What need for concern?
The elder withdrew at once, recorded his name, and sent him to work, providing him with wages according to the standard rate.
At that time, Śāriputra manifested a person who became the foreman among the laborers.
Later, the Venerable One, perceiving through his insight that the man's faculties were mature, went to the place of labor and sat down calmly beneath a tree.
At that time, those non-Buddhists, having initially found an opportunity, each felt joy in their hearts and desired to approach;
however, their leader, wielding a staff, drove them back so that they could not advance.
Exhausted and suffering from the labor, he then cried out:
"O Great Holy One! Save me!"
"Save us!
Śāriputra said, "You are weary;
you may rest for yourselves."
The non-Buddhists said:

"This Great Honored One, when we harbored murderous intent and plotted against his life, now recognized us and caused our efforts to cease; we are truly ashamed and fearful, having nothing further to say."

At that time, Śāriputra observed his remorse and, knowing that the time for his faculties and nature to ripen had arrived, called him forward and preached the Dharma to him; he then expounded for him the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhists' view of a self—resembling twenty mountain peaks—was completely shattered without remainder by the vajra-like wisdom, and they immediately attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
He spoke again:
"Venerable One!
I wish to leave the household life for the sake of the True Dharma and become a monk."

Śāriputra accepted him and ordained him as a śramaṇa. Gradually he progressed in his practice, diligently maintaining the holy life (brahmacarya). Seeing through the cycle of saṃsāra to its ultimate end, he exhausted all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship. His mind became equanimous like space; he viewed gold and earth as no different. Having renounced worldly gain, he attained great cooling peace and became worthy of receiving all offerings from Śakra and the various devas.

At that time, after Śāriputra had converted the non-Buddhists, he and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada together took a single cord, each grasping one end, and measured out the entire boundary of the great site for the vihāra.
The realms having been fixed, the karmic retribution experienced by the householder Anāthapiṇḍada manifested as a golden palace appearing in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Not understanding the noble intention, the householder said to Śāriputra:
"This vihāra is not intended for the arhats alone; it is for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Śāriputra said,
"What I originally practiced was precisely for the sake of the Tathāgata and the Arhats.
He then addressed the elder, saying:
"This land of yours has already manifested as a divine reward.
He then lent him his divine eye so that he might see for himself.
Upon seeing this, the elder was filled with immeasurable joy and wonder, whereupon he again gave rise to the highest grade of resolve.

Śāriputra then took one end of the cord himself and had the elder take the other end; they divided the sixteen great halls and sixty small chambers therein, so that the respective dwellings for the Buddha and the Saṃgha were each determined, and those golden palaces were transformed into magnificent jeweled adornments.
The Venerable One lent him his supernormal powers and caused him to see once more.
The householder, filled with joy, exclaimed to himself:
"This deed of mine shall surely bring forth such benefits of merit and virtue."

As the elder personally beheld that his future merit and retribution would be successively and increasingly manifold, he redoubled his diligence in the task; having dismantled the palace halls, he further prepared all the necessary articles for their enjoyment within.
When the work on the vihāra was finished, he again addressed the Venerable One,
saying, "What is the measure of the World-Honored One’s walking and standing?
The Venerable One replied:
"Use the ritual of a Wheel-Turning King.

Thereupon, the elder traveled from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha, constructing a palace every ten *krośas* along the way to serve as a place for the Tathāgata to rest, and establishing treasuries to store all items for his use.
He further appointed stewards to guard them constantly, sprinkling white sandalwood water daily to purify them, waiting upon the Tathāgata to ensure they were fragrant and clean.
In every place, he ensured that all preparations were made with such thoroughness.
Once the tasks were completed, he immediately dispatched a person to Rājagṛha to invite the Buddha and his assembly, instructing the messenger:
"When you arrive there, speak on my behalf as follows:"

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and addressed him, saying: "I hope you are free from illness and affliction, that your daily life is light and easy, and that you dwell in peace and happiness.

The vihāra I have established is now fully prepared; I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will look upon me with compassion and deign to descend. For the remainder of this life, I shall offer saṃghāṭī robes, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, bedding, and various requisites, ensuring they are never lacking. O Buddha, the Truly All-Knowing One, I pray that you will witness my earnest devotion."

The messenger, having grasped the meaning of these words, went to the presence of the Buddha and reported the elder’s words in full to the World-Honored One, further extending his request with redoubled devotion.
Having conveyed his message, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and stood reverently before him.
For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to others, the Buddha granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had definitely accepted the invitation, the messenger returned quickly to Śrāvastī to see the elder and said to him:
"The World-Honored One remained silent; he will certainly come to grace us with his presence."
The householder was filled with joy and thereupon arranged parasols, banners, precious incense, and exquisite flowers at various points along the way to welcome them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"O Arhats and others, you may proceed together to attend the invitation of Anāthapiṇḍada."

The Buddha, surrounded by the great assembly before and behind him, departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded toward Śrāvastī. Looking back and forth at his left and right, he addressed the Arhats and others:

"This retinue of mine is disciplined, free from desire, well-liberated, and consists of Arhats—the very family of the Buddha. They are like a bull-king among a herd, like an elephant-king surrounded by elephants, a lion-king surrounded by lions, a swan-king surrounded by swans, or a golden-winged garuḍa-king surrounded by garuḍas;
they are also like students following a teacher, the sick seeking a physician, soldiers supporting a general, or merchants relying on their leader."

Furthermore, it is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King surrounded by a thousand sons; like the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by gandharvas; like the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka surrounded by kumbhāṇḍas; like the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa surrounded by hosts of nāgas; like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by yakṣas; like the Sun God surrounded by a thousand rays; like the Moon God surrounded by the lunar mansions; like Śakra surrounded by his host of gods; and like Brahmā surrounded by the assembly of Brahmās;
even as the *śiśumāra* fish dwells within the great ocean, or as the Sea God gathers together all the waters.

The body of the Tathāgata is fully perfected with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; adorned with radiance, it illuminates all things like the light of a thousand suns. His gait is majestic, like a mountain of jewels, and he is endowed with great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all other such dharmas.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having accomplished such supreme majesty and virtue, and being accompanied by his retinue of liberated ones, traveled by stages to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to convert beings.

Then, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada, together with his family and attendants, each holding banners, streamers, precious parasols, and exquisite incense and flowers, went out from the city of Śrāvastī to welcome the World-Honored One and the great assembly of sages from afar.
Furthermore, elders, commoners, and citizens of the land—whether men or women—a multitude of hundreds of thousands, also came forth to welcome him;
additionally, countless devas in the void rejoiced and offered praise.

At that time, as the World-Honored One entered the city gate, he stepped upon its threshold with his right foot. Thereupon, the great earth shook in six ways, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the world. Celestial drums resounded spontaneously, and a rain of various heavenly flowers fell—namely, *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, and even *mandārava* flowers from the kalpa-trees. Furthermore, fine powders of exquisite fragrances such as agallochum, sandalwood, and *tamaraka* were showered down; moreover, within the houses, various kinds of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

The blind gained sight, the deaf heard sounds, the mute were able to speak, and those with incomplete limbs all attained wholeness. Those who were deluded and intoxicated became sober; those who had consumed poison found peace; those who harbored mutual hatred reached reconciliation; those who were bound and fettered attained liberation; those who were pregnant gave birth; and even the poor obtained abundant wealth.
When the World-Honored One entered the city, there were hundreds of thousands of such auspicious signs, portents, and beneficial occurrences.
Upon arriving at the house of the elder, the Buddha and the great assembly sat down in due order.
All the kinsmen and attendants of the elder, whether close or distant, came to burn incense, scatter flowers, prostrate, and make offerings.
When these various rites were completed, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada took up an incense burner and led the Buddha, the World-Honored One, into the vihāra.
The Buddha ascended the precious throne, and all the Arhats likewise took their seats.

At that time, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada took a golden pitcher, intending to pour water over the World-Honored One’s hand—which was marked by a web-like membrane—but as he poured the water, it would not come forth.
The elder reflected:
"Could it be that I committed unwholesome karma in the past,
such that this has come to pass today?"
The Buddha told the householder:

"There is no unwholesome karma; it is simply because you have already offered this site as a monastery to a Perfectly Enlightened One in the past that you must not harbor a fixed mind thinking, 'I am now able to give. If you depart from this [attitude], the water will surely flow out."
The householder replied,
"It is as the Buddha has taught.
Having spoken these words, the water in the jar made a sound endowed with the five virtues.
Having poured water over the Buddha’s hands, he said, "May the Buddha act according to his will.
He further addressed him, saying,
"Please grant us a name."
At that time, the youth Jeta was also present in the assembly of the Buddha, and he thought to himself:
"If the Buddha knows [my name], he will mention it first.
In accordance with his thoughts, the Buddha established the name of the vihāra as Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma.
Having heard this, the youth Jeta’s joy and delight toward the Tathāgata redoubled; he further adorned his gate with the four precious substances.
It was for this reason that the name Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma was established.

At that time, the Great King Prasenajit, the sovereign of Śrāvastī, heard that the Buddha had traveled through his kingdom and, having accepted the invitation of the elder Anāthapiṇḍika, was residing in the monastery. Overjoyed and leaping with delight, he went to the Buddha’s presence and praised the World-Honored One with various words. Having prostrated, circumambulated him, and sat to one side, he spoke as follows:

"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama knows the characteristics of his own mind and has realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The śramaṇa Gautama delights in discourse according to the Dharma; whatever mind he possesses may be called 'false' and may be called 'right,' and it can perform both good and evil deeds. Yet these mental characteristics have no coming or going; they cannot be known and cannot be described—this is a most profound dharma."
"How can this be known?

The Buddha said, "What the King has spoken is indeed the truth. That mind may be called 'deviant' and may also be called 'righteous'; it can perform good and it can perform evil. Yet the characteristics of this mind have no coming or going; they cannot be known and cannot be described—this is a most profound dharma."
"I know this mind; I have realized unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The king said, "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
Why do you speak in such a manner?

There were the elders Kāśyapa, Māṭhara, Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Bhāradvāja, Vāṣpa, and Mahānāman; even though they understood the nature of the mind, they did not yet realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
How can it be that a śramaṇa, young and having only recently left the household life, claims to have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
The Buddha said, “Great King!
Do not speak thus. There are four things in the world that must not be treated with contempt.”
What are these four?
First, one must not treat a prince with contempt;
second, one must not treat a small dragon with contempt.
Third, one must not treat a small fire with contempt;
fourth, one must not treat a small Saṃgha with contempt. Why is this?

Now, that prince was born of the Kṣatriya caste, endowed with the marks of royalty and possessed of great merit; as he grows to maturity, he will surely succeed to the sovereign throne. Yet the foolish, lacking wisdom, think him insignificant and treat him with contempt; they shall fall into calamity at that royal station and have no cause for regret.

Furthermore, as for dragons, their nature is inherently venomous and malevolent, and their manifestations are inconsistent; they may conceal their massive bodies to assume small forms. If a foolish person fails to recognize this and treats them with contempt or provokes them, the dragon will in an instant become enraged and retaliate by inflicting harm.

Furthermore, fire can burn everything; one must not treat it with contempt even when it appears small, for if a person treats it lightly, it will surely spread later, utterly destroying villages, mountains, and forests.

Furthermore, the Sangha maintains purity and self-restraint; though they may be young, they must not be treated with contempt. Realizing the Path and attaining the fruits of realization does not depend on being old or young, nor does it distinguish between those who have been in the order for a long time or recently, or between the noble and the humble. Worldly people, lacking wisdom, fail to discern between the ordinary and the holy; when they encounter an Arhat, they immediately give rise to insults and humiliation. The retribution for such offenses is like cutting off the crown of a *tāla* tree, from which no new growth can ever arise; even through diligent repentance and apologies, the transgression cannot be extinguished.

At that time, King Jayasena, having heard the Tathāgata’s exposition of these four dharmas, received them with deep faith and repented of his transgressions. He then prostrated himself, placing his head at the Buddha’s feet, offered his apologies, circumambulated him, and withdrew with joy.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had completed his work of transforming and benefiting beings in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he desired to travel to the city of Kapilavastu.
King Śatānīka, having received the Buddha’s transformative guidance, developed a firm mind of devotion and sent an envoy with a letter to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Your Crown Prince Siddhārtha has realized the unsurpassed flavor of the nectar of the Dharma; both those within and beyond the world have now received his salvation."
Upon hearing this, King Śuddhodana immediately reflected:
"Although I rejoice that my son has attained perfect enlightenment, if I were now to dispatch a messenger, he would surely be converted and leave the household life."
Supporting his chin with his hand, he examined the matter closely and repeatedly.
At that time, there was a great minister named Upananda, who, seeing the king in such a state, addressed him, saying:
"Great King!"
"Why do you prop your chin in your hand and appear unhappy?
The king replied, "It is not that I am unhappy;
I am simply preoccupied with a certain matter."

King Prasenajit has sent a letter informing me that Prince Siddhārtha has already attained perfect enlightenment and is currently at the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery in Śrāvastī, where he has a thousand disciples, all of whom are arhats.

"When I previously departed for the sake of those ascetic practices, I dispatched people to search for me who have not returned to this day; if I were to send a messenger now, it would certainly be one that never returns again—how, then, can such a thing be known?"
That Siddhārtha is intelligent and wise, surpassing all others; who would not place sincere faith in whatever he says? It is for this reason that I have reflected upon the matter.
Upananda then addressed the king, saying, "I now request leave to depart; I pray you do not worry.
The king said:
“I have always held only you in my thoughts; if you can act thus, it would truly be a great blessing.
The King then personally composed a letter by hand, saying:

“Sarvārthasiddha is my own biological son. Having grown weary of afflictions, he has renounced his kingdom to leave the household life in order to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
Having heard that one achieves the Way and transforms sentient beings, my mind of contemplation continues day and night without interruption.
Now, while others obtain happiness, I alone suffer; it is like a great tree that grows from the earth—once it possesses roots and sprouts, it ultimately hopes for fruit.
Your heart’s desire has been fulfilled; you should now recall your former vow and what you said in the past:
"If I do not realize the path of unexcelled, tranquil enlightenment, I swear never again to enter the city of Kapilavastu."
"Since your great practice is already perfected, you ought to take pity on me and my retinue.
Having received the letter from the King, Udāyin quickly went to Śrāvastī and proceeded to the vihāra.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he said:
“World-Honored One!
Your father, King Śuddhodana, has sent a letter to the Buddha.”
Having finished speaking, he offered it up.
The Buddha personally accepted it, opened the seal, and read its contents; after a short while, he remained silent.
Then, Upananda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now request the World-Honored One to depart from the city of Kapilavastu.
The Buddha said,
"I shall go."

Upananda immediately prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to pay his respects; having bowed, he bowed again and again until he was exhausted, and then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if you depart, I shall say no more; yet if you do not depart, I must insistently entreat you to go."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Upananda:
"The Buddha’s eye is pure and can see; he is one who is free from all attachment.
He sees the boundless and does not go; how could you possibly lead him there?"
The Buddha’s eye sees the boundless; he who is unattached to craving has no destination even by the power of diligence—how could you lead him away?
If a person’s mind is undisturbed, he likewise cannot be overcome.
Boundless is the wisdom of the Unconquerable One; how can you proceed with steadfastness?
If a person attains that which cannot be overcome, there is likewise nothing that can overcome them.
Since the Buddha’s power of progress and stride are boundless, by what stride can you proceed with steadfastness?
Then Upananda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to take these spoken verses and present them to King Śuddhodana.
The Buddha told Upananda:
"I do not think so," he replied.
Again [the other] asked:
"If it is not so, then what is your intention?"
The Buddha said,
"I wish for you to leave the household life.
He spoke again:
"I previously made an agreement with the King that if I were to see the Buddha, I must certainly return.
The Buddha said, "Do not break your agreement;
you may go as you wish. However, there is no obstacle to shaving your hair and donning the dyed robes."
Upananda said:
"When the World-Honored One was still a bodhisattva, he yet relied upon the instructions of his parents and teachers; how could I now dare not rely upon their teachings?"
"Now I seek to leave the household life; I pray that the Buddha will deliver me.
The Buddha immediately ordained him as a śramaṇa at that very moment.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Upananda! You may go now;

however, upon reaching the gate of the palace in your own country, you must not enter immediately. Stand outside the gate and request an audience with the king. Whether he asks your name—saying 'I am the Śākya bhikṣu'—or whether he summons you, only then may you proceed forward."
Furthermore, if one should ask:
"Are you truly a śramaṇa of the Śākya clan?
one should immediately answer:
"It is true. If one asks:
"Is Sarvārthasiddha also like this image?"
He replied,
"It is likewise.
He asked again:
"Has Sarvārthasiddha come? He replied, "He has."
"When will that be? He replied,
"It shall be seven days from now."
Having spoken thus, he departed;
even if one were to remain, one would not be permitted to stay.
The king said:
"If Sarvārthasiddha comes, will he stay within the palace?
He replied, "He will not stay."
The King asked:
"In what place do you delight to dwell?
He replied:
"Whether in forests, fields, or dwelling in vihāras.
If one asks:
"What is meant by a vihāra?"
"You may then report this in detail, just as you did regarding the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery.
After the Buddha had thus instructed him, Upananda was about to depart.
The Buddha spoke to him again:
"A king’s single word brings wealth and honor; when a celestial being conceives a thought, everything is obtained. All noble beings are likewise.

By means of the Buddha's supernatural power, Upananda reached the city of Kapilavastu in an instant. Abiding in right mindfulness as instructed by the Buddha, he arrived at the palace gate and stood there, not proceeding further.
He said to the gatekeeper, "You may report this:
a Śākya bhikṣu has come to the gate but does not enter.
The King then commanded:
"Call him in. When Upananda was summoned, he immediately entered.
As soon as Śuddhodana saw him, he asked in astonishment:
“Upananda, have you gone forth?
He replied,
“I have gone forth.”
The king said,
"What did you report to me when you were departing? He replied:

"I obey your command immediately; originally, I had no intention of leaving the household life. Yet, through the majestic power and skillful means of the World-Honored One, I have been transformed and enlightened. A Buddha appears in the world but rarely, and the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Even a prince has renounced his supreme sovereignty; how could a lowly servant like me persist in my attachment?"

The king’s words seemed to reproach him, yet his heart was not truly angry; moreover, because the king’s demeanor was extraordinary, he did not treat him as a former minister. He immediately ordered [the prince] to ascend the hall, took his hand to comfort him, and commanded an attendant to spread a seat and provide water for washing, before offering him medicinal broth, fruits, and other refreshments.

Uṇṇābha’s deportment was extraordinary and his conduct followed established norms; his speech was invariably deliberate and thorough, and his disposition was exceedingly harmonious and pleasant. As the King gazed upon Uṇṇābha for the first time—shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes—their conversation continued for so long that he completely forgot the purpose of his visit to inquire after the Buddha.
Upon arriving here, he asked again:
"Does my son Sarvārthasiddha possess such auspicious marks and dignified deportment as these?
He replied:
"To liken me to the Buddha is like comparing a mustard seed to Mount Sumeru, or a cow's footprint to the great ocean, or even the light of a small window-opening to the radiance of the sun."
Upon hearing these words, the king thought of his son; he suddenly fainted and fell to the ground, and only after a minister sprinkled water on his face did he regain consciousness.
After a long while, he asked again:
"Has my son come?"
He replied, "Come.
He spoke again:
“When will he arrive? “Seven days hence.
The king immediately issued an edict to purify the inner palace and to solemnly adorn the halls in preparation for the arrival of the World-Honored One and the assembly of noble disciples.
Upananda said to the Great King:
"If the World-Honored One comes, he will not stay within the palace.
The King said:
“Where do you take pleasure in dwelling?
“If not in the forest wilds, then I dwell in a vihāra.
The king said:
"What is meant by a 'vihāra'?
Ūnāyana then informed the king of the vihāra's layout, saying:

"There are sixteen main halls and sixty small chambers; the World-Honored One resides in the center while the noble assembly is distributed throughout. All necessary articles and utensils have been made fully complete."

Having heard these words, the King dispatched a messenger to the Nyagrodha Grove with instructions to begin work immediately and set a deadline for completion; he had it constructed according to the same plan as the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, yet adorned it with double the amount of precious jewels.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One dispatched Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:

"You should announce to the assembly of bhikṣus: 'I now wish to go to the city of Kapilavastu; you should each take up your saṃghāṭī robes and alms bowls, and proceed to convert and benefit my parents and kinsmen.'"
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having received the Buddha’s command, fully announced the Buddha’s words to all the arhats and others.

The Buddha, leading the great assembly, departed from the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery and proceeded toward the city of Kapilavastu at the invitation of his father, the king, surrounded by the arhats in front and behind.
The Buddha then looked around and addressed the Arhats and others, saying:

"These followers of mine are disciplined, free from desire, well-liberated, and are Arhats—the true retinue of the Buddha. They are like a bull king among his herd; like an elephant king surrounded by elephants; like a lion king surrounded by lions; like a king of geese surrounded by geese; like a king of garuḍas surrounded by garuḍas;
and again, like students following their teacher, the sick seeking a physician, soldiers supporting their general, or merchants relying on their leader."

Furthermore, it is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King surrounded by a thousand sons; like the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by gandharvas, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka surrounded by kumbhāṇḍas, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa surrounded by hosts of nāgas, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by yakṣas;
like the Sun God surrounded by a thousand rays, the Moon God surrounded by the multitude of stars, Śakra surrounded by his host, and the Brahmā King surrounded by the Brahmā assembly;
even as the *sītimī* fish dwells within the great ocean, or as the Sea God gathers together all the waters.

The body of the Tathāgata is fully perfected with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; it is adorned with radiance that illuminates all things like the light of a thousand suns. His gait is majestic, like a mountain of jewels, and he is endowed with great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and all other such dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed along the road with his retinue, traveling by stages for the sake of conversion until he reached the Rohitaka River, not far from the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue and high and low officials, was by the riverbank. They had prepared precious parasols, banners, and streamers; they struck gongs and blew conchs, extensively arranging musical performances. Burning incense and scattering flowers, they gazed expectantly toward the World-Honored One.

Furthermore, from the Rohitaka River to the Nyagrodha Grove, and throughout the city and its suburbs, the King commanded the commoners and citizens to prepare the way in advance. He ordered that all mounds, ruins, sand, and gravel be removed, replacing them with pure earth and sprinkling it with scented water. At intervals according to the distance, incense burners were placed so that as the Buddha passed by, they might offer worship by burning incense.

At that time, the officials, commoners, elders, men, and women of the city of Kapilavastu each took up exquisite incense and flowers and stood by the roadside to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
The multitude of people all said:
"The World-Honored One was formerly a prince and has now attained Buddhahood.
They were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, desiring to behold his majestic demeanor.
Furthermore, he had this thought:
"What should be the ritual when father and son meet?
If the son bows to the father, it is no different from worldly custom; if the father bows to the son, it would not accord with the rites of the state."
"The Prince practiced the Way, underwent asceticism, and attained Buddhahood; he must surely be distinct from the world.
The multitude of people was so dense that there was no space between them on the road.
