When the Buddha and his holy assembly were about to reach the riverbank, he knew that the King’s retinue were all at that spot, and he reflected to himself:
"Now, in the city of Kapilavastu, the royal father, his kinsmen, and the common people each think to themselves:
'When the Prince departed, he was surrounded before and behind by hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, and traveling through the air, he went to the Snowy Mountains to practice the path.'"
Furthermore, he said:
"Having already attained perfect enlightenment and leading the assembly to transform and guide others, what is so extraordinary about returning to my kingdom now on foot?
I should now manifest my supernormal powers for the King, my father, to see, and cause the people to marvel with joy."

When the king and his retinue beheld the great assembly with their own eyes, they were about to hasten forward to welcome the World-Honored One. At that moment, the Buddha entered *samādhi* and emerged from the midst of the empty space in the eastern quarter, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. Sometimes water flowed from the upper part of his body while fire issued from the lower; at other times, fire issued from the upper part of his body while water flowed from the lower. Furthermore, he emitted great radiance from within his body—blue, yellow, red, white, and vermilion—all mingling together in various colors like crystal, each reflecting and penetrating the others. This was likewise so for the southern, western, and northern quarters.

Furthermore, each of the bhikṣus manifested supernatural powers, leaping upward to a height of seven *tāla* trees; the World-Honored One likewise manifested a body therein. While the manifestations of the bhikṣu assembly were not uniform—some reaching six *tāla* trees, some five, some four, some three, two, or one—the Buddha always rose higher, distinct from the multitude.
Having thus manifested himself, the Buddha and his holy assembly suddenly vanished; in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, they were already back at their original location.
The king and his retinue felt redoubled faith and devotion, and went forward to welcome them.

When the King saw that the great assembly was all clad in saffron robes and their outward appearances were so similar, he could not initially distinguish who was the World-Honored One and who were his disciples.
Then, Upananda led King Śuddhodana before the World-Honored One; upon seeing him, the King still regarded him with the affection due to a son.
Upananda said to the king: "The Tathāgata has severed the habitual tendencies of affliction and attained mastery over the mind;

like the sun illuminating the world while abiding in space, he rides the vehicle of True Suchness to realize supreme enlightenment and perfect the ten powers. Possessing all-knowledge, his marks and signs and radiant light are pure and illuminate all things; he is sovereign over all dharmas and benefits beings boundlessly."
"I entreat the King to take refuge and seek the Noble Path.

When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he was awakened to the truth and believed with deep conviction. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage at the Buddha’s feet and spoke this verse:
"When you were born, the great earth shook; The tree’s shadow covered your body, not following the sun."
"Furthermore, with the universal eye he observes all sentient beings; for this reason, I prostrate at the feet of the Most Honored One.
At that time, the assembly of Śākyas saw King Śuddhodana prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
Then some said:
"How is it that the World-Honored One turns his back on worldly dharmas to transform sentient beings?
When the King heard this public discussion, he addressed them, saying:
“Have you not heard?

When Siddhārtha was born, the great earth shook in six ways, and a brilliant light shone everywhere throughout all worlds. Even those places of pitch darkness where the sun’s rays do not reach, nor even the light of majestic deities can penetrate—this light illuminated them all. The sentient beings dwelling in those dark places, who had fallen there due to their evil karma, suddenly saw one another because of the radiance and each said:
‘When did other beings ever appear here before?’”
At that time, I prostrated at the feet of the Most Honored One.

Before Siddhārtha had gone forth into homelessness, he went to sit beneath a Jambu tree; pure and free from desire, having abandoned unwholesome states and severed all conceptualization and doubt, he dwelt joyfully in a tranquil meditative absorption. While the shadows of all other trees shifted with the sun, the shadow of the Jambu tree remained fixed, shading his body.
Having already seen this, I was struck with extraordinary wonder, and at this moment I again prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet.
This prostration of mine is now the third.
Thus ends the twelfth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-saṃghabhedavastu-mahāsūtra*.
The Sūtra of the Mahāvaṃsa Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Commissioner for Dispersing the Grandees, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, having spoken these words, King Śuddhodana had a thought arise in his mind and suddenly shed tears.
He further spoke a verse, asking the World-Honored One:
"In the past, when I dwelt within the palace, Many people provided me with protection; Now, having renounced my home and left the city, I am alone and have no one to rely upon."
“In the midst of the fearsome mountains and wilds, how can one body remain?
The World-Honored One replied:
“The ten abodes of the noble ones—I have fully established myself in them all.”
"Bound fast, now you are liberated; you do not dwell in the palace of a human king.
The King said:
"An elephant bed adorned with gold and jewels was where you once lay to rest;"
"In these mountains and wilds there are only grasses and trees; how can one sleep in peace?
He replied:
"The bedding of liberation, adorned with the factors of enlightenment;"
"Sleeping is most pleasant and refreshing; there is no heat or affliction whatsoever.
The King said:
"Elephants, horses, and palanquins—those upon which you formerly traveled in and out;"
"How can one now proceed upon this ground of all thorns?
He replied:
"I have the chariot of supernormal power; by riding it with diligent effort, I go back and forth."
"Though he traverses all stages, he is not obstructed by the thorns of affliction.
The King said:
"The exquisite garments of the Kṣatriyas adorned his body in the past; he was once sovereign."
"Now this kashaya is a coarse garment; how can you endure wearing it?
He replied:
"The samghati is a coarse garment, the robe worn by the Muni in the mountains."
"Once he has put it on, auspicious signs arise, and all who see him are deeply pleased.
The King said:
"He eats from vessels of gold and jewels, always consuming the most excellent flavors."
"Now that you yourself carry the alms-bowl, what do you know of the food you eat?
He replied:
"The flavor of the Dharma in meditative equipoise is supreme; by eating it, one attains liberation."
"Having already severed worldly craving, he wanders to transform others out of compassion for the world.
The King said:
"The milk-sugar water was sweet and delicious; in the past, I drank it without ever being satiated."
Regarding the cold and hot, clear and turbid waters you now drink—how do you distinguish them?
He replied:
“The water of the King’s noble abundance is what the people of the world vie to drink.”
"Having drunk, my defilements may increase; as for me, there is no delight [in this].
The King said:
"The precious palaces and towers were formerly inhabited according to one's heart's desire."
Now dwelling alone in the mountain forests, how can one be free from fear?
He replied:
“Having severed the root of afflictions, no fears shall arise.”
"Even the atom and the self do not exist; / Thus I dwell in peace wherever I am.
The King said:
"With pure and wondrous fragrant water, / You have always bathed in the past;"
"Now, here alone amidst the mountains and wilds, who bathes the King of Munis?
He replied:
"Scented with the fragrance of precepts and immersed in the water of Dharma, the virtuous person bathes constantly."
"Purifying oneself to reach the other shore—this is what the immeasurable sages have taught.
The King said:
"In the past, my body was anointed with exquisite perfumes, and I wore garments of Kāśi silk;"
"Always dwelling within the inner palace, how could one be separated from that which is not fitting?
He replied:
"The fragrance of the precepts is most exquisite; it is used as an ointment for the adornment of the body."
"I am no longer deluded now; I have cast off my precious robes and ornaments.
The king asked:
"Where can one find disdain? Where is there anything to fear?"
Regarding the state of non-action and the state of action, I now ask that you please explain them.
He replied:
"The three phenomena of old age, sickness, and death are terrifying; do not treat them with negligence."
"One should seek only pleasant objects; one should find joy in being free from worldly affairs.
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he was filled with immeasurable joy and praised him, saying:
"Well-born scion of the Śākya clan, you are entirely unstained by the eight worldly dharmas."
Again, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata and further reflected:
"I have gained a great benefit, for my son has realized such meritorious qualities."
The King and his retinue escorted the World-Honored One into the Nyagrodha Grove Monastery.

At that time, once the World-Honored One had arrived at the monastery and ascended the Dharma seat, the King, the ministers, and even the commoners surrounded him in reverent gazing; the devas in the void rejoiced and offered praise.

The Buddha observed the minds and dispositions, as well as the spiritual faculties, of each member of the assembly; having known them as they truly were, he extensively expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, King Śuddhodana and the Śākya multitude, numbering seventy-seven thousand people, all realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
The World-Honored One further observed where the conditions were ripe;
it was at the Brahmānuvartana Forest that the time was right to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha and the great assembly all proceeded to that place, followed by immeasurable multitudes who came to listen to the Dharma.

The World-Honored One extensively expounded the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths; thereupon, seventy-six thousand people, including King Droṇodana, the Śākya assembly, and even humans and devas, further realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.

The World-Honored One proceeded again to the Rohitaka Forest, where there were likewise immeasurable devas, humans, Śākyas, retinues, commoners, and citizens who followed the Buddha to listen to the Dharma.

The World-Honored One extensively expounded the Four Noble Truths as before; seventy-five thousand people, including King Amṛtodana, the Śākya assembly, and others up to the humans and devas, realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Among them, some realized the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and some realized the fruit of *arhat*.
Some gave rise to the mind of *śrāvaka-bodhi*, some gave rise to the mind of *pratyekabuddha-bodhi*, and some gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, there were those who left the household life, severed all afflictions, and subsequently realized the fruit of *arhat*, even down to those who gave rise to the mind of the Three Refuges.

At that time, having witnessed the World-Honored One manifesting supernatural transformations and preaching the sublime Dharma, Devadatta—having no realization of his own—conceived a heart of envy and uttered unwholesome words, saying to the assembly of Śākyas:
"All blind people delight in such illusory transformations; I am capable of performing all such illusory feats."
There was a member of the Śākya clan named Pramāṇārtha, who said to Devadatta:
"Do not utter such evil words regarding the Great Man, the World-Honored One."
Devadatta immediately fell silent.
At that time, King Śuddhodana reflected:
"In the past, devas and asuras were the objects of offerings for the world; now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, he is truly the one who receives the world's reverence and offerings."
A young man of the Śākya clan spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha, saying:
“The Great Sage and Great Being of the Śākya clan, Can rain down the sublime Dharma’s nectar;
He rescues those fallen into darkness, Opening the gate of liberation as a guide.”
At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing this youth’s verse in praise of the Buddha, was deeply moved with joy; yet, as he had not yet seen the Truth in its reality, he said only:
"The World-Honored One is a Great Man endowed with great majestic virtue; who else has such a noble son as I do?"
The World-Honored One reflected:
"King Śuddhodana, my father, does not perceive the truth; this is due to two things:
first, his own mind."
"Second is the discriminating mind.
If one can leave this behind, one will be able to see reality.
The Buddha, observing that Mahāmaudgalyāyana had a karmic connection with King Śuddhodana from a previous life, said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You must employ skillful means to transform King Śuddhodana, causing him to abandon the grasping of a self.
Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately went to the king's residence.

Upon seeing the Venerable One, the king’s heart was filled with joy. At that moment, the Venerable One entered *samādhi* and vanished from before the king, appearing instead in the empty space to the east, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

Furthermore, his body emitted light of five colors, which, like crystal, were transparent and mutually reflective; sometimes water issued from his upper body while fire issued from his lower body, and sometimes fire issued from his upper body while water issued from his lower body—thus he manifested various such supernatural transformations.
As it was in the east, so it was in the south, west, and north.
Having performed these supernatural transformations, he vanished into the void and, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, was already before the King.
The King asked,
"Among the disciples of the Buddha, is there anyone else like the Venerable One?
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke this verse:
“The disciples of the World-Honored One possess great majesty; Mastery over the three knowledges and six supernormal powers is theirs.
Arhats liberated from the three realms— Śrāvaka sages like me are many.”

At that time, King Śuddhodana had initially believed that only the World-Honored One possessed such powers, and the mark of self-attachment remained constantly in his mind; however, once Mahāmaudgalyāyana had manifested these supernatural transformations, he realized that even his disciples possessed such realization, and through this, the King’s sense of self was extinguished.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, employing skillful means, formed a worldly thought:
"How might Brahmā, Śakra, and the gods of the Pure Light Heaven come, so that I may preach the Dharma for them?"
"What do you think?
The mind of the Tathāgata cannot be known by śrāvakas or bodhisattvas. Why is this so?
Even the minds of worldly beings as lowly as ants can be made to know [the Buddha's mind], let alone those of the devas."
Thereupon, Śakra addressed the devaputra Viśvakarman, saying:
"Transform the Nyagrodha Grove into a great Dharma assembly; within it, let the terraces, palaces, and pavilions all be furnished with lion thrones, adorned throughout with various precious gems.
Furthermore, open four gates, each embellished with the four kinds of jewels, and command the Four Great Heavenly Kings to guard them."

Then the devaputra Viśvakarman, receiving the command of Śakra, transformed the great assembly with various kinds of magnificent adornments according to Śakra’s instructions, and further appointed the Four Great Kings as gatekeepers.
Having performed these transformations, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "The Dharma assembly is now complete; I pray that the Buddha will proceed there.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with his own retinue, as well as Brahmā, Śakra, the gods of Pure Radiance, and countless hundreds of thousands of other beings, returned to the Nyagrodha Grove.
Once the Buddha had arrived, he entered the precious hall, ascended the lion throne, and immediately preached the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana and King Śuddhodana went together to the place where the Buddha was.
Upon reaching the gate of the Dharma assembly, the Venerable One entered directly, while the King stopped.
The King said,
"Why do you obstruct me?"
He replied, "The Buddha is preaching the Dharma for the gods of the Pure Light Heaven and others; ordinary people are not permitted to attend the assembly.
The King said:
"What noble being are you, staying here guarding the gate?
He replied,
"I am the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
Then the king asked,
"If it is so at the eastern gate, would it be possible at the southern gate?
He replied:
"I do not know.
Having arrived at the southern gate, he was again unable to enter, whereupon the king asked: "Why is this so?"
He replied, "The Buddha is preaching the Dharma for the gods of Pure Light; ordinary people are not permitted to attend the assembly.
He asked again:
“Who are you, O worthy one, staying here guarding the gate?
He replied, “I am the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka; therefore, I guard the southern gate.”
The king thought to himself, "If I go to the western gate, I shall likely be able to enter.
Yet, upon arriving there as well, he was not permitted to enter; the king then questioned him further:
"Why is it so? He answered as before.
Again he asked:
"What noble being are you? He replied,
"I am the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa."
King Śuddhodana sighed deeply and lamented:
"The gap between the holy and the mundane is such that even though we are near, we are as far apart as the distant.
Since his longing to see the Buddha was so intense, he went again to the northern gate; however, upon arriving there, he was stopped just as before and not allowed to enter.
The king then spoke in a stern voice to the gatekeeper, saying,
"Is this not the Worthy and Holy One, the Heavenly King of the North?
The gatekeeper replied:
"I am Vaiśravaṇa. Upon hearing these words, King Śuddhodana was on the verge of fainting; he then reflected:
"Though we were once close kin, we are now distant; my sense of personal attachment has from this moment been extinguished."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, knowing their lack of discrimination and observing that their emotional distress was extreme— fearing that if he did not see them at that time, they would meet with impermanence—

the Buddha employed his supernatural powers to transform the towers, pavilions, halls, and even the walls so that they all became made of pure, translucent crystal, such that one could see through from inside to outside without any obstruction.
Upon seeing the Buddha, the king’s heart was filled with supreme joy; he immediately prostrated himself and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One employed various skillful means to transform his father, the king, causing him to abandon the notion of self and eliminate conceptual discrimination, and then extensively expounded for him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Having heard this, the King’s twenty mountain peaks of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) were shattered and utterly destroyed by the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*), and he immediately realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
The King reflected:

"What I have now realized was not obtained by gods, nor by sages, nor by my father, nor by my mother, nor by any beloved kinsmen; it must have been brought about through filial devotion toward the Tathāgata."
He further reflected:

"Throughout my past cycles of birth and death in saṃsāra, my accumulated bones have formed mountains and my blood and tears have formed oceans; having even fallen into the various evil realms, today I have finally entered the gate of liberation and joined the ranks of the noble path."
Again he spoke, saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"In the past, I practiced countless asceticisms, disregarding my own body and life for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; now I seek even more excellent celestial retribution.
The Buddha then thought with compassion:
"Why does the King now seek such a reward?"
Then King Śuddhodana rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and addressed him, saying:

"I now wish to invite the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones to partake of a meal in my palace tomorrow morning; I pray that, out of great compassion, you will all deign to accept this invitation."
The Buddha remained silent.
Knowing that he had given his consent, the king paid his respects and returned home.
As soon as he arrived at the palace, he summoned King Śuddhodana and addressed him, saying:
"I have realized the Way and take no pleasure in the royal throne; you shall receive the consecration and govern the kingdom in my stead.
King Śuddhodana asked, "When did you realize it?"
He replied,
"I have just gone to the Nyagrodha Forest to hear the Dharma and have attained realization.
King Śuddhodana said:
"I had already attained realization when the World-Honored One first arrived at that grove; as for the king’s request that I take his place, I truly cannot.
He then issued a summons to King Droṇodana, saying:
"You may receive the consecration and succeed me in governing the kingdom."
He replied, "In the Brahmā-vyūha forest, I heard the Dharma and realized the fruit; as for what you call 'acting as a regent,' I truly do not delight in it.
He then spoke again to King Amṛtodana:
"Accept this consecration and govern the kingdom on my behalf.
He replied, "In the Lohitaka Forest, I heard the Dharma and realized the fruit; now, I have no desire to dwell upon the royal throne."
King Śuddhodana asked, "If this is so,
who then shall be made to guard the ancestral altars?
All the kings replied:
"Among the Śākya clan, there is one of noble virtue who may be appointed to guard it.
Having concluded this deliberation,
King Śuddhodana said:
"Order the relevant authorities immediately to prepare various kinds of rare delicacies and food and drink, ensuring they are exceedingly fragrant and delicious.

He further decreed that the interior and exterior must be purified and all pungent or impure things removed; upon the main hall, pure mats and exquisite garments were to be spread, and seats for the Tathāgata and the assembly of holy ones were to be arranged. Furthermore, incense, flowers, and pure water vessels were to be provided so that nothing was lacking or incomplete.
When morning arrived, he dispatched a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is now prepared; we pray that the Buddha and the assembly will deign to descend and accept our invitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the assembly of sages in front and behind, proceeded to the royal palace to receive the offerings of food.
When the Buddha arrived at the palace gate, the king and his retinue held censers and burned incense, escorting the World-Honored One inside.
Once the Buddha had ascended his seat, the assembly of noble ones took their places in succession.
Then King Śuddhodana, together with his retinue, having completed their prostrations, inquiries, and praises, personally offered various kinds of food and drink as an act of worship.
When the meal was finished and the washing and rinsing completed, the King Śuddhodana’s heart’s desire was fulfilled.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana took a golden pitcher and poured water over the World-Honored One’s hand, saying:
“I offer this Nyagrodha Grove monastery; may the Buddha accept it as he pleases.”
When the water emerged from the jar, five kinds of virtuous sounds resounded.
The Buddha also bestowed a blessing, saying:
"By the merit of this offering, may the King and the Śākya clan obtain all that they seek, according to their wishes."

When the king and his retinue heard these words, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew, while the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones returned to the vihāra.
On a later day, the World-Honored One again accepted a meal at the royal palace. The king’s attendants said to one another, “Now, those on the World-Honored One’s left and right are all elderly;
their auspicious marks and dignified deportment are truly worthy of veneration. Yet, they are not yet suitable to serve the World-Honored One.”
"One should select from the Śākya clan a youth who is virtuous and excellent, and have him renounce the world to attend upon the Buddha at his side; thus it would be fitting for our noble lineage.
At that time, King Śuddhodana issued a decree to his kinsmen and both internal and external ministers:

"Now that Sarvārthasiddha has relinquished the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to practice asceticism and become a Great Dharma King, each of you should select a worthy son to renounce the world and serve as an attendant to the World-Honored One, thereby perfecting this noble undertaking."
At that time, King Droṇodana had two sons: the first was named Aniruddha, and the second was named Mahānāman.
That Mahānāman was capable of managing the affairs of state, yet he was greedy for wealth and profit.
Aniruddha constantly resided within the palace, enjoying pleasures as he pleased.
At that time, King Droṇodana issued an imperial decree and summoned Mahānāma, saying:
"You must renounce the household life to carry out the King's command."
The son said:
"If I do not leave the home life, let that Āniruddha, who constantly enjoys pleasures within the palace, be the one to go forth.
His father said:
"Do not speak of that son's merit," [the father] said.
The son replied, "This is permitted by the affection of my parents; if he truly possesses merit, it may be tested."
The father asked,
"How should one test him?
The son replied:
"The usual practice is to send food with a full dish; now you may send it with an empty one.
If he possesses merit, food will appear naturally.
The father then sealed an empty dish before his son's face and ordered a palace lady to deliver it.
He cautioned him, saying:
"If he asks what food there is, simply reply that there are various kinds inside.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived this matter through his divine insight and thought: "In the past, Aniruddha once offered food to a Pratyekabuddha; how can I ensure that he has no food today?"
He then transformed various kinds of exquisite and delicious foods to fill those empty plates.
When the female servant arrived there, Aniruddha asked, "What is this?"
The palace lady felt resentment in her heart and, disregarding his admonition, replied:
"There is nothing.
Then Aniruddha thought to himself:
"How can my parents send an empty tray?
he thought, and upon opening the seal to look inside, he found it filled with extraordinary delicacies rarely seen by men; their fragrant aroma pervaded the entire garden.
Aṅgulimāla was also deeply perplexed and asked the woman,
"Was there originally food?
Or was it originally an empty plate?"
The girl said,
"An empty bowl," and then she proceeded to offer this food to her parents.
When the parents saw the food, they were also greatly astonished; they then showed this food to Mahānāma, saying:
"Look at this food; it was produced by his miraculous power."
"That Ārūḍha is beloved by all people; I said his great merit was not due to your power, and though you did not believe me at first, it is now proven.
Mahānāma said to his parents, "Since he possesses such great merit, let him go forth into the religious life; as for me, I have no merit and am not one who would go forth."
The parents then said to Aniruddha, "The King has now issued a decree; will you renounce the household life?
He replied:
"What benefit is there in leaving the household life?
What fault is there in remaining at home?
His parents asked.
"One who has left the household life should realize *nirvāṇa* and is worthy of receiving the foremost offerings among gods and humans.
Whether one remains at home or has left the household life, if they truly abandon desire, they likewise receive offerings from gods and humans;
however, if one remains at home while falsely claiming to have left the household life, they shall experience the retribution of the three evil realms."
He replied, "I have already understood the gains and losses of both the renunciant and the householder; now I wish to leave the home life to fulfill Your Majesty's command.
His parents said to him:
"Your words are most excellent.
At that time, Aniruddha had a contemporary named King Bimbisāra, with whom he shared a deep mutual understanding; he therefore went to him and made his declaration.

Upon reaching the gate of the Wise King's palace, he heard the sound of lute-playing; however, encountering a broken string such that the five notes were incomplete, Aniruddha, who was skilled at the lute, halted his progress and stood still, waiting for the instrument to be tuned before sending someone inside to announce his arrival.
The Wise King invited him to enter and said to Aniruddha,
"When did you arrive? He replied:
"The lute strings have just been broken and I have already reached the gate; I am waiting for them to be tuned before allowing you to enter and report your arrival.
The Worthy King praised this as excellent, took his hand, and invited him to sit, saying:
"Why have you come here now?"

He replied, "King Śuddhodana has issued a decree that members of the Śākya clan shall renounce the householder’s life; his intention is that his kinsmen may attend upon the Buddha. Because you have long admired the virtuous, he has come to inform you."

The Wise King said, "As soon as the imperial decree was issued, I immediately learned of it; since you have left the household life, I shall go with you as well, so you may stay the night at my residence."
Aṇiruddha stopped immediately upon these words.
The Wise King had a place prepared for him to lie down, but when night came, he could find not even a moment’s peace in sleep.
When they met again the following morning, the Wise King asked:
"Did you sleep peacefully?
He replied,
"I did not sleep peacefully."
He asked again,
"For what reason is it thus?
He replied:
"The bedding spread upon my bed is a garment touched by the sick; for this reason, I am unable to sleep in peace.
The Worthy King immediately summoned the attendant in charge and asked him about the circumstances from which it had been obtained.
He replied, "When Your Majesty was first born, it was prepared as a surplus; later, due to illness, it was already used.
The Wise King sighed and said:
"Excellent! A wondrous son has been born to this Śākya clan.
He further said:
"I have renounced the world; Devadatta shall succeed me to the throne.
He then ordered his attendants to call for Devadatta.
When he had arrived, he asked him:
"We have all gone forth into homelessness by imperial decree; we do not yet know what you intend to do now.
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself, "If I say that I will not go forth, it will cause Prince Sudatta to likewise refrain from going forth."
He then spoke these deceptive words:
"I, too, shall go forth into the homeless life.
At that time, King Śuddhodana quickly submitted a formal petition to King Śuddhodana, and the king issued an edict to announce it both within and without his realm:
"Now it is known that the noble Prince, Aniruddha, Devadatta, and five hundred members of the Śākya clan have all gone forth as monastics.
After this edict was issued, everyone both inside and outside the palace rejoiced; only Devadatta was personally distressed, thinking to himself:

"I originally devised a stratagem intending to cause the noble Prince to go forth, yet now he has perhaps broken his word and incurred the fault of lying, which will prevent me from attaining the throne in the future."
Thereupon, Vīradatta followed the crowd and went forth from the household life.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, wishing to let future generations know the nobility of his lineage, issued a proclamation to both the inner and outer courts: "Adorn all streets and thoroughfares, as well as the city moats, making them all exceptionally magnificent; spread pure earth and sprinkle scented water.
Furthermore, arrange banners, streamers, parasols, and canopies, and scatter flowers and burn incense to welcome the noble Prince and the five hundred Śākya clansmen as they pass through."

The parents of each of those Śākyas individually prepared viewing platforms by the side of the roads and at the gates of the city; they also summoned physiognomists to examine each of their sons, asking, "Which one among them is fit to renounce the world?"
"Who could not be so? The Wise King was the first to emerge, and the physiognomist praised him, saying:
'If he leaves the household life, he will surely realize the Noble Path.'"
When Aniruddha subsequently departed from the city, the physiognomist likewise declared:
"He shall attain sainthood before long.
When Devadatta went out to the city gate, the jeweled crown upon his head suddenly fell to the ground; having seen this, the physiognomist said: "This man of evil karma is certain to enter hell."
Furthermore, there was a man of unwholesome character named Sāgarāyus; as soon as he reached the threshold of the gate, the donkey let out a harsh cry, and the diviner knew it:
"This man has committed verbal karma by slandering the śrāvakas; when the fruit ripens in the future, he will certainly fall into the evil realms."
Upānanda came out next; as he was mounting his elephant at the entrance of the gate, a jeweled necklace fell to the ground, which he then dismounted himself to pick up with his own hands.
A physiognomist remarked, "This stingy person shall enter hell."

In this manner, each of the five hundred Śākyas emerged from their homes; the physiognomists all observed them and reported in detail to their parents everything concerning their good and evil fortunes.

Then the Śākya multitude departed from the city of Kapilavastu and traveled through the gardens and groves until they reached the place where the Buddha was staying. Each of them addressed the Buddha, requesting to leave the household life and become renunciants.
The World-Honored One reflected:
"Now, although these members of the Śākya clan have sought to leave the household life, some possess the aspiration and delight [in it], while others do not.
The Buddha then ordained them as bhikṣus by means of the four dharmas.

At that time, King Śuddhodana had an attendant named Upāli, who was skilled at shaving hair. The king immediately dispatched him to shave the heads of the Śākya assembly; however, upon arriving there, he refused to shave them, displaying a look of distress and weeping bitterly.
The Wise King asked,
"Why is this so? Upāli replied:
"I serve but one person and am not subject to the commands of the multitude; I would rather give up my life than shave my hair.
The Wise King admonished him, saying:
"Do not speak such words. You serve by the King's command and are not subject to the multitude's bidding; herein lies a great benefit, so please do not be distressed."
King Bimbisāra again employed a skillful means to address the Śākya assembly, saying:

"Now that you have gone forth, your jeweled crowns, exquisite robes, and ornaments shall henceforth serve no purpose; place them all together in one spot and give them to Upāli. Upon hearing this, he may perhaps rejoice at receiving them."
When the robes and crowns had all gathered, they formed a great heap; at that time, Upāli immediately shaved their hair.
Upon seeing that the Śākya assembly consisted entirely of youths who had renounced their wealth and status, he thought, "I now belong to a lowly clan; what is there for me to long for?"
"It would be fitting to cast off that affection and depart from afflictions, thereby escaping the calamity of the cycle of birth and death.
Thereupon, he rested his chin upon his hand and deliberated thus repeatedly.
The Venerable Śāriputra saw him and asked,
"Why do you rest your chin in your hand?
You seem to be unhappy."
He replied, "It is not that I am unhappy; it is that I have something on my mind.
He then related the facts of the matter in detail to Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said to him, "The World-Honored One’s deliverance knows no distinction between noble and humble; now is precisely the right time, and you should act with vigor.

Knowing in advance that Upāli’s faculties were fully matured, Śāriputra brought him before the Buddha. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid his respects and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Upāli now wishes to leave the household life within the True Dharma; we pray that the Buddha will look upon him with compassion.
The Buddha addressed Upāli, saying:
"You have attained the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

As soon as the Blessed One had finished speaking, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord and the saffron robe was donned upon his body. After seven days, his hair and beard grew back again; his majestic deportment was as dignified and orderly as that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing. He himself spoke this verse:
"I have now, before the Tathāgata, Sought to go forth from home into the True Dharma."
The Buddha said: "Having attained the holy life (brahmacarya), my beard and hair fell away of their own accord, and the saffron robe was likewise donned upon my body.
This very thing originated from roots of goodness; it has now reached maturity today, and thus I have become a bhikṣu."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:

"From now on, those who have left the household life shall observe the order of seniority according to the sequence of their years since ordination (*varṣāgra*), maintaining the distinction between the honorable and the humble; this practice shall continue until the future without fail."
Thereupon Upāli looked levelly at the Śākyas.
Then that King Bhadrika paid homage to the assembly in succession, but when he came before Upāli, he refused to prostrate himself and addressed the World-Honored One:
"Upāli is now my attendant; for me to prostrate myself before him would be improper."
The Buddha said, "Since you have left the household life, you should eliminate the notion of 'self. He is a senior elder; you ought to extend him your respectful salutation.
As soon as King Bhadrika prostrated, the earth shook in six ways.
Next, Devadatta also refused to pay homage and again came to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One who has left the household life should eliminate the notion of 'self. Since he is a senior elder, it is appropriate that you prostrate at his feet."
Thereupon, among the Śākyas, there was none who did not pay homage.
The bhikṣus each harbored a doubt in their minds:
"Now that Prince Bimbisāra has prostrated himself, the earth shook in six ways; what is the cause and condition for this?"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will untangle this web of doubts.
The Buddha said:
“In a past age, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king who ruled over it named Brahmadatta; his realm was prosperous and its people were happy.”
At that time, there was a courtesan in that city named Vārā, whose physical appearance was so exquisite and dignified that she was envied by all.
A man named Sunāramanavaka went to her place and expressed his mutual affection;
the woman then replied:
"He said, 'If you have five hundred gold coins, you may come to see me.

This man was so impoverished that he could not fulfill his request; however, by employing other expedient means, he became intimate with him. Eventually, they moved to live as neighbors, whereupon he would offer flowers and fruit. Later, during a seasonal festival when men and women performed music, they adorned themselves and wore flowers, each displaying their own beauty."
Then Vajra gave rise to this thought:
"If Sunāramanava were to come here, we could enjoy pleasure together.
In a short while, he arrived.
The woman was delighted and said, "Take these flowers and let us make music for you.

On this day, Sunāramanava had important business; his mind was extremely distressed, and he did not sleep throughout the night. When dawn was about to break, he fell into a deep sleep and did not wake; by the time people had gathered all the finest flowers, he obtained only śirīṣa flowers.
As he was about to give it to her, she was displeased and immediately spoke this verse:
"Your discipline is not diligent in action; you are indolent and heavy with sleep.
While the multitude gathers fine flowers, you have obtained only a śirīṣa flower."
Again he said to her:
"Seek other flowers.

At that time, it was the first month of autumn and the summer heat still lingered; yet she went out again to search for flowers, and by midday, as she gathered them and sang songs, she was not at all aware of the heat.

It happened that King Brahmadatta had entered the grass and gone to the forest to avoid the heat; suddenly he heard singing. He sent men to search for the source, and having found him, he summoned him and said to him:
"The sunlight shines down like fire burning the brain; how is it that you sing without feeling any distress at all?"
He then replied with a verse:
"Because my mind was deluded, the sun did not shine upon me;
because there were few matters to attend to, I did not perceive suffering."
At that time, the king reflected:
"This flower-gatherer can speak eloquently.
He then detained him to converse with him.
The king said, "I have come here from the heat seeking coolness; you may speak so as to dispel my burning distress.
Sunāramanava was naturally possessed of wisdom, and his words were to the king's liking; he then spoke of the benefits of military conquest, which struck a chord in the king's mind.
Upon hearing this, the king marveled at its rarity and immediately forgot his feverish distress. He addressed his ministers, saying:
"What national law exists whereby the highest reward is granted to one who risks their very body and life for the sake of a consecrated Kṣatriya king?"
The minister replied, "He may be granted to the Crown Prince.

Thereupon, he commanded the ministers to confer the investiture upon him to occupy that position. He notified both the inner and outer courts to prepare the ceremonies according to established protocol. The prince proceeded with due rites to the Spring Palace to assume the status of the designated heir. All his daily provisions were nothing but precious gems, and the bedding in his sleeping quarters was of extraordinary quality.
Sūnāramanavaka thought to himself:
"If the Crown Prince is such as this, it is clear that his status is supreme.
Thereupon, a covetous mind arose and he desired to plot for the Great Treasure; as soon as he conceived this thought, he immediately became aware of it himself.
"Am I such a person that I can speak of receiving a future retribution?
Because of this, he felt remorse and could not find peace in his bed; he then spread a coarse mat and lay upon the bare ground.
When morning dawned, the king immediately dispatched a messenger to observe his movements; seeing Sunāramanava lying upon the ground, he quickly returned and informed the king:
"This is not the crown prince, but merely a man of low status!"
The King asked,
"How do you know?
He reported the matter in full to the King.
The King said, "This is a man of great wisdom; he is no commoner.
He then ordered him to be summoned so that he might inquire into the reason for this.
The king asked,
"What is the meaning of not sleeping on a bed at night but lying upon the ground?
He replied:
"Your nobility is not ultimate; that is why I do not find it pleasing.
The King asked, "What is your intention?"
"I now wish to leave the household life.
The king spoke again, saying:
"I am not yet aware of this matter."
"What is meant by 'leaving home' (renunciation)? What are its merits?
He replied:

"Practicing with rigorous austerity in a secluded place, without a noble teacher and without seeking companions, one contemplates conditions, investigates principles, and realizes the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha."
The king immediately praised him as excellent and released him to enter the religious life.

Later, having realized the fruits of the Path, he came before the king and manifested miraculous signs in the midst of the sky. Upon witnessing this, the king conceived deep faith and devotion; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he offered his respectful salutation and spoke this verse:
"Excellent is the man of wisdom, Who cannot be bound by evil karma."
"Seeking the practice of tranquility, he realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Having spoken this verse,
he further said:
"If there are any *maṇavaka*s who leave the household life to seek the Way, I shall rejoice in them.

At that time, there was a close minister named Gaṅgāpāla; having heard this verse, he was filled with extraordinary joy, memorized it in his heart, and admonished himself against greed and attachment.
Thereafter, the king also exhorted himself, distancing himself from palace life and taking great pleasure in solitude.

Later, when Kṣāntivādin learned of the king’s joy, he requested to leave the household life. Having received the king’s permission, he took his leave and departed; he soon reached a deep mountain where he encountered an ascetic seer, and following him, he studied the Way with diligent application and exertion, eventually realizing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
He came directly before the king and manifested his supernatural transformations.
The king then asked, "Have you attained such merit as this? He replied:
"I have realized it.
The king, believing he had realized the state of an *ārya*, prostrated at his feet; as soon as his head touched the ground, the earth shook.
At that moment, the king’s mother perceived that this was not genuine and spoke a verse (*gāthā*) to Gaṅgapāla:
"If one fundamentally leaves the household life, Pays homage and serves the śramaṇas,
Practices silence and diligence, And undergoes ascetic practices, one becomes a pratyekabuddha."
"All sins shall be eternally extinguished, and all meritorious deeds shall arise;
thereafter, throughout all worlds, you shall extensively bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The King Brahmadatta of old was none other than the present-day King Bimbisāra; Gaṅgāpāla was Upāli.
Just as the earth trembled when he prostrated in the past, it is no different today when he pays his respects."
"O Bhikṣus!
These various matters of the past and the present, I shall now explain to you once more in detail; you who hear this should believe it with earnest attention."
When the bhikṣus heard this teaching, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness;
they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew. The Mahāsudarśana Sūtra, Scroll Thirteen.
